papers.authors: Morello A, Coletta L, Barchi M, Rizzo F, Zigiotto L, Sarubbo S, Garbossa D, Avesani P, Cofano F.
papers.abstract: Background and objectives Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) has the highest short-term mortality among stroke subtypes, and progress in treatment has been hindered by the limited accuracy of current prognostic tools. We investigated whether white matter functional disconnection severity, estimated using a normative lesion network mapping framework integrating direct electrical stimulation and resting-state functional MRI data from previously published independent Data sets, improves prediction of 6-month functional outcome measured with the modified Rankin Scale (mRS). Methods We analyzed 97 patients with spontaneous ICH. Ordinal logistic regression models were used to evaluate the association between domain-specific disconnection severity and 6-month mRS, and to compare traditional functional outcome in patients with primary intracerebral hemorrhage and ICH scores with connectivity-enriched models incorporating disconnection measures. Results White matter functional disconnectivity was significantly associated with 6-month functional outcome (mRS; P < .001; Nagelkerke's R2 = 0.507). Integrating disconnection severity into the functional outcome in patients with primary intracerebral hemorrhage and ICH scores improved predictive performance in both cases (Nagelkerke's R2 = 0.615 vs 0.389 and 0.651 vs 0.434, respectively), with the connectivity-enriched ICH score achieving the strongest overall fit across all models tested. Exploratory analyses showed associations between domain-specific disconnection severity, residual functional deficits, and early mortality. Conclusion Assessment of white matter functional disconnection severity seems to be a promising approach for predicting long-term disability after ICH, although prospective validation in larger multicenter cohorts is required before clinical implementation. The findings suggest that different brain networks exhibit variable vulnerability to injury and differential potential for functional recovery.
keywords: Functional Outcome In Patients With Primary Intracerebral Hemorrhage

papers.title: Midlife and Late-Life Alzheimer Disease Blood Biomarkers and 11-Year Cognitive Decline.
papers.authors: Smith JR, Pike JR, Lu Y, Walker KA, Sullivan KJ, Windham BG, Thyagarajan B, Mielke MM, Lutsey PL, Hughes TM, Knopman DS, Gottesman RF, Mosley TH, Coresh J, Deal JA, Sharrett AR, Palta P.
papers.abstract: Background and objectives Plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer disease (AD) neuropathology (amyloid-β42 to amyloid β40 [Aβ42/40] ratio, phosphorylated tau at threonine [p-tau181]), neurodegeneration (neurofilament light [NfL]), and neuroinflammation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) in late-life are associated with cognitive decline. Whether these biomarkers in midlife are predictive of subsequent cognitive decline, and whether they are associated with different cognitive domains, is uncertain. In this study, we investigated associations of midlife and late-life plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP with late-life change in domain-specific (memory, language, and executive function) and global cognitive function. Methods We performed a prospective cohort analysis of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study (ARIC-NCS). Outcome follow-up was from ARIC visit 5 (2011-2013) to visit 9 (2021-2022). We included all individuals from ARIC field centers (Jackson, Mississippi; Forsyth County, North Carolina; Washington County, Maryland; and Minneapolis suburbs, Minnesota) with biomarkers measured from stored specimens in midlife (visit 3, 1993-1995, mean age 59.0 years) and late-life (visit 5, 2011-2013, mean age 76.8 years). Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were measured with the Quanterix Simoa platform and standardized to visit 3 to facilitate cross-biomarker comparisons of their rate of change from midlife to late-life. We estimated change in memory, language, executive function, and global cognition factor scores from visit 5 to visit 9 with linear mixed-effect models. Results In 1,515 included participants, 60.7% (n = 920) were female and 25.5% (n = 387) were Black. Each SD increase in p-tau181 in midlife was significantly associated with faster late-life memory decline (β = -0.030 [95% CI -0.059 to -0.001] SD. Midlife Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP were not associated with subsequent decline in any cognitive domain. In late-life, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were significantly associated with faster decline in different cognitive domains, with the strongest associations seen with memory (β = -0.091 [95% CI -0.123 to -0.058] SD; β = -0.064 [95% CI -0.106 to -0.023] SD; and β = -0.048 [95% CI -0.082 to -0.013] SD, respectively). Discussion Midlife p-tau181 was associated with faster 11-year memory decline beginning 20 years later in the ARIC cohort, which underscores a potentially long prodromal phase of cognitive decline that could precede dementia onset. In late-life, biomarkers for AD, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation were associated with faster decline across different cognitive domains, but associations remained strongest for p-tau181 and memory.

papers.title: A Primer on COL4A1/COL4A2-Related Cerebral Small Vessel Disease for Neurologists.
papers.authors: Alten B, Ullman NL, Porcari G, Sloane KL, Cristancho AG, Rothstein A.
papers.abstract: COL4A1 and COL4A2 encode type IV collagen, a principal structural component of basement membranes, and pathogenic variants in these genes cause a multisystem small vessel vasculopathy with prominent cerebrovascular involvement. Despite increasing recognition with the expansion of genetic testing, COL4A1/2 -related cerebral small vessel disease remains underrecognized in clinical practice, in part due to its striking phenotypic heterogeneity. Presentations span a broad clinical spectrum-from asymptomatic individuals or incidental imaging findings to recurrent ischemic events, intracerebral hemorrhage, and catastrophic perinatal brain injury-and may occur across the lifespan. In this narrative review, we provide a clinically oriented framework for recognizing and managing COL4A1/2 -related cerebral small vessel disease. We integrate underlying molecular mechanisms of type IV collagen dysfunction with vascular pathophysiology, highlighting how impaired basement membrane integrity leads to a dual hemorrhagic-ischemic phenotype. We describe characteristic neuroimaging patterns, including microhemorrhages, white matter hyperintensities, lacunes, and dilated perivascular spaces, and emphasize their anatomic distribution and clinical relevance. Given the systemic nature of the disorder, we also review key extracerebral manifestations-including ocular, renal, and musculoskeletal features-that serve as important diagnostic "red flags." We outline practical considerations for clinical care, including indications for genetic testing, initial diagnostic evaluation, and longitudinal management strategies tailored to neurologists. Particular emphasis is placed on individualized decision-making around antithrombotic therapy, hemorrhage risk mitigation, and surveillance for complications such as intracranial aneurysms. Illustrative multigenerational cases are incorporated to demonstrate genotype-phenotype correlation, incomplete penetrance, and common diagnostic pitfalls. By providing a mechanism-informed and clinically actionable synthesis, this review aims to improve recognition, reduce misdiagnosis, and guide management of COL4A1/2 -related cerebral small vessel disease.

papers.title: Seizures Secondary to Aconitum Plant Poisoning: a case report.
papers.authors: Zhao Z, Zhang J, Du J, Liu L, Rao G, Zhou M.
papers.abstract: Background Aconitum plant poisoning typically manifests as isolated early cardiotoxicity or late neurotoxicity. However, the dynamic temporal evolution from arrhythmia-driven cardiogenic syncope to true epileptic seizures mediated by direct central nervous system injury remains rarely documented and poorly characterized. Case presentation We report a 53-year-old Han Chinese male who presented with ventricular tachycardia rapidly degenerating into ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest following ingestion of homemade Aconitum kusnezoffii (caowu)-infused liquor. Initial convulsions were tightly coupled with malignant arrhythmias, consistent with cardiogenic syncope. After successful resuscitation, hemoperfusion, and restoration of stable sinus rhythm, the patient developed breakthrough generalized tonic-clonic seizures on hospital days 4-6. Electroencephalography performed during sedation withdrawal revealed bilateral occipital spike-and-slow and sharp-and-slow waves with focal epileptiform discharges, confirming direct central nervous system neurotoxicity rather than recurrent cardiac ischemia. A mechanism-based, staged treatment strategy was employed: early advanced cardiac life support and hemoperfusion targeted cardiotoxicity, while sodium valproate and acetylglutamine were administered for antiepileptic prophylaxis and neuroprotection. The patient was discharged on day 13; antiepileptic therapy was successfully tapered and discontinued at 3 months without seizure recurrence, with normalization of electroencephalography and electrocardiography. Conclusions This case provides the first systematic documentation, validated by electroencephalography, of the transition from cardiogenic convulsions to true epileptic seizures in Aconitum alkaloid poisoning. The findings highlight the critical role of pharmacokinetic-driven central nervous system retention in delayed seizure onset and underscore the necessity of prolonged neurological monitoring, early electroencephalography evaluation for late-onset convulsions, and sustained antiepileptic prophylaxis to reduce mortality and long-term neurological sequelae. Key clinical message Aconitum plant poisoning may manifest as early cardiogenic syncope and convulsions secondary to malignant arrhythmias, progressing in the late stage to genuine seizures caused by central nervous system (CNS) injury. Effective management requires a staged treatment strategy targeting both cardiotoxicity and neurotoxicity, with a focus on stabilizing cardiac rhythm and providing neuroprotection as needed.

papers.title: Amygdala neurofeedback as an adjunct to residential dialectical behavior therapy for borderline personality disorder: a pilot randomized controlled trial.
papers.authors: Hofmanová M, Santangelo PS, Kleindienst N, Schmahl C, Paret C.
papers.abstract: Background Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterized by affective instability and amygdala hyperreactivity. Although dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) reduces symptoms and amygdala-related abnormalities, many patients show only partial remission. Real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) amygdala neurofeedback (amy-NF) directly targets hyperactive limbic responses and has shown promise in uncontrolled trials. We examined whether amy-NF adds benefit to inpatient DBT. Methods Thirty-six mid-therapy people with BPD and clinically significant residual symptoms (BSL-23 > 1.5) were randomized to DBT plus amy-NF (n = 23) or DBT alone, termed treatment as usual (TAU = 13). Post-treatment assessments were completed by 15/9 (amy-NF/TAU), with 15/8 and 12/7 completing the 3- and 6-month follow-ups. Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) of daily-life affective instability served as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included self-reports, amygdala responses during two fMRI tasks, and resting-state fMRI. Assessments occurred at pre-, post-, 3-, and 6-month follow-up. Results Participants successfully downregulated amygdala activity during neurofeedback. EMA showed improvements in negative affect, inner tension, and affective instability over time, without consistent superiority of amy-NF. Self-reports likewise showed no additional benefit of amy-NF, and BSL-23 scores increased after discharge in both groups. Amy-NF was associated with transient pre-post reductions in amygdala activity during both viewing and regulation in the emotion regulation task, and with more stable amygdala reactivity over time than TAU in the faces task. Resting-state analyses showed transient pre-post increases in amygdala connectivity with precuneus and dorsomedial frontal regions in amy-NF. Conclusions Amygdala neurofeedback is feasible and reduced amygdala activity in BPD, but did not yield additional clinical benefit when delivered alongside intensive residential DBT, although the small sample may have limited power to detect such effects. Trial registration The study protocol was preregistered 2020/03/26 on ClinicalTrials.gov and received the ID NCT04333888.

papers.title: Multiomics Profiling Supports Cathepsin B as a Protective Factor in White Matter Hyperintensities and Cognition.
papers.authors: Rivier CA, Diaz-Perez S, Bories G, Huo S, Clocchiatti-Tuozzo S, de Havenon A, Debette S, Sheth KN, Sansing LH, Falcone GJ.
papers.abstract: Background White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are a common brain magnetic resonance imaging marker of cerebral small vessel disease and a major risk factor for stroke and dementia, yet the molecular mechanisms governing lesion formation remain incompletely understood. We sought to identify circulating proteins that lie upstream of WMH and influence related clinical manifestations. Methods We conducted a 4-stage proteogenomic study. Stage 1 tested a WMH polygenic risk score against 2923 plasma proteins in 52 560 UK Biobank participants (mean age, 56.8 years, 53.9% female, 94.0% White), and candidate proteins against WMH volume in the neuroimaging subset (n=5443; mean age 54.2 years, 53.5% female). Stage 2 applied bidirectional Mendelian randomization, colocalization, and local genetic correlation using cis protein quantitative trait locus and cis expression quantitative trait locus instruments from plasma, vascular, and brain tissue. Stage 3 analyzed single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 8 postmortem periventricular white matter samples (4 WMH lesions, 4 controls; mean age, 81 years; 50% female). Stage 4 tested circulating and genetically predicted protein levels against general cognitive ability. Results Stages 1 and 2 converged on CTSB (cathepsin B) and ECHDC3 (enoyl-coenzyme A hydratase domain-containing 3). Higher plasma CTSB was associated with lower WMH volume (β=-0.09 [95% CI, -0.13 to -0.05]; n=5260), and Mendelian randomization estimates were directionally consistent across all 5 instrument sets (plasma protein quantitative trait locus β=-0.052 [95% CI, -0.064 to -0.040]), with concordant effects on white matter microstructure, perivascular spaces, and lacunar stroke. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing showed CTSB downregulation within lesions, predominantly in astrocytes (log2 fold change=-1.70) and oligodendrocytes (log2 fold change=-0.48; both false discovery rate P <1×10-20 ). Higher plasma CTSB (β=0.061 [95% CI, 0.010-0.112]; n=5193) and a cis protein quantitative trait locus polygenic score (β=0.031 [95% CI, 0.009-0.054]; n=8884) predicted better cognitive performance. ECHDC3 showed no consistent association beyond stage 1. Conclusions Multimodal proteogenomic evidence nominates CTSB as a lesion-suppressed protein associated with lower WMH burden and better cognition, and a candidate therapeutic target for cerebral small vessel disease.

papers.title: Extended field-of-view two-photon imaging in the deep brain of freely behaving mice using lightweight microfabricated corrective optics.
papers.authors: Nardin C, Sattin A, Curreli S, Letti G, Maddalena L, Nacci L, Fellin T.
papers.abstract: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions. Miniaturized two-photon microscopes (MINI2Ps) enable deep brain imaging in freely moving animals when coupled with gradient index (GRIN)-based microendoscopes. However, intrinsic optical aberrations in GRIN-based microendoscopes degrade spatial resolution and limit the effective field-of-view (FOV). Here, we address these limitations using lightweight microfabricated optics to correct GRIN aberrations during deep brain MINI2P imaging. The aberration corrected system demonstrated improved and more homogeneous axial resolution across the FOV, resulting in more than fourfold increase in effective FOV. We applied the corrected system to the ventral posteromedial thalamus in freely moving mice and performed optical mapping of head direction (HD) tuned cells. These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus. Combining the MINI2P with aberration corrected GRIN-based microendoscopes is a powerful approach for large-scale and high-resolution functional imaging of deep brain circuits during naturalistic behavior.

papers.title: Multiscale neural signatures of long-lag repetition learning: a simultaneous fNIRS-EEG study.
papers.authors: Ren J, Noah A, Zhang X, Gracco V, Joanisse M, Bajracharya A, Rueckl JG, Buchweitz A, Koirala N, Hirsch J, Pugh K.
papers.abstract: Significance Repetition-based learning supports word recognition and reading fluency, yet its neural mechanisms remain poorly understood, particularly where deficits in consolidating repeated linguistic input may underlie reading and language difficulties. Establishing reliable neural markers of repetition-based learning is a critical first step toward characterizing the phenotypes of these difficulties in children. Aim We developed a whole-brain simultaneous functional near-infrared spectroscopy-electroencephalography (fNIRS-EEG) approach to capture fast temporal electrophysiological and spatially accurate hemodynamic signals during long-lag repetition learning. Approach Thirty participants performed a semantic judgment task with words repeated across four runs with intervening items, modeling repetition demands central to reading instruction. A multimodal decoding framework integrating electrophysiological, hemodynamic, and cross-modal fNIRS-EEG correlation features was used to classify repetition-based learning. Results Repeated words showed response time reductions. EEG captured a frontal N400-range repetition-related negativity and attenuation of alpha-beta suppression, reflecting changes in recognition-related and post-recognition processing. fNIRS revealed left inferior frontal and superior temporal efficiency increases alongside right supramarginal activation, suggesting integrative processing. Multimodal classifiers outperformed unimodal classifiers, indicating that each modality captured complementary aspects of learning. Conclusions Combining fNIRS and EEG with multimodal machine learning provides a richer characterization of repetition-based learning than either modality alone, establishing a framework for phenotyping language learning capacity and identifying neural markers of reading difficulties in pediatric populations.

papers.title: Altered glymphatic system measures and functional network connectivity in autism spectrum disorder: A longitudinal study examining associations with prognosis.
papers.authors: Zhang M, Luo T, Zhao S, Li L, Jiang Y, Duan X, Situ M, Huang Y.
papers.abstract: Aim Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by social deficits and repetitive behaviors, yet prognostic biomarkers remain elusive. This study investigated the interplay between glymphatic function and functional network connectivity (FNC) in ASD and their longitudinal associations with clinical outcomes. Method This combined cross-sectional and two-year prospective longitudinal study included 50 ASD children and 50 controls. Glymphatic function was assessed using the along the perivascular space (ALPS) index and global blood-oxygen-level-dependent to cerebrospinal fluid (gBOLD-CSF) coupling, alongside FNC analysis. Results Cross-sectionally, ASD participants showed significantly reduced ALPS index, gBOLD-CSF coupling, and widespread FNC reductions. Longitudinally, among the 40 ASD participants who completed follow-up, glymphatic function increased over time. Greater increases in ALPS were correlated with greater reductions in ADOS-CSS. In the symptom-improved subgroup, four FNC connections (including DMN-DAN) increased over time. In contrast, no consistent pattern was found in the non-improved group. Baseline inter-network connectivity measures were associated with ADOS-CSS reduction in univariate analyses, but the multivariate model was not significant. Mediation analysis showed an indirect association between baseline gBOLD-CSF coupling and long-term ADOS-CSS reduction via DMN-DAN FNC reduction (indirect effect = -0.22, 95% CI [-0.42, -0.07]). Conclusion These findings indicate that glymphatic function and FNC are altered cross-sectionally and improve longitudinally in parallel with symptom changes in ASD and suggest that baseline gBOLD-CSF coupling is indirectly associated with long-term clinical improvement through DMN-DAN connectivity. Together, these results highlight the potential of glymphatic and functional connectivity measures as prognostic imaging markers in ASD.

papers.title: Effects of postmortem interval on myelin integrity in rhesus macaque brain tissue.
papers.authors: Novoseltseva A, Robinson R, Niziolek P, Jang A, Xie T, Tiwari A, Abdelhakeem A, Nicks R, Lucas Y, Yang Q, Mortazavi F, Boas D, Wang H, Moore TL, Rosene DL, Bigio IJ.
papers.abstract: When conducting microscopy of human brain sections, the postmortem interval (PMI) introduces myelin-related artifacts that can confound neuropathological interpretation, yet the extent and detectability of these changes remain poorly characterized. This study examined the impact of controlled PMI on myelin integrity in rhesus macaque brain tissue using advanced optical imaging approaches. Brains from five aged rhesus macaques (20.5-28.5 years) were maintained at 4°C and analyzed at 0, 24, and 72 h postmortem. Myelin integrity in white and gray matter was assessed using quantitative birefringence microscopy to measure relative retardance and polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography to quantify scattering coefficients, retardance, and volumetric features. Increasing PMI was associated with progressive myelin degradation, reflected by significant reductions in relative optical retardance in white matter (p < 0.01) and gray matter (p < 0.001), alongside increased scattering coefficients in both regions (p < 0.001). Morphological analyses revealed a marked increase in myelin defects per mm2 with longer PMI (p < 0.001), characterized by swellings, vesicles, and structural discontinuities. These findings demonstrate that PMI causes significant detectable myelin changes, which can be quantified using optical imaging techniques, providing critical implications for interpreting postmortem neuropathological studies (especially with human brain tissues) and establishing a need for standardized PMI considerations in research protocols to ensure accurate pathological assessment in neurological disease investigations.

papers.title: Individualized Theta Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation Modulates Mnemonic Discrimination and ERP Responses to Positive Information in Individuals With Elevated Depressive Symptoms.
papers.authors: Huang X, Zhou M, Wang C, Huang Y, Wang W, Shao J, Mao J, Li J, Zhang L, Ye R, Zhu C, Tian Y, He K, Yu F, Wang K.
papers.abstract: Individuals with elevated depressive symptoms often show impairments in positive memory processing. This randomized, double-blind study investigated whether individualized theta-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) using an OFC-oriented montage modulates mnemonic discrimination and ERP responses to positive information. Sixty-one individuals with elevated depressive symptoms received either real or sham stimulation before completing an emotional mnemonic discrimination task. Behavioral results showed that lure discrimination increased following real stimulation but not sham stimulation. EEG results showed that real stimulation modulated ERP responses during positive memory encoding and retrieval, as reflected by increased late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes during encoding and altered early retrieval-related ERP amplitudes. These findings suggest that individualized theta-tACS may influence both mnemonic discrimination performance and neural responses to positive information.

papers.title: A multi-atlas ensemble learning framework for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis.
papers.authors: Liang S, Zhang Z, Du W, Gu F.
papers.abstract: Objective. Clinical autism spectrum disorder (ASD) relies on subjective scales and neuroimaging, with traditional approaches suffering from high subjectivity and insufficient feature extraction, increasing misdiagnoses risk.Approach. To improve the diagnostic accuracy, we propose a multimodal ASD prediction network (APN) that integrates resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging with non-imaging data. Algorithmically, we first introduce a novel cumulative distribution divergence score (CDDS) feature selection method based on the multi-atlas functional connectivity (FC), which quantifies statistical distributional differences between positive and negative samples, effectively addressing the limitations of the traditionalF -score in overlapping or weakly discriminative features. Building upon this, we adapt existing deep learning (DL) paradigms to construct a deep neural architecture (variational autoencoder-denoising autoencoder (VAEA)), combining a variational autoencoder (VAE), a denoising autoencoder, and a multilayer perceptron. The combination of these modules is non-trivial: the novel CDDS first purifies the high-dimensional feature space, enabling the VAEA to learn robust latent probabilistic representations via unsupervised pre-training without suffering from the curse of dimensionality. This is followed by the supervised fine-tuning to optimize parameters. We further incorporate demographic factors including age, full-scale intelligence quotient, and gender via a late-fusion strategy to prevent them from being overshadowed by imaging features, thereby enhancing the discriminability. FC features from three atlases including AAL, CC400, and Dosenbach160 are weighted and integrated to achieve the effective multi-source fusion.Main results. We conduct 10-fold cross-validations on the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) dataset, and the proposed APN achieves 81.63% accuracy, 81.89% sensitivity and 81.46% specificity, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Interpretability analysis identifies hippocampus, amygdala, and cingulate gyrus as strongly ASD-associated regions, offering neural mechanistic insights.Significance. This study provides an efficient, objective, and interpretable multimodal DL framework for ASD assisted diagnosis, with substantial clinical application and neuroscience value.

papers.title: Involuntary facial muscle activity during imagined vocalisation contaminates EEG and enables emotion decoding.
papers.authors: Tang Y, Corballis PM, Hallum LE.
papers.abstract: Objective. Decoding imagined speech from electroencephalography (EEG) recordings is potentially useful for brain-computer interfaces. Previous studies have focused on decoding semantic information from EEG, leaving the decoding of emotion - an important component of human communication - largely unexplored.Approach. Here, we report two experiments involving participants tasked with overt (n = 14) or imagined (n = 21) emotional vocalisation in five different categories: anger, happiness, neutral, sadness, and pleasure. Throughout, we recorded 64-channel EEG; we computed time-frequency features and used a logistic-regression classifier to evaluate emotion decoding accuracy. In five participants, we also recorded facial surface electromyography (sEMG) during imagined vocalisation, and studied the contamination of EEG by sEMG.Main results. Our results show that emotion can be decoded from single-trial EEG recordings of both overt (78.1%, chance = 20%) and imagined vocalisation (36.4%). The high-gamma band (50 to 100 Hz) and lateral EEG channels (T7, T8, and proximal) were important for decoding. sEMG analysis indicated that involuntary facial muscle activity contributed to these spectral and spatial patterns during imagined vocalisation. We identified a prominent muscle-induced pattern over lateral EEG channels - the railroad cross-tie pattern - showing greater activation during imagined happy vocalisations. We conclude that involuntary facial muscle activity is associated with certain emotion categories (i.e. happiness) and contributes to the decoding of emotion from single-trial EEG recordings.Significance. This study provides converging EEG and sEMG evidence demonstrating that involuntary facial muscle activity occurs during imagined vocalisation and is modulated by emotion, producing emotion-specific EEG contamination patterns. Although we focused on imagined vocalisations, the EMG patterns we observed closely resembled EEG patterns commonly reported in emotion decoding studies, raising concerns about involuntary facial muscle activity in such work.

papers.title: Impact of depth-of-interaction and spatially-variant point-spread-function model on the performance of ultra-high resolution brain PET.
papers.authors: Zeng T, Najmaoui Y, Zhang J, Volpi T, Fontaine K, Chemli Y, Hu Y, Gallezot JD, Sun C, Lu Y, El Fakhri G, Carson RE, Marin T.
papers.abstract: Objective. To implement a spatially-variant point spread function (VarPSF) model for the NeuroEXPLORER (NX) brain positron emission tomography (PET) scanner in the open-source Yale Reconstruction Toolkit for PET, and investigate the interplay between depth-of-interaction (DOI) resolution and resolution modeling.Approach. PSF parameters were estimated from simulated and physically measured point sources. Three primary DOI configurations were evaluated: eight-layer DOI (8DOI), two-layer DOI (2DOI), and no DOI (noDOI), with an additional 4DOI comparison in the off-center simulated Derenzo study. Reconstructions using VarPSF, a spatially-invariant PSF measured at the field-of-view center (SinglePSF), and no PSF modeling (noPSF) were assessed using simulated Derenzo and brain phantoms, a physical Derenzo phantom, and one non-human primate (NHP) scan.Main results. In simulated and physical Derenzo studies, VarPSF yielded higher peak-to-valley ratios than SinglePSF and noPSF at the final evaluated iterations, with pronounced gains at large radial offsets. In the simulated brain phantom, VarPSF reduced the estimated transverse blur by 0.3 mm relative to SinglePSF and 0.5 mm relative to noPSF in 2DOI, and by 0.6 mm and 0.8 mm, respectively, in noDOI. In the NHP study, VarPSF improved contrast and structural delineation with reduced DOI encoding at approximately matched white-matter coefficient of variation, while its incremental benefit over SinglePSF was small with 8DOI at clinically relevant iteration settings.Significance. Spatially-variant PSF modeling can partially compensate for limited DOI information. The findings motivate combining modest DOI capability with accurate resolution modeling, while further validation is required for redesigned detectors and fully corrected acquisitions. The open-source implementation enables controlled investigation of the complementary roles of DOI encoding and resolution modeling.

papers.title: Video EEG in pediatric epilepsy: Diagnostic significance and association between frequency band power and cognitive impairment severity.
papers.authors: Li B, Wu F.
papers.abstract: Objective This study aimed to compare video electroencephalogram (VEEG) and routine electroencephalogram (EEG) in childhood epilepsy diagnosis and analyze the correlation between EEG frequency band power and cognitive impairment severity. Methods One hundred and sixty children suspected of having epilepsy underwent routine EEG and VEEG examinations. Diagnostic efficacy and detection rates were compared. Cognitive function was evaluated in 80 children diagnosed with epilepsy, who were allocated into normal intelligence (35 cases), borderline intelligence (25 cases), and intelligence-impaired (20 cases) groups. Clinical data, EEG parameters, and their correlation with cognitive impairment were analyzed. Results VEEG showed higher sensitivity, accuracy, and negative predictive value, and detection rates of epileptiform discharges, synchronous clinical seizures, and clinical symptoms than routine EEG (p < 0.05). Clinical characteristics and EEG parameters differed among the three groups (p < 0.05). The relative power of δ and θ bands and the awake and sleep discharge indices were positively correlated with cognitive impairment severity (r = 0.300, 0.643, 0.622, and 0.456), whereas α and β band power were negatively correlated (r = -0.515 and -0.410) (all p < 0.001). Conclusion VEEG demonstrated higher diagnostic performance than routine EEG, and EEG frequency band power was correlated with cognitive impairment severity.

papers.title: Toward early dyslexia screening through handwriting: A trustworthy XAI-enhanced deep learning framework.
papers.authors: Matthias SL, Lau J, Tang YM, Geda MW.
papers.abstract: Dyslexia, a prevalent learning disorder, significantly impairs children's ability to process written language, often leading to challenges such as letter reversals, inconsistent spacing, and scrambled writing sequences. Early detection is critical for timely intervention, yet traditional diagnostic methods such as behavioral assessments and neuroimaging-are either time-consuming, subjective, or prohibitively expensive. Recent advances in deep learning offer promising alternatives, particularly through handwriting analysis, which is non-invasive and scalable. However, the "black-box" nature of many deep learning models raises concerns about interpretability, a key requirement for clinical and educational adoption. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework combining a custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and an Attention mechanism to detect dyslexia from handwriting samples. The study uses handwriting samples from adolescents aged 12-15 with an established dyslexia diagnosis and a control group. It therefore provides a proof-of-concept for handwriting-based classification and a foundation for early screening, rather than a validated early screening tool. The CNN extracts spatial features, while GRUs model temporal patterns in writing sequences. The Attention mechanism highlights the most discriminative regions for screening. To enhance transparency, Explainable AI (XAI) techniques such as Grad-CAM, LIME, and feature scatter plots are added to provide visual explanations of the model's decisions. Evaluated on a dataset of 3170 handwriting images from dyslexic and non-dyslexic students, the model achieved 99.5% accuracy using leave-one-out cross validation, outperforming pre-trained models like ResNet-50. Ablation studies confirmed the CNN's pivotal role while GRUs and Attention provided complementary improvements. These findings demonstrate technical feasibility; however, the model has not yet been evaluated in younger, undiagnosed children, and conclusions about early screening utility should therefore be interpreted with caution. XAI visualizations, such as Grad-CAM and LIME, offer interpretable saliency maps, and the results show that the predictions made by the model depend on the regions where known dyslexic characteristics, such as irregularities in letter curvature, spacing, and alignment, often occur.

papers.title: Decoding Spatial Attention in the Cocktail Party Problem Using Whole-head High-Density fNIRS.
papers.authors: Duwadi S, Rogers D, Boyd AD, Carlton LB, Zhang Y, Gaona AK, Pathiyaparambath AD, Chaudhury R, Magee G, Zimmermann BB, O'Brien WJ, von Lühmann A, Boas DA, Yücel MA, Sen K.
papers.abstract: Spatial attention is critical for solving the cocktail party problem, a longstanding problem in neuroscience and artificial speech recognition. The ability to decode where humans are attending in a cocktail party like scene would empower applications in brain computer interfaces and assistive devices such as hearing aids. Here we demonstrate that, in an overt attention task, the attended spatial location can be decoded robustly from single trial hemodynamic responses, using a whole head high density fNIRS system. We also identify critical brain regions that make the highest contribution to decoding accuracy. Specifically, we find that decoding based on a small fraction of channels located within the left and right inferior parietal lobule (IPL) achieves maximal decoding accuracy comparable to all channels. Decoding fell close to chance in a covert auditory condition in which participants held central fixation while attending to the same talkers, indicating that auditory attention alone without orientation is not sufficient for decoding. Finally, control experiments suggest that overt-condition decoding is influenced by sustained eye position/gaze direction, not eye movement. These results support the development of fNIRS-integrated BCIs and assistive devices controlled by overt spatial attention.
papers.summary_zh: 该研究关注能否用全头高密度fNIRS从单试次血流动力学反应中解码“鸡尾酒会”场景下受试者所注意的空间位置。研究采用外显注意任务，并设置要求保持中央注视的隐蔽听觉条件及控制实验。结果显示外显条件下解码稳健，仅用左右顶下小叶（IPL）内少量通道即可达到与全部通道相当的准确率；隐蔽条件下解码接近随机水平，提示缺乏朝向的纯听觉注意不足以支持解码。控制实验提示外显条件解码受持续眼位/注视方向而非眼动影响，作者据此认为结果支持开发由外显空间注意控制的fNIRS脑机接口与助听器等辅助设备。

papers.title: White matter-guided transtemporal corridors: An anatomical blueprint for safe access through the temporal lobe.
papers.authors: Bilgin B, Yuncu ME, Karadag A, Bozkurt B, Tanriover N.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
papers.abstract: Background Transtemporal approaches provide access to deep temporal and intraventricular lesions but may traverse critical white matter pathways, making tract-aware planning important for minimizing postoperative deficits. Therefore, the microsurgical anatomy of commonly used transtemporal corridors, the fibers encountered along each approach, and their tract-specific risk profiles should be defined to guide corridor selection. Methods Three formalin-fixed cadaveric brain specimens (six hemispheres) were dissected, proceeding stepwise from the cortical surface to the ventricular system. Results Posterior superior temporal gyrus approaches lay close to the arcuate fasciculus (AF) and superior longitudinal fasciculus, with the middle longitudinal fasciculus encountered at a deeper plane; trajectories toward the roof of the temporal horn or atrium approached the optic radiation (OR) and Meyer's loop. Middle temporal gyrus and inferior temporal sulcus corridors lay adjacent to the OR-particularly Meyer's loop-and the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) within the sagittal stratum. Inferior temporal gyrus approaches remained distant from the AF and uncinate fasciculus (UF), with the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF) most closely related to the trajectory, while the OR and IFOF remained superior and medial. The transsylvian corridor traversed the temporal stem near the UF and central IFOF, with superior extension toward the ventricular roof placing Meyer's loop and the OR at risk. Conclusion Safer transtemporal surgery depends on the relationship between the surgical corridor and associated fibers, rather than the cortical entry point alone. These findings provide an anatomical framework for white matter-guided planning and tract-sparing corridor selection.

papers.title: An efficient convolutional neural network model for classifying positive affective states from EEG data considering sleep condition.
papers.authors: Gazan MK, Moghaddamnia S, Habiboglu MG.
papers.abstract: Background The recognition of affective states from EEG recordings considering the sleep condition can be an important supporting tool in therapy and in the treatment of psychological or psychiatric disorders. New method Since sleep deprivation changes EEG characteristics, a two-stage framework is developed for affective state classification. First, a classification between "Normal Sleep" (NS) and "Sleep-Deprived" (SD) is conducted using resting-state EEG data. The data are then fed into one of two newly proposed, lightweight Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to recognize four affective states. Results In the first stage, CNN-BiLSTM achieves 95.96% accuracy under window-level splitting and 70.46% under subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation, while in the second stage the proposed models achieve 93.40% (NS) and 90.95% (SD) under window-level splitting, and 38.98% (NS) and 38.97% (SD) under cross-validation. The lower subject-independent accuracies reflect the class imbalance and the clustering of scores near the class boundaries, which make cross-subject four-class generalization challenging. Comparison with existing methods As existing studies mostly classify momentary emotions without addressing sleep conditions, direct comparison with prior work is difficult; we therefore benchmarked our framework against several established baseline models, including SqueezeNet, EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, Support Vector Machine, and Random Forest. Conclusions This study suggests that considering physiological states can improve multi-class classification of affective states from time-varying neurophysiological signals such as EEG. The framework performs strongly under window-level evaluation, whereas its performance under the stricter subject-independent setting is more limited and should be interpreted accordingly. It can nonetheless contribute to more comprehensive research in affective neuroscience.

papers.title: Basic-level category processing advantage in fear generalization and its modulation by threat-conditioned stimulus diversity: Behavioral and event-related potential evidence.
papers.authors: Zhang P, Li J, Wu S, Li H, Weng Y, Zheng X.
papers.abstract: Category-based fear generalization refers to the extension of acquired fear responses to novel stimuli sharing categorical cues with a threat stimulus. Categories are organized into superordinate, basic-level, and subordinate levels, which differ in cognitive processing advantages; however, whether this categorical advantage influences fear generalization remains unclear. Experiment 1 used a discriminative fear conditioning paradigm, employing subordinate exemplars of birds and measuring tools as the threat-conditioned stimulus (CS+) and the safety-conditioned stimulus (CS-), respectively. During the generalization test, we included generalization stimuli sharing either the same basic-level category (GSBasic ) or the same superordinate category (but different basic-level category) as the CS+. Fear generalization was assessed via shock expectancy ratings and skin conductance responses. Experiment 2 manipulated CS+ diversity (high vs. low) in the same task while recording electroencephalography to examine its moderating role. Behaviorally, acquired fear generalized more robustly to GSBasic than to GS sharing the same superordinate category (GSSuperordinate ). Participants in the high-diversity group showed higher shock expectancy ratings for both the CS+ and GSBasic than those in the low-diversity group. Event-related potential results revealed that GSBasic elicited P2 and N400 amplitudes comparable to those of the CS+, and exhibited more positive P2 and less negative N400 amplitudes than GSSuperordinate and CS-. Moreover, only the CS+ and GSBasic elicited more positive LPP amplitudes than CS-. These findings suggest that early attentional allocation, late semantic processing, and motivational attention collectively constitute the electrophysiological basis of the basic-level category processing advantage in fear generalization, offering implications for the intervention of anxiety disorders.

papers.title: Reversal of refractory epilepsy in an adult with GAMT deficiency: A case report and comparative literature review.
papers.authors: Sung WH, Chen H, Hsu CW, Tsai MH.
papers.abstract: Objective Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive creatine biosynthesis disorder. Reports specifically focusing on adult patients remain scarce. Methods We report a 52-year-old female (the oldest documented case of GAMT deficiency to date) presenting with severe intellectual disability, refractory epilepsy, and adult-onset disease progression. Whole-exome sequencing identified novel compound heterozygous GAMT variants (c.265_267del and c.253G>T), and magnetic resonance spectroscopy confirmed cerebral creatine depletion. Remarkably, initiating oral creatine supplementation at age 52 achieved complete seizure freedom, normalization of the electroencephalogram (EEG), and significant motor function recovery. Results A comprehensive review revealed that untreated adult patients face a high risk of progressive neurological deterioration. Compared to the pediatric cohort, adults exhibited a significantly higher prevalence of movement disorders (69.2% vs. 33.1%, p < 0.001) and a trend toward a higher prevalence of epilepsy (92.3% vs. 74.2%). Especially, atonic seizures (drop attacks) are particularly characteristic of adult GAMT deficiency, with EEGs frequently demonstrating background slowing, multifocal epileptiform discharges, and electrodecremental patterns. Significance This study underscores that continuous disease progression and prolonged neurotoxicity still could compromise the well-being of adult GAMT deficiency patients. Accurate diagnosis is essential for adults presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) phenotype, as even late treatment for GAMT deficiency can still dramatically alleviate the epileptic burden and reverse motor decline. Plain language summary We report the oldest known adult diagnosed with GAMT deficiency. Our case demonstrates that starting creatine treatment even at age 52 can dramatically reduce seizures and restore motor function. Literature shows that untreated adults suffer from more severe epilepsy and movement disorders than children, with symptoms worsening over time. These findings highlight the critical need for genetic testing in adults with unexplained severe epilepsy; timely creatine supplementation can halt cognitive decline and significantly restore quality of life.

papers.title: Frequent involvement of cingulate and insulo-opercular regions in sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy: A multimodal presurgical study.
papers.authors: Zhu F, Shi XR, Weng SW, Delazer L, Fearns N, Arafat T, Lv RJ, Hu WH, Zhang C, Koepp M, Wang Q.
papers.abstract: Objective Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) is classically considered a frontal lobe epilepsy; however, accumulating evidence suggests that hypermotor seizures may arise from multiple frontal and extrafrontal regions. We characterized the anatomical distribution of best available localizations in patients with SHE using multimodal presurgical data. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 17 patients with clinically diagnosed SHE who underwent comprehensive evaluation, including long-term video-electroencephalographic (EEG) monitoring, 3-T high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography, and, where indicated, magnetoencephalography, stereo-EEG (SEEG), and surgical assessment. Best available anatomical localizations were assigned using a hierarchical multimodal framework incorporating surgical, SEEG, and concordant noninvasive findings. Their anatomical distribution was subsequently assessed at the cohort level. Results Sixteen patients (94.1%) had an assigned best available localization. Cingulate or insulo-opercular regions were involved in 11 of 16 patients (68.8%), whereas the remaining cases were localized to other frontal regions. In a sensitivity analysis restricted to 10 patients with SEEG-defined and/or surgically supported localizations, six involved cingulate or insulo-opercular regions. All patients were MRI-negative. In contrast, MRI-positron emission tomography fusion provided regionally informative anatomical findings in 16 of 17 cases and contributed to multimodal localization. Interictal epileptiform discharges were identified in 15 patients, whereas regionally informative ictal scalp EEG patterns were observed in eight; ictal interpretation was frequently limited by rapid propagation, movement-related artifacts, and delayed EEG onset. Focal cortical dysplasia-related histopathological findings were identified in five of seven resected specimens, whereas interpretation in two was limited by prior thermocoagulation. Significance These descriptive findings indicate that cingulate and insulo-opercular regions were frequently represented among the identified localizations in this presurgical cohort. Multimodal evaluation integrating electroclinical, imaging, and invasive findings may support presurgical localization in MRI-negative SHE.

papers.title: Empagliflozin in Lafora disease: A first-in-human 6-month pilot study with electroclinical and FDG-PET findings.
papers.authors: d'Orsi G, Liantonio A, Imbrici P, Lolli G, Dinoi G, Conte E, Altomare CD, Ciccone F, Calò E, Perrone E, Cazzanelli G, DEFEAT‐LD Study Group, Carella M.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
papers.abstract: Objective Lafora disease (LD) is a rare, fatal neurodegenerative epilepsy with no approved treatments. Empagliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, has shown neuroprotective actions in preclinical models through modulation of glycogen metabolism, induction of a pseudo-ketogenic state, improved mitochondrial efficiency, and reduction of excitatory neurotransmission. Based on this rationale, we conducted a first-in-human pilot study of empagliflozin in two genetically confirmed LD patients. Methods Two patients with genetically confirmed LD received empagliflozin 10 mg/day for 6 months. Serial assessments included safety and tolerability, seizure frequency, myoclonus severity, electroencephalographic findings, neuropsychological and motor evaluations, brain MRI, and quantitative FDG-PET with regional Z-score analysis. Results Empagliflozin was safe and well tolerated, with no serious adverse events. Seizure frequency, myoclonus, and overall clinical status remained largely stable over 6 months, although some neuropsychological and motor measures showed variable changes between patients. EEG background activity and spike index were largely unchanged. Brain MRI showed stable mild cortical atrophy in both patients. In contrast, FDG-PET revealed progressive and spatially expanding cerebral hypometabolism in both patients, with worsening regional Z-scores, particularly in the parietal and precuneus regions. Significance In this first-in-human, 6-month pilot study, empagliflozin showed acceptable short-term safety and feasibility in LD, but no definitive conclusions on efficacy can be drawn. The dissociation between relative electroclinical stability and progressive metabolic impairment suggests that quantitative FDG-PET may represent a sensitive biomarker for monitoring disease trajectory in this ultra-rare epilepsy.

papers.title: Three-hinge gyri link individualized folding topology to cortical and superficial white-matter diffusion organization
papers.authors: Chen M, Dong X, Cheng J, Hu D, Liu T, Zhu D, Li G.
papers.abstract: Individual differences in cortical folding are a hallmark of human brain anatomy, but what this variability reflects in the underlying tissue remains unclear. Three-hinge gyri (3HGs), where three gyral crests converge, provide an individualized higher-order folding landmark for probing this relationship. Using 7T diffusion MRI in six postmortem hemispheres, we found lower mean, axial, and radial diffusivity and higher fractional anisotropy at 3HGs than at matched gyral crowns, with the principal tensor pattern replicated in 414 age-matched in vivo adults. Diffusivity differences extended across the cortical ribbon, whereas anisotropy- and fiber-related differences strengthened toward and beneath the white surface. Ex vivo , diffusion measures also varied with gyral-skeleton degree, and streamlines sampled beneath 3HGs preferentially reached other 3HGs. These findings link individualized folding topology to cortical and superficial white-matter diffusion-inferred tissue properties, providing tissue-level context for understanding the microstructural correlates of individual folding variation.

papers.title: Speech Tracking in fMRI Reveals a Distinct Response to Sentence Boundaries During Comprehension
papers.authors: Levy-David O, Tikoschinski R, Reichart R, Zion Golumbic E, Deschamps I, Agmon G.
papers.abstract: Psycholinguistic research and linguistic theory suggest that comprehending continuous speech involves segmenting it into sentences. Yet, direct neuroimaging evidence for this process remains scarce, partly because sentence boundaries coincide with acoustic, prosodic, lexical, and syntactic changes. Here, we used whole-brain fMRI to test whether sentence boundaries elicit a neural response beyond these accompanying speech properties during spontaneous speech comprehension. We modelled BOLD responses to sentence-final words alongside continuous regressors characterizing accompanying speech properties. This approach revealed sensitivity to continuously varying features of speech across multiple brain regions. Notably, the acoustic envelope predicted BOLD responses in bilateral primary auditory cortices. Responses associated with prosodic breaks and emphasis were found in right temporal cortex, syntactic bottom-up node count in the left superior temporal sulcus, and word concreteness in the parahippocampal gyri. Critically, sentence-final words were associated with an increased activation in right temporal regions, after accounting for acoustic, prosodic, lexical, semantic and syntactic properties. These findings provide evidence for a neural response to sentence boundaries consistent with active sentence segmentation. More generally, this study demonstrates the value of continuous-regressor modelling for investigating speech comprehension with fMRI.

papers.title: Brain FACTs: A same-section workflow for Fiber Architecture, Cytoarchitecture and cell Types in large-scale brain sections
papers.authors: Kooijmans RN, Axer M, Graessel D, Amunts K.
papers.abstract: Understanding the human brain's multiscale organization requires linking cells, connections and architecture, yet conventional methods are incompatible within a single specimen, and inter-individual variability confounds cross-brain comparisons. Multiple-label immunohistochemistry for different cell types has been applied in interleaved sections but remains challenging within a single large human brain section and, has never been combined on the same tissue with 3D polarized light imaging (3D-PLI) for three-dimensional fiber architecture. Here we introduce a sequential multimodal workflow integrating 3D-PLI, multiplex chromogenic immunohistochemistry and Nissl staining on the same large human brain section, preserving each technique's quality and specificity. The method was validated on vervet monkey and Wistar rat sections. The resulting paired high-resolution images eliminate inter-subject variability and enable direct micron-scale mapping of fiber tracts relative to molecularly defined cell types, yielding previously inaccessible insights such as molecular identification of white-matter components, refined cortical layering and cytoarchitectural disambiguation.

papers.title: Time at Home for Whom? Unequal Returns of Paid Family Leave for Infant White Matter and Language Development
papers.authors: Lazarus MF, Nelson CA.
papers.abstract: Paid family leave (PFL) may give parents more time with infants, ease financial strain, and support stable routines. Although PFL has been linked to child development, little is known about neural pathways that might underpin its benefits or whether associations vary across families. Using data from 274 infants in the HEALthy Brain and Child Development Study, we examined associations of maternal and paternal PFL with language ability at 12 months and white matter microstructure at 6 months. We tested whether associations varied by the corresponding parent’s education. Neither maternal nor paternal PFL was directly associated with language scores or fractional anisotropy in the left arcuate, inferior longitudinal, or uncinate fasciculus. Maternal education moderated associations between maternal PFL and fractional anisotropy in the arcuate ( p = .014) and inferior longitudinal fasciculus ( p = .003; n = 148). In both tracts, PFL was associated with higher fractional anisotropy only among infants whose mothers had relatively high education. No comparable pattern emerged for language, the uncinate fasciculus, or paternal PFL. Findings suggest that the neurodevelopmental correlates of PFL may depend on family resources rather than operate uniformly across families, underscoring the need to pair paid leave with additional supports and resources. Lay Summary Paid family leave may give parents more time at home, steadier daily routines, and less financial worry in the months after a birth, all of which could change the care an infant receives. But these benefits may not be equal across families. In a national study of infants, we examined whether paid leave taken by mothers, fathers or partners was related to early language skills and to the organization of brain pathways involved in language. Paid leave was not directly related to language scores or brain development overall. However, maternal paid leave was associated with more mature organization in two language-related brain pathways only among infants whose mothers had higher levels of education. No similar pattern was found for father or partner leave. These findings suggest that paid leave alone may not reduce early developmental disparities, and that policies offering paid leave may need to be paired with additional support for families with fewer resources.

papers.title: Agency and Embodiment Provide Dissociable Benefits to Perception, Metacognition and Neural Processing During Active Sensing
papers.authors: Tang Z, Dowsett J, Taylor P, Ferreiro DN, Pecka M.
papers.abstract: Metacognition, judging how reliable our own perceptual decisions are, is central to adaptive behavior. Such judgments hinge on the reliability of the sensory evidence on which that decision is based, and active sensing through self-directed exploration is known to improve perception itself. Yet, how agency, the authorship over self-initiated actions, and the processing of the sensory consequences, which is implicit to active sensing, modulate metacognition and its calibration, remains unknown. Whether physical embodiment adds to this beyond virtual exploration is similarly unclear, yet relevant both for daily life and for self-monitoring in agentic AI. Here, we combined a naturalistic auditory search paradigm with mobile electroencephalography. Twenty participants performed a target-detection task under three conditions: active embodied exploration, active screen-based exploration, and passive listening to replays of their own trials, while we obtained steady-state auditory evoked potentials (SSAEPs) to characterize stimulus-locked neural responses. We find that both agency conditions improved accuracy, metacognitive sensitivity, and overall SSAEP amplitude relative to passive listening, indicating that agency, rather than whole-body movement, drives these enhancements. Crucially, however, embodiment uniquely grounded both the target-evoked neural response and the subjects’ confidence to immediate sensory evidence. Thus, agency alone broadly enhances perceptual and neural processing, but embodiment specifically anchors confidence, neurally and behaviorally, to the present. Significance Statement How well we judge the reliability of our perception, called metacognitive sensitivity, matters more than ever, as we increasingly are presented with information passively through screens rather than gathering it actively via self-initiated exploration. Does actively seeking information sharpen self-monitoring, and does the medium (body vs. screen) matter? We show that active search enhances metacognitive sensitivity and brain responses alike, whether embodied or screen-based. Only embodied search, however, anchors self-evaluation to the present: Behaviorally, embodiment facilitates coupling of confidence tracking directly to current evidence rather than the previous trial’s outcome, while neuronally, it enhances responses in frontal brain regions during periods of heightened subjective confidence. This embodied grounding of self-monitoring may prove pivotal for building reliably agentic AI systems.

papers.title: Autoencoder-based anomaly mapping and visualization of white matter deformation with application to glioma cases
papers.authors: Shams B, Fekonja LS, Vajkoczy P, Picht T, Aydogan DB.
papers.abstract: Introduction Gliomas can alter white matter pathways, causing structural deformation and functional impairments. However, there is no method to map these structural alterations across the whole brain to support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework based on a convolutional autoencoder that learns geometry-preserving streamline embeddings for mapping structural connectivity anomalies Methods We trained and validated the autoencoder on 100 million synthetic streamlines and evaluated the anomaly-mapping pipeline using data from 118 healthy subjects. We analyzed how different tractography algorithms affect anomaly scores and demonstrated its feasibility in five glioma patients using multi-shell and single-shell diffusion MRI. Results Latent-space distances strongly associated with native-space geometric distances ( R ² = 0.82–0.98), supporting preserved streamline geometry in the learned embeddings. Anomaly scores varied with both the input and reference tractography methods. Patient anomaly maps showed elevated scores near gliomas and extending distally along affected pathways. These whole-brain anomaly maps were generated within minutes. Conclusion The framework offers a practical way to quantify and visualize geometric deviations in whole-brain tractograms, providing novel insights beyond current network and microstructural analyses, with relevance to clinical applications where white matter deformation is pertinent.

papers.title: Movie Watching for Individual Functional Brain Network Estimation in Adolescents
papers.authors: Godfrey KJ, Grimsrud GJ, Ramirez JS, Corlett A, Houlihan K, Byington N, Gell M, Kretsch S, Dosenbach NU, Barch DM, Gordon EM, Greene DJ, Mueller BA, Betzel RF, Fair DA, Conelea CA, Tervo-Clemmens B, Nelson SM.
papers.abstract: SUMMARY Precision functional mapping (PFM) reveals stable individual differences in brain functional network organization and holds promise for advancing neuropsychiatric clinical care. PFM requires sufficient high-quality and densely sampled functional MRI data at the individual level that is typically acquired during the so-called resting state while passively fixating on a crosshair. However, crosshair fixation acquisitions can be challenging especially for pediatric or patient populations, where alternatives like movie watching might be used to improve data quality and reduce participant burden. Here, we compare the use of resting state crosshair fixation and movie watching fMRI data to derive individual-specific functional brain network topography using PFM data (28–38 minutes of low-motion fMRI data per-participant per-condition) in nineteen adolescents (12-18 years) with a range of transdiagnostic psychiatric diagnoses. Network assignments were largely conserved between crosshair fixation and movie watching, with a smaller subset of reproducible network reassignments which were overwhelmingly border shifts between neighboring networks. This suggests largely conserved global structure of functional network topography between crosshair fixation and movie watching, though border shifts can compound into variable estimates of cortical network size particularly for movie positive (language, salience, and parietal memory) and movie negative networks (default mode, action mode). Functional network assignments derived from movies and crosshair were also similarly individual-specific and consistent within common neuromodulation targets including dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and somatomotor cortex. Key results were replicated in independent pediatric consortia data (Healthy Brain Network, n = 466, 6-22 years) and reproduced across independent PFM data sessions. Acknowledging individual differences and level of analysis, we conclude that movies are a viable alternative to resting state crosshair fixation for individual network definitions.

papers.title: Aging effects on retrospective and naturalistic encoding of time and their relationship with memory
papers.authors: Fricker F, Buzi G, Morantin M, Doidy F, Clochon P, Bordas R, Leroy N, D’Argembeau A, van Wassenhove V, Hinault T.
papers.abstract: In everyday life, attention is not explicitly directed toward time. Yet, we can reconstruct how long an experience lasted from the memory traces it left behind, a process intertwined with episodic memory and subjective experience. As both memory and temporal processing change with advancing age, investigating aging effects could provide critical insights on these reconstructive processes. In this study, 31 younger (aged 24±3) and 36 older (aged 69±6) healthy adults completed two EEG sessions: 1) a resting-state recording followed by an unexpected retrospective time estimation, and 2) a video-based prospective duration estimation task where participants encoded and judged the duration of 50 naturalistic videos (2-32s) varying in eventfulness. Using a cycle-by-cycle burst analysis of alpha (α: 8-12 Hz), we examined oscillatory correlates of both retrospective temporal judgement and prospective temporal processing. Behaviorally, both groups reconstructed short intervals similarly, but older adults produced longer prospective duration estimates than younger adults for longer video clips (16-32s), particularly under low-eventfulness. Regression analyses also showed that individual differences in older adults’ prospective duration judgments were influenced by both their retrospective time estimation and episodic memory abilities, especially for longer videos. At the neural level, resting-state α-burst dynamics were higher in older adults and predicted, with α-power, longer retrospective estimates in older adults. Additionally, resting-state α-burst activity predicted α-burst during video encoding in both groups. Together, these findings reveal that individual α-power and α-burst dynamics could constitute memory-based time-tracking mechanism that aging reshapes in ways that manifest behaviorally under naturalistic conditions.

papers.title: Cortex-wide single-cell activity mapping in freely moving mice
papers.authors: Guo C, Xie M, Qiu G, Lu J, Liu Y, Qu L, Huang Y, Guo Z, Tian J, Lin J, Zhang B, Zhang X, Zhao J, Liu X, Long H, Ma J, Zhou B, Ye X, Zhao P, Cao J, Lin Z, Zhang Z, Deng W, Wang J, Wu W, Wang J, Peng X, Zhao S, Na S, Li H, Liu W, Fu Q, Guo ZV, Zhao W, Chen L.
papers.abstract: How the cortex supports complex, naturalistic behavior can be revealed only in freely moving animals. Although head-mounted microscopes promise access to the neural dynamics underlying such behavior, fundamental trade-offs among field of view, spatial resolution, device weight, and background contamination have prevented cortex-wide single-neuron recording, leaving distributed cortical coordination largely inaccessible. To meet these challenges, we introduce COMET (C ortex-wide O bservational M iniature E pifluorescence T echnique ) , a 3.75-g head-mounted mesoscope that integrates an aberration-controlled wide-field optical design, uniform high-efficiency excitation and single-coaxial power-and-data transmission with an end-to-end denoising and signal-extraction pipeline. This enables cortex-wide calcium imaging at single-cell resolution in freely moving mice. COMET captures activity from >15,000 layer 2/3 neurons per 5-min recording over fields of view up to 10 mm in diameter while preserving natural behavior. Benchmarking against benchtop two-photon microscopy demonstrates high spatial concordance of detected neurons and matched event-level calcium dynamics. We apply COMET to social interaction to quantify region-specific engagement and to an auditory trace fear-conditioning task that requires natural movement and behavioral expression, revealing time-ordered changes in regional firing-rate structure and functional connectivity preceding a global conditioned response. COMET provides an open, lightweight hardware–software framework for linking single-neuron activity to cortex-scale network dynamics during freely expressed behaviors under changing internal or external conditions.

papers.title: Concordance and Association of Kidokoro MRI Scores at 32 and 40 Weeks Postmenstrual Age with Neurodevelopmental Outcomes in Very Preterm Infants.
papers.authors: Bonezzi L, Biagioni T, Fiori S, Luke C, George JM, Colditz PB, Fripp J, Ware RS, Pannek K, Boyd RN.
papers.abstract: Background and purpose Early identification of neurodevelopmental risk in very preterm infants is critical for timely intervention. The Kidokoro MRI scoring system offers a semiquantitative approach to evaluating brain abnormalities. This study aimed to assess the agreement of Kidokoro scores obtained in the same infants at 32 and 40 weeks postmenstrual age, and their association to cognitive, language, and motor outcomes at 24 months corrected age. Materials and methods A cohort of 187 very preterm infants (median 28+5 weeks gestational age; 55% boys) underwent structural MRI at 2 time points: early (median 32+2 weeks) and term-equivalent age (TEA; median 40+5 weeks), using 3T scanners. Scans were scored independently using a modified version of the Kidokoro system. Bland-Altman analysis assessed agreement between early and TEA scores. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were assessed at 24 months using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition (Bayley-III). Multivariable linear regression models evaluated the predictive value of MRI scores, adjusting for sex, gestational age, birth weight centile, and socioeconomic status. Results Early MRI scores were consistently higher than TEA scores (mean difference: 1.9; 95% CI, 1.6-2.2), with WM scores showing the largest discrepancy (mean difference: 1.68; 95% CI, 1.46-1.90), primarily due to the myelination delay item. Excluding this item reduced the difference to 0.32 (95% CI, -0.01 to 0.64). Early and TEA Kidokoro Global Brain Abnormality Score (GBAS) were negatively associated with Bayley-III cognitive and motor, but not language scores. Higher GBAS were associated with lower cognitive (early: β = -0.67 [95% CI, -1.23 to -0.11], partial R 2 = 0.03; TEA: β = -0.60 [95% CI, -1.15 to -0.06], partial R 2 = 0.03) and motor scores (early: β = -1.04 [95% CI, -1.67 to -0.41], partial R 2 = 0.06; TEA: β = -1.18 [95% CI, -1.78 to -0.58], partial R 2 = 0.08). Reduction in GBAS from early to TEA correlated with higher motor scores (β = 1.02 [95% CI, 0.03-2.02], partial R 2 = 0.02). WM abnormalities were linked to poorer motor outcomes at both time points. Conclusions Kidokoro scores at early and term-equivalent time points are associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes at 24 months. Global abnormalities and WM scored at either time points, or their longitudinal changes are significantly linked to motor outcomes. Refinement of the scoring system for the early assessment may enhance clinical utility.

papers.title: Novel Neuroimaging Biomarker of Cortical Gray/White Border Integrity in Blast-Related Mild Traumatic Brain Injury.
papers.authors: Andreu Arasa VC, Fortenbaugh FC, Knoff AA, Fortier CB, Milberg WP, Salat DH.
papers.abstract: Background and purpose Recent studies suggest that blast or mid-impact neurotrauma are characterized by scar-border forming astrogliosis at the gray-white matter junction. Individuals with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) and blast trauma have increased neuroinflammation and impairment of axonal remyelination on postmortem histopathology. However, there are currently only limited methodologies to use in the assessment of the cortical gray/white interface using in vivo neuroimaging. The purpose was to investigate the gray-white matter contrast (GWC) at the gray-white matter junction that may be linked to neuroinflammation/astrogliosis in the setting of blast exposure and/or mTBI, through 3D T1-weighted MPRAGE images. Materials and methods Post-9/11 veterans (n =723) from the Translational Research Center for TBI and Stress Disorders completed MRI. Participants were grouped into 4 categories: participants with a history of blast-related mTBI (blast-mTBI), participants with a history of mTBI due to other mechanical forces (blunt-mTBI), participants with a history of close blast exposure but no mTBI, and those without a history of lifetime mTBI or close blast exposure. MRI data processing for morphometry and cortical surface mapping was done using FreeSurfer image analysis. Signal intensities in gray and white matter along the cortical and white matter interface were used to calculate mean GWC value. Results Veterans in the blast-mTBI group showed diffuse patterns of increased GWC relative to the other groups, particularly in the frontotemporal lobes. This effect was driven primarily by a greater number of high GWC regions in the blast-mTBI group compared with the no-neurotrauma and blunt-mTBI groups. Conclusions There was diffuse increased GWC on MR in the blast-mTBI group compared with the no-neurotrauma, close blast exposure, and blunt-mTBI groups. These findings may be linked to astrogliosis and neuroinflammation in patients with blast-mTBI. Histopathologic correlation with imaging findings will be necessary to better understand these effects.

papers.title: The Effects of Cognitive Load on Intergroup Empathy Biases [Registered Report Stage 1, Version 2]
papers.authors: Franks JE, Gutsell JN.
papers.abstract: Accurate and quick judgments of others’ mental and emotional states are crucial for social interaction. However, these judgments can be compromised by social biases, especially while cognitive demands are high and cognitive resources are low. Empathy is not always allocated to everyone equally, especially when the target is considered an outgroup member. One factor that may exacerbate such empathy biases is cognitive load, as cognitive load has been shown to increase ingroup biases and impair empathizing. This study investigates whether high cognitive load and racial outgroup membership interact, potentially worsening behavioral and self-reported indicators of empathy bias. To our knowledge, the present work is the first to directly manipulate cognitive load during intergroup empathizing, examining its effects on two distinct, yet interacting, routes of empathy—experience sharing and mentalizing. Mentalizing (cognitive empathy) and affective experience sharing (emotional empathy) activate different brain networks but interact during social situations, necessitating separate examination within the same paradigm. Using an empathy task designed to test racial empathy biases, we integrate behavioral and self-report measures to capture empathy dynamics in response to naturalistic stimuli. This approach allows us to test how group biases and cognitive load independently and jointly affect mentalizing and experience sharing.

papers.title: Baroreflex control of heart rate at rest and during exercise in microgravity conditions.
papers.authors: Perrone MA, Caminiti G, Aracri M, Volterrani M, Iellamo F.
papers.journal: The Journal of sports medicine and physical fitness
papers.abstract: One of the most important features of prolonged weightlessness is a progressive impairment of muscular function. Physiological modifications related to exposure to microgravity, e.g. altered blood volume distribution, impaired myocardial function, and a decrease in stroke volume, in addition to the alterations in muscular function, contribute to the reduced physical exercise capacity commonly reported after space flight. The interplay between muscular, hemodynamic and body fluid modifications occurring in microgravity could alter also the neural mechanisms of cardiovascular regulation both in resting conditions and during exercise in comparison to those that are normally operating on the ground. Indeed, an impairment in arterial baroreflex control of heart rate has been reported in the resting state during spaceflight. Moreover, cardiovascular and autonomic responses to exercise have been reported to be either impaired or preserved after simulated or actual microgravity conditions. Differences in results might depend on different experimental settings: the majority of studies on exercise in microgravity have been conducted using handgrips as a convenient model of muscular exercise. However, microgravity-induced muscular impairment involves mainly the antigravity muscles, i.e. leg muscles, which are those primarily involved in the reduced exercise capacity and hence are more representative of the marked changes in the musculoskeletal system induced by microgravity. This brief review aims to summarize current knowledge on baroreflex control of heart rate in resting and exercise conditions in microgravity.

papers.title: Exploring the Neural Mechanisms of Acupuncture Stimulation in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Protocol for a Randomized, Sham-Controlled, Multimodal Neuroimaging Trial.
papers.authors: Sim J, Choi KS, Lee DH.
papers.abstract: Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by restricted and repetitive behaviors and disturbances in social communication and interaction. Currently, there is no fundamental treatment for ASD, with only a few medications available for use on a limited basis to manage concomitant neuropsychiatric symptoms. The primary therapeutic goal of such treatments is to alleviate symptoms while maximizing the functional independence and quality of life of affected individuals. Many complementary and alternative medicine therapies have been reported to have effects on ASD symptoms; however, evidence is insufficient to confirm their clinical effectiveness. Acupuncture has traditionally been used as a complementary intervention to manage various neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases, including ASD, in East Asia. However, how acupuncture stimulation modulates neural activity at the macroscale level in individuals with ASD remains largely unknown. Objective This study aims to elucidate disease-related brain alterations and explore the acute neural mechanisms underlying acupuncture stimulation in patients with ASD and in typically developing (TD) individuals, using a multimodal neuroimaging approach. Methods This study was designed as a randomized, sham-controlled trial.
