The Bayes Factor (BF) reflected moderate, strong or very strong evidence (BF = 3.0;20;1.5⋅102 respectively). In the 24 included patients, prominent focal volume loss, iron deposition, ventricular enlargement and myelin damage (BF:2.0⋅102 ) were observed peripheral to the initial 24-hour DWI lesion at long-term FU MRI. In the basal ganglia nuclei, very strong evidence of focal volume loss (BF > 8.1⋅102 ) and moderate to very strong evidence of iron deposition (BF: 5.0 to 2.7⋅102 ) were observed at long-term assessment. Higher systolic blood pressure was associated with reduced long-term ventricular atrophy (BF:5.8). Long-term differences in ipsilateral versus contralateral hippocampal volume difference (BF:8.0) and iron deposition (BF:4.1) were moderately associated with QoL. Long-term subtle yet widespread demyelination and iron deposition were observed, and these changes correlated with long-term recovery.

papers.title: Pericyte loss and endothelial activation define distinct vascular states in cerebral small vessel disease.
papers.authors: Chagnot A, Jaime Garcia D, McQuaid C, Cholewa-Waclaw J, McDade K, Dando O, Wardlaw JM, Smith C, Montagne A.
papers.abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) is a leading cause of stroke and vascular cognitive impairment, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying microvascular dysfunction in human disease remain incompletely understood. In particular, the relationship between pericyte alterations and endothelial activation, two key features of blood-brain barrier dysfunction, remains unresolved. Here, we performed a quantitative single-vessel analysis of the human cortical microvasculature across increasing cSVD severity and ageing. Using multiplex immunohistochemistry combined with spectral unmixing and automated image analysis, we analysed 11,409 microvascular fragments from post-mortem brain tissue derived from 20 cases. Endothelial cells, pericytes, and endothelial activation were assessed using PECAM-1, PDGFRβ, and VCAM-1, respectively. Microvascular density and diameter differed between cortical grey matter and the underlying white matter, with white matter vessels being less dense and wider in controls. While vessel diameter remained stable across cSVD severity groups, microvascular density increased with cSVD severity and age in the white matter. At the molecular level, PDGFRβ signal decreased markedly with increasing cSVD severity, consistent with reduced pericyte coverage. This reduction was observed in both grey and white matter and correlated with disease severity and age. Notably, intermediate severity groups displayed marked heterogeneity, with vessels exhibiting either preserved or markedly reduced PDGFRβ signal. In parallel, endothelial markers PECAM-1 and VCAM-1 increased significantly with disease severity, reflecting endothelial activation. Unsupervised Gaussian mixture clustering of marker expression identified three vascular states characterised by (i) preserved PDGFRβ signal with low endothelial activation, (ii) reduced PDGFRβ signal without endothelial activation, and (iii) reduced PDGFRβ signal combined with endothelial activation. These clusters broadly aligned with neuropathological severity but revealed heterogeneity not captured by post-mortem diagnosis alone. Together, these findings suggest that pericyte alterations and endothelial activation are partially dissociated processes in human cSVD and identify distinct microvascular phenotypes across disease severity. These cross-sectional observations provide a framework for future longitudinal and experimental studies to determine their temporal and mechanistic relationships.

papers.title: Neuropathic Pain: From Mechanisms to Therapeutic Interventions.
papers.authors: Dai Y, Tan M, Yuan M, Zhou H, Xie Q, Zeng J, Yang Y, He X, Song S.
papers.abstract: Neuropathic pain is caused by injury or disease of the somatosensory system. It involves peripheral nerve injury, central sensitization, transmitter imbalance, glial activation, and large-scale network remodeling. Despite substantial advances in pain biology, clinical assessment continues to rely predominantly on patient-reported symptoms, sensory examination, and conventional neurophysiological testing, approaches that often fail to delineate the predominant biological mechanisms underlying pain in individual patients. Recent advances in sensory phenotyping and multimodal imaging have enabled in vivo characterization of abnormalities at the receptor, neuroinflammatory, and circuit levels, thereby providing a foundation for mechanism-based stratification and more individualized therapeutic decision-making. This review summarizes neuropathic pain from clinical stratification to mechanism-based imaging and therapeutic intervention. We describe key clinical dimensions, including sensory gain, sensory loss, peripheral and central pain generators, mixed nociceptive-neuropathic pain, central sensitization, and autonomic or small-fiber modifiers. These dimensions help explain why patients with the same diagnosis may show different symptoms and treatment responses. We also review major molecular mechanisms, including glutamatergic overactivity, GABAergic and glycinergic disinhibition, monoaminergic remodeling, and neuroimmune modulation. These changes reshape spinal, thalamocortical, limbic, salience, reward, cerebellar, and descending control circuits. Peripheral nerve ultrasound and MR neurography can help identify structural peripheral pain generators. PET, MRS, MRI, DTI, fMRI, EEG, and multimodal imaging can assess receptor availability, neurotransmitter balance, neuroinflammation, white matter integrity, and network connectivity. These imaging tools may link clinical phenotypes with biological mechanisms and help define mechanism-based subtypes. Imaging biomarkers may also support treatment selection, treatment monitoring, neuromodulation targeting, and translational trial design. This framework supports a shift from symptom-based assessment to mechanism-guided precision care for neuropathic pain.

papers.title: Diffusion Basis Spectrum Imaging of Tissue Microstructure and Early Treatment in Multiple Sclerosis.
papers.authors: Kaewsanit A, Luna A, Judge B, Shelley N, Friedrichsen K, Rajamanickam J, Tu Z, Wang Y, Benzinger TLS, Wang Q, Brier MR.
papers.journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology
papers.abstract: Objective Conventional MRI cannot resolve the coexisting pathological processes within multiple sclerosis tissue. Diffusion Basis Spectrum Imaging decomposes the diffusion signal into fiber, cell, and hindered ratios indexing axonal integrity, cellularity, and extracellular space, respectively. We asked how these ratios differ between early relapsing and established non-relapsing disease, change with early treatment, and relate to disability, and secondarily, whether lesions form reproducible microstructural subtypes. Methods Thirty-seven participants underwent multi-shell diffusion MRI: 11 healthy controls, 15 treatment-naïve relapsing, and 11 non-relapsing patients. Thirteen were rescanned ~3 months after starting high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy. Metrics were extracted from normal-appearing gray and white matter and lesions (core, rim, and perilesional white matter); Gaussian mixture model clustering of per-lesion fiber, cell, and hindered ratios identified lesion subtypes. Results Treatment-naïve relapsing patients showed reduced normal-appearing white matter fiber (p = 0.04) and elevated hindered ratios (p = 0.02) versus controls. Lesions had lower fiber and cell ratios and higher hindered ratio than within-subject normal-appearing white matter (all p < 0.001). After treatment, lesional fiber ratio increased (p = 0.01) while lesional and gray matter cell ratios declined (both p = 0.02). Lesional cell ratio was higher in relapsing than non-relapsing patients at the core (p = 0.03) and rim (p = 0.04) but not perilesionally; treatment-related improvement was similar across compartments. Clustering yielded four reproducible subtypes (edematous-hypocellular, moderately cellular, actively inflamed, structurally preserved); the inflamed subtype predominated in relapsing and the edematous-hypocellular in non-relapsing disease. Interpretation Diffusion basis spectrum imaging distinguishes relapsing from non-relapsing disease by lesion-body cellularity and detects treatment-related changes in fiber and cell compartments. Reproducible, hypothesis-generating lesion subtypes support its use for in vivo lesion phenotyping.

papers.title: Robust and replicable effects of ageing on resting-state brain electrophysiology measured with MEG.
papers.authors: Quinn AJ, Pitt J, Kohl O, Gohil C, van Es MWJ, Nobre AC, Woolrich MW.
papers.abstract: Non-invasive recordings of brain electrophysiology provide credible insights into decline in neuronal functioning with age. New approaches are required to translate these results into compelling clinical metrics and meet the global challenge of preserving brain health in ageing. Changes in neuronal dynamics with ageing are observable in the power spectra of EEG and MEG recordings. Highly promising candidates for electrophysiological markers have been identified, but progress is hindered by substantial methodological variability across studies. This makes it challenging to establish a clear consensus on the frequency, location, and direction of any single reported effect within the larger body of research. We estimate a full-frequency whole-head profile of the ageing effect on eyes-closed resting-state MEG using the GLM-Spectrum. This data representation is easily sharable, facilitates meta-analyses, and provides a framework for estimating statistical power of age effects for future study planning. We use this to show that the effect of age replicates across open-access MEG datasets and is robust to modelling of common covariates. Distinct components within the full-frequency profile have different effect sizes, indicating that sample-size planning for ageing effects must consider the specific features of interest. The frequency profile of ageing is strongly robust to a range of common covariates and partially robust to modelling of grey matter volume. We establish that what seems a well-powered study may become underpowered when analyses target an age effect that is linearly separable from an age-relevant covariate such as grey matter volume. These results provide a pathway towards formal comparison and assessment of candidate markers for brain health in ageing.

papers.title: Attenuated alpha state transitions and disrupted repetition-dependent temporal adaptation in mild cognitive impairment
papers.authors: Wang X, Zhu Y, Zhang J, Zheng Z, Yu M.
papers.abstract: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) may involve impaired dynamic regulation of brain states that is not captured by conventional resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We quantified occipital alpha (8–12 Hz) transitions during three repeated eye-opening/eye-closure cycles in 60 healthy controls (HC) and 77 participants with MCI. Eye-state events were refined from frontal ocular artifacts. Transition magnitude was measured by the log-transformed post-/pre-event energy ratio, and transition success by the expected direction of alpha change. For canonical transitions meeting prespecified fit-quality criteria, mono-exponential fitting yielded transition onset (t onset ) and the post-onset time constant (τ). MCI showed weaker alpha suppression during eye opening, weaker alpha enhancement during eye closure, and lower odds of transition success. No significant group difference in τ was detected within the canonical quality-controlled subset. In contrast, t onset showed significant Group × Trial interactions in both conditions: HC developed later onset during eye opening and earlier onset during eye closure across repetitions, whereas MCI showed no comparable change. These findings suggest reduced alpha state-transition capacity and altered repetition-dependent temporal organization in MCI.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks for subject-specific recovery of travelling-wave structure in resting-state fMRI
papers.authors: Pouya TL, Sotero RC.
papers.abstract: Resting-state BOLD fluctuations show reproducible spatiotemporal propagation that is not accounted for by conventional zero-lag functional connectivity. Travelling wave analyses based on phase gradients or statistical decomposition have problems when multiple wave generators overlap or when wave origins have to be localized. This work introduces a wave-informed physics-informed neural network that represents the parcellated BOLD signal as a superposition of seven spatially extended damped travelling wave generators, each periodically re-excited at its own characteristic frequency and fixed at initialization to one of the seven canonical Schaefer resting-state networks. A soft anatomical prior derived from each subject’s diffusion-tensor structural connectivity is included to encode the hypothesis that white-matter pathways constrain wave direction. The pipeline is validated on synthetic data by three simulation studies, creating the operating envelope, and then applied to 41 cognitively normal participants of the ADNI 3 cohort. A within-subject ablation showed that mean alignment between recovered wave directions and underlying white-matter geometry increased by a small but statistically detectable amount when using the structural prior (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, p = 0.026), with exploratory network-level effects most evident in the visual, dorsal-attention, and salience/ventral-attention networks. The contribution is a network-anchored parametric inverse method returning subject-specific propagation descriptors from short resting-state scans.

papers.title: Awake resection of temporal encephalocele associated with drug-resistant epilepsy: illustrative case.
papers.authors: Ondrušová P, Timárová G, Pakosová E, Buvala J, Hrebeňárová B, Hollý V, Drajnová Z, Jezberová M, Koblížek M, Konečná M, Ojemann SG, Šteňo A.
papers.abstract: Background The association between temporal encephaloceles (TEs) and drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) is well recognized, yet the literature regarding therapeutic management remains scarce and largely retrospective. Reported strategies vary from conservative approaches to extensive resection of encephaloceles including the adjacent epileptogenic zone (EZ). Surprisingly, although the EZ may be localized within or adjacent to eloquent areas, surgeries under awake conditions have not been described. One plausible explanation is the potential risk of intraoperative pain during surgical manipulation in the area of the richly innervated basal dura. Observations The authors present a case of a 23-year-old right-handed male with a left-sided TE associated with incapacitating DRE lasting 8 years. Preoperative evaluation, including 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography, suggested a large EZ within the dominant temporal lobe. An awake resection of the encephalocele and the EZ was performed; electrocorticography was utilized to tailor the resection extent. Speech and language functions were tested during the entire procedure. Surgical manipulation during encephalocele resection did not cause any discomfort. No postoperative neurological deficit was observed; the long-term seizure outcome is Engel class II. The patient returned to work. Lessons In selected cases in which the EZ adjacent to TEs involves eloquent areas, awake resection may be safely performed. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26699.

papers.title: Aging and Hearing Loss in Emotional Prosody Processing: Divergent Neural Adaptation and Behavioral Performance
papers.authors: Lin Y, Lu Y, Ding H, Zhang Y.
papers.abstract: Emotional prosody perception is vulnerable in later adulthood, yet the contributions of central aging and peripheral hearing loss remain unclear. Across two experiments, we combined event-related potentials (ERPs) , time-frequency analyses and behavioral measures to examine how aging and hearing sensitvity shape emotional prosody processing. Experiment 1 used acoustically matched speech and nonspeech stimuli in a passive oddball paradigm to assess preattentive processing. Experiment 2 examined explicit emotion identification and implicit stimulus judgment to evaluate goal-directed performance and its associations with neural responses. Aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between emotions and lower behavioral efficiency, alongside enhanced P3a amplitude. Older adults also responded more slowly than younger adults during emotion identification. Hearing sensitivity showed no significant main effect on accuracy or reaction time, despite associations with delayed early neural processing and stronger theta- and alpha-band activity. Hearing-related neural effects were most evident in older adults and varied across emotions and stimulus types. Brain–behavior associations were selective: reduced mismatch negativity (MMN) was associated with slower responses during stimulus identification, whereas longer MMN latencies were associated with lower accuracy and slower responses during emotion identification. These findings indicate that aging and hearing loss have distinct yet interacting associations with emotional prosody processing, with neural responses not necessarily corresponding to behavioral performance. We propose an “asymmetric adaptation” account in which neural responses to degraded auditory input reorganize selectively across processing stages and contexts, potentially explaining this neural-behavioral divergence and informing more sensitive assessment of socioemotional communication in later adulthood.

papers.title: Associations Between Resting-State EEG Delta-band Activity at Selected Parietal Electrodes and Cognitive Changes Following Transcutaneous Auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation in Patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment: An Exploratory Analysis.
papers.authors: Wang L, Ouyang H, Zhang J, Lu X, Zhang S, Zhao Y, Liang Y, Hao L, Wang Y, Rong P.
papers.abstract: Introduction Transcutaneous auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation (taVNS) may improve cognition in Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), but its electrophysiological correlates remain unclear. We explored whether parietal delta-band changes were associated with cognitive changes following taVNS. Methods This exploratory secondary analysis included 26 participants with MCI from a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial (taVNS, n = 14; sham, n = 12) who had valid resting-state EEG data at baseline and Week 24. Absolute and relative 1-3 Hz delta power at Pz, P1, P2, and P5 were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA and EEG-cognitive correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. Results Absolute delta power showed significant time effects at all four electrodes after FDR correction (all q = 0.008). Relative delta power at Pz showed an uncorrected group effect (F = 5.007, p = 0.035; q = 0.218). In the taVNS group, MoCA-B improvement was positively associated with relative delta-power changes at P1, P2, and P5 (r = 0.629-0.652, p = 0.012-0.016), whereas AVLTN7 improvement was negatively associated with absolute delta-power changes across Pz, P1, P2, and P5 (coefficients = -0.418 to -0.613, p = 0.020-0.048). Although these correlations did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons, they showed a relatively consistent direction across multiple electrodes. Discussion Relative and absolute delta power may reflect complementary aspects of spectral modulation. The convergent cross-electrode associations provide preliminary EEG evidence linked to cognitive response to taVNS. Conclusion Parietal delta-band power may represent a candidate electrophysiological marker of cognitive change following taVNS in MCI. These exploratory findings support further validation of predefined EEG biomarkers in larger, prospectively powered studies. Clinical trial registration http://www.chictr.org.cn (ID: ChiCTR2000038868).

papers.title: Clinical Efficacy and Electrophysiological Mechanisms of Closed-Loop Neuromodulation for the Treatment of Drug-Resistant Epilepsy
papers.authors: Wang Z, Hu T, Xie H, Zhang D, Sun Y, Zhang J, Cui X, Zheng J, Yu J, Zhang S, Song X, Wang M, Gao X, Li B, Zhao X, Zhang Z, Zhang Y, Liu W, Li W.
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate the clinical efficacy of closed-loop neuromodulation for drug-resistant epilepsy and to characterize its electrophysiological mechanisms by combining intracranial and scalp EEG, thereby providing experimental evidence for optimizing treatment protocols and identifying multidimensional efficacy biomarkers. Methods Eight patients with drug-resistant epilepsy who underwent closed-loop neuromodulation implantation were enrolled and followed for 12–24 months. Clinical efficacy was evaluated using the seizure reduction rate and the responder rate. Linear mixed-effects models and within-subject Spearman rank correlation analyses were used to systematically characterize the population-level associations and inter-individual heterogeneity between stimulation parameters and clinical efficacy. Interictal intracranial EEG (recorded before stimulation onset and at 12 months postoperatively) and scalp EEG (international 10–20 system) were collected, and power spectral density and the phase lag index were used to quantify frequency-band-specific EEG activity and brain functional connectivity, with correction for multiple comparisons. Results At 12 months postoperatively, the overall seizure reduction rate was 56.3% (P < 0.05), with a responder rate of 75.0%. At 24 months, the reduction rate increased to 75.0% (P < 0.05) and the responder rate reached 85.7%, indicating a progressive, cumulative improvement in efficacy with treatment duration. At the population level, no significant independent associations were found between stimulation amplitude, frequency, pulse width, or target changes and the seizure reduction rate, and the parameter–efficacy relationship exhibited marked inter-individual heterogeneity. Intracranial EEG revealed significantly increased gamma and high-gamma band power after treatment (Cohen's d > 0.8, large effect sizes), with no significant changes in the low-frequency bands. The high-gamma band exhibited a heterogeneous network reorganization pattern characterized by significantly enhanced functional connectivity within the epileptogenic zone and suppressed long-range propagation pathways. Scalp EEG showed diffuse changes, with significantly increased whole-brain delta power and significantly decreased beta power, whereas inter-electrode phase synchrony showed no statistically significant differences across frequency bands. Gamma-band power changed in opposite directions between intracranial and scalp EEG. Conclusion Closed-loop neuromodulation is a safe and effective treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy. Its efficacy accumulates over time and is patient-specific, with no universally optimal programming parameters. The electrophysiological mechanism is closely related to the plastic reorganization of epileptic networks induced by chronic targeted stimulation: the increased intracranial gamma/high-gamma power suggests functional restoration of local parvalbumin (PV)-positive inhibitory interneuron microcircuits in the epileptogenic zone, with the excitation–inhibition balance re-established toward a physiological steady state; the heterogeneous changes in high-gamma connectivity may limit the transregional propagation of epileptiform discharges. The scalp EEG pattern of enhanced slow-wave and attenuated fast-wave activity reflects an overall downregulation of whole-brain cortical excitability. The opposite changes in intracranial and scalp gamma-band power may provide key experimental evidence for a deeper understanding of the mechanisms of closed-loop neuromodulation and for establishing a multidimensional electrophysiological biomarker system for efficacy evaluation.

papers.title: TMS-EEG Investigation of Cortical Activity Induced by Individualized rTMS in Patients with Prolonged Disorders of Consciousness
papers.authors: Zhang Y, Yan X, Zhu Z, Du J, Cao L, Song W, Wang Y.
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective To establish an individualized repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) target selection protocol based on resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) directed functional connectivity for patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (pDoC), and to explore the underlying electrophysiological mechanisms using transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with EEG (TMS-EEG). Methods We enrolled 42 pDoC patients and randomly assigned to an individualized rTMS group, a conventional rTMS group, and a sham stimulation group. The individualized rTMS group selected the target with stronger directed functional connectivity between F3 and Pz as the stimulation site based on Granger causality analysis. The conventional rTMS group received random stimulation at either F3 or Pz. Both active groups received 10 sessions of high-frequency rTMS over 10 consecutive days, while the sham group underwent sham stimulation. Behavioral improvement and cortical connectivity were assessed before and after treatment using the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) and TMS-EEG, respectively. Results CRS-R scores significantly increased in both the individualized and conventional rTMS groups ( p < 0.05), whereas no significant improvement was observed in the sham group ( p > 0.05). TMS-EEG analysis demonstrated that the amplitudes of N100 and P180 components significantly increased post-treatment in both active groups ( p < 0.05), with no statistically significant changes in the sham group ( p > 0.05). Global mean field amplitude (GMFA) significantly increased post-treatment in both active groups ( p < 0.05). Specifically, significant increases were found in the 1-100 ms and 101–200 ms time windows post-treatment in both active groups ( p < 0.05). Additionally, the individualized rTMS group showed a significant increase in the 201–300 ms window ( p < 0.05), which was not observed in the conventional group ( p > 0.05). No significant differences were found in the sham group across any time windows (1-100 ms, 101–200 ms, 201–300 ms, 301–400 ms, 401–500 ms; p > 0.05). Correlation analyses indicated that the change in CRS-R score positively correlated with the change in N100 amplitude in both the individualized ( r = 0.82, p < 0.001) and conventional ( r = 0.79, p = 0.001) treatment groups. Similarly, the change in CRS-R score positively correlated with the change in P180 amplitude in the individualized ( r = 0.77, p = 0.0002) and conventional ( r = 0.62, p = 0.025) groups. Conclusion Individualized rTMS based on resting-state EEG directed functional connectivity is more effective in promoting consciousness recovery in pDoC patients. Compared to conventional rTMS, this approach may better facilitate the sustained propagation of post-stimulation cortical activity along residual consciousness networks and promote integration during middle-to-late stages. This study provides preliminary evidence supporting the transition of neuromodulation therapy for pDoC from fixed-target interventions to individualized precision regulation. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05682248. Ethics approval : Ethics Committee of Xuanwu Hospital, 2022[022].

papers.title: Interpretable Frequency-Aware Deep Learning for Multi-Class EEG Classification of Neurological Disorders
papers.authors: Bunterngchit C, Baniata LH, Baniata MH, Atwan JM, Alali M, Alsharaiah MA, Kang S.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) records cortical activity with high temporal resolution without radiation and at low cost, which makes it a practical signal for automated screening of neurological disorders. Deep learning classifies EEG with high accuracy, but most models distinguish only two conditions and give no account of their decisions, which limits their use in screening and decision support. This paper presents SpectraXAI, an interpretable frequency-aware deep learning model that assigns resting-state EEG to four diagnostic categories: Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia, and healthy control. The model filters each EEG window into the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands and processes every band in a separate convolutional branch with squeeze-and-excitation recalibration. Softmax-weighted band attention and temporal attention then combine the spectral and temporal evidence, and the same attention weights are intrinsic explanations of each prediction. Under a subject-disjoint evaluation protocol that prevents window leakage, the model reached 94.43% accuracy, 96.74% balanced accuracy, and 93.82% macro-F1 on 20,760 windows from 173 unseen subjects while using only 0.10 million parameters. An ablation study confirmed that the attention modules account for most of the improvement over a plain convolutional baseline. Attention weights, feature-attention heatmaps, Grad-CAM, and t-SNE embeddings trace each decision to specific frequency bands, time segments, and learned features, therefore the frequency structure that drives the accuracy also makes the predictions inspectable.

papers.title: Cranial Electrotherapy Stimulation for Fibromyalgia in Veterans: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Feasibility Study of Resting-State Functional Connectivity Magnetic Resonance Imaging to Evaluate Pain and Treatment Response.
papers.authors: Woodbury A, Martini R, Ree A, Huang CYO, Denmon C, Vernon M, Lukemire J, Ramos J, Kim KSJ, Cui X, Stevens J, Krishnamurthy V, Guo Y, Napadow V, Rauch SAM.
papers.abstract: Background Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder frequently co-occurring with depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and insomnia, particularly in veterans, and safer nonpharmacological therapies are needed. Cranial electrotherapy stimulation, also referred to as cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES), may help with anxiety and sleep, but its effect on pain is unclear. This feasibility study evaluated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to identify neural correlates of pain and treatment response for CES effects on fibromyalgia pain in veterans. Methods In a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial at a single US government hospital, veterans aged 20 to 60 with fibromyalgia were assigned to active or sham in-home CES, stratified by sex. Participants self-administered CES for 60 minutes daily over 12 weeks. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was acquired at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks with clinical outcomes, including the Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale (DVPRS), National Institutes of Health (NIH) Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) measures, and tests of physical function. Results Forty-eight participants were randomized (25 active, 23 sham) and 47 were analyzed. Both groups showed significant improvements in DVPRS pain (-1.88 ± 2.2) and pain interference with sleep (-2.25 ± 2.8), mood (-1.88 ± 2.6), activity (-1.83 ± 2.4) and stress (-1.77 ± 3.0) at 12 weeks versus baseline (P < .01), with significant between-group differences only in sleep (P = .04). Neuroimaging revealed significant increases in connectivity between the cerebellar 7b seed and the left occipital fusiform gyrus (0.079 ± 0.1) left lingual gyrus (0.063 ± 0.08), and right lingual gyrus (0.058 ± 0.08) for the CES group and decreases in the sham group (-0.088 ± 0.1; -0.121 ± 0.08; and -0.135 ± 0.1), respectively. No adverse events occurred. Conclusions Both groups improved similarly in pain and function, though new analgesic usage was more prevalent in the sham group. Neuroimaging revealed differential changes in cerebellar-sensory-visual networks and baseline patterns distinguishing responders from nonresponders, supporting feasibility and design of larger, adequately powered CES trials in fibromyalgia.

papers.title: Microglial dynamics associate with the spatial pattern of tau deposition in early Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Öchsner M, Brendel M, Franzmeier N, Trappmann L, Zaganjori M, Ersoezlue E, Kurz C, Haeckert J, Utecht J, Schirge PM, Papazov B, Pogarell O, Janowitz D, Buerger K, Ewers M, Palleis C, Weidinger E, Biechele G, Schuster S, Finze A, Eckenweber F, Rupprecht R, Rominger A, Goldhardt O, Grimmer T, Keeser D, Stoecklein S, Dietrich O, Bartenstein P, Levin J, Höglinger G, Perneczky R, Rauchmann BS.
papers.abstract: Background Neuroinflammation is implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis, yet how changes in TSPO PET signal are associated with tau deposition, and how brain network architecture shapes this relationship remain poorly understood. Methods We conducted a prospective, multimodal neuroimaging study in 56 participants: 35 amyloid-positive individuals across the AD spectrum (ADS) and 21 amyloid-negative healthy controls (HC). Amyloid status was classified primarily by CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 and, when eligible CSF was unavailable, by baseline amyloid PET. Participants underwent TSPO PET using [18 F]GE-180 and resting-state fMRI at baseline. A longitudinal subgroup additionally underwent follow-up tau PET using [18 F]PI-2620 (n = 24) and repeat TSPO PET (n = 18) approximately 18 months later. Results Baseline TSPO did not differ significantly between groups. Baseline TSPO was associated with regional tau in both groups; the reciprocal association between tau and TSPO change was numerically weaker in AD, but this group difference was not statistically significant. Connectivity to baseline-TSPO epicenters was associated with higher tau in both groups, whereas connectivity to TSPO-change epicenters was associated with lower tau in AD but not controls (group-by-connectivity interaction p < 0.001, participant-level slope difference p = 0.012), a dissociation replicated in independent participants. Conclusion These findings suggest that connectivity to established versus emerging TSPO epicenters carries distinct spatial information about tau in the AD spectrum, a pattern shaped by functional brain connectivity and absent in healthy controls. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06224920).

papers.title: Quran Memorization as a Naturalistic Neurocognitive Training Paradigm: A Quality-Weighted Evidence Synthesis in Student Populations.
papers.authors: Souissi A, Sayed MA, Alghamdi HA, Ahmed Abdelsattar H, Zemni B, Ben Saad H.
papers.abstract: AimWe aimed to quantitatively synthesize observational evidence on the association between memorization (Hifz ) and cognitive and mental health outcomes in students, using a quality-weighted evidence synthesis approach.MethodFor observational studies published between 2005 and 2026, a systematic multi-database search was carried out using PubMed/Medline , Scopus , ScienceDirect , and Google Scholar . The direction, strength, and consistency of the evidence across predetermined outcome domains were measured using a quality-weighted vote-counting synthesis. Seven observational studies involving 690 students were included.ResultsA statistically significant positive association between Hifz and at least one cognitive or psychological outcome was identified in 5 of 7 studies (71.4%). One study identified a neutral result, and one study (Magnetic Resonance Imaging morphology outcome) was reclassified as uncertain. No study reported a significant negative association. The quality-weighted evidence score was W = 71.5%, corresponding to moderate evidence. Memory performance, intelligence quotient, and quality of life showed the most consistent positive associations. Several studies reported more favourable cognitive or psychosocial outcomes among participants with higher levels of Quran memorization, although the observational design precludes causal interpretation.ConclusionQuality-weighted synthesis (W = 71.5%) indicates generally favourable associations between Hifz and cognitive and psychological outcomes in students. Although all studies included were conducted in students rather than clinical rehabilitation samples, emerging neurophysiological and clinical research on Quranic engagement provides a preliminary rationale for investigating its cognitive-linguistic and neurorehabilitation potential. Accordingly, Hifz is considered as a promising, culturally sensitive, hypothesis-generating model of intensive cognitive-linguistic practice that warrants rigorous prospective evaluation in neurological populations.

papers.title: An EEG-based framework for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis via single-channel multi-entropy fusion and ensemble learning.
papers.authors: Li J, Ling C, Peng Y, Yu Y, Feng G, Du W, Chen R.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers. Part H, Journal of engineering in medicine
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, and its early diagnosis is vital for timely intervention. However, most existing EEG-based diagnostic methods rely on multi-channel devices confined to hospital settings, limiting their accessibility for community screening. To address this gap, this study aims to develop a lightweight processing approach for portable, low-cost devices to support early AD diagnosis using single-channel EEG data, integrating signal purification with complementary entropy-based feature extraction and ensemble learning. Specifically, EEG signals are first decomposed into five brain rhythms (δ, θ, α, β, γ) using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) is then applied to extract Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) from the selected rhythm. Four entropy measures, including Differential Entropy (DE), Singular Spectral Entropy (SSE), Fuzzy Entropy (FE), and Sample Entropy (SE), are subsequently extracted from each IMF to construct the Multi-IMF Entropy Matrix (MIMFEM). After that, an ensemble learning framework combining five classifiers is designed to discriminate AD patients from healthy controls (HCs). The proposed method is evaluated on two public datasets using Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV). Using single-channel EEG data, our approach achieves classification accuracies of 97.92% on the Florida-based dataset and 81.54% on the AHEPA dataset, with corresponding F1-scores of 97.87% and 82.86%, respectively. These results, achieved with limited data sources, show that our approach provides an effective, practical solution for single-channel wearable AD screening and addresses the critical need for low-cost, accessible early diagnostic tools, advancing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare through a lightweight model.

papers.title: Altered Fronto-Cingulate Connectivity During Social Competition and Cooperation in Adolescents With Major Depressive Disorder: An fNIRS Hyperscanning Study.
papers.authors: He Y, Wang Y, Jiang S, Liang F.
papers.abstract: Background Major depressive disorder (MDD) in adolescence is characterized by high prevalence (24.3% in China) and social dysfunction, particularly in competitive and cooperative behaviors. This study used fNIRS hyperscanning to explore cortical connectivity alterations during parent-adolescent interactions in adolescent MDD. Methods Thirty-three MDD adolescents (DD) and 29 healthy controls (HCs) completed competitive/cooperative maze tasks with parents under 52-channel fNIRS. Wavelet coherence analyzed functional connectivity (FC) in prefrontal/motor regions, which provides undirected connectivity estimates. Group × task effects were tested via GLMM and FDR correction. Results (1) Competition: DD exhibited hyperconnectivity in emotion regulation circuits between right opercular inferior frontal gyrus and left triangular inferior frontal gyrus (rIFGoperc and lIFGtriang, p = 0.047) but hypoconnectivity in executive networks between left dorsal superior frontal gyrus and left precentral gyrus (lSFGdor and lPreCG, p = 0.040). (2) Cooperation: DD showed enhanced motor-cognitive integration between right supplementary motor area and right middle frontal gyrus (rSMA and rMFG, p = 0.036) but impaired socioemotional processing between right triangular inferior frontal gyrus and left dorsal superior frontal gyrus (rIFGtriang and lSFGdor, p = 0.033). Task modulation: Within DD, cooperation preferentially engaged emotional resonance networks between right inferior orbital frontal gyrus and right medial superior frontal gyrus (rORBinf and rSFGmed, p = 0.031) while competition was associated with enhanced coupling in self-monitoring circuits between left dorsal superior frontal gyrus and right opercular inferior frontal gyrus (lSFGdor and rIFGoperc, p = 0.047). Conclusions Adolescent MDD involves context-dependent neural deficits in social cognition, suggesting targets for neuromodulatory interventions.

papers.title: Zero Echo Time Functional MRI in Humans: Technical Demonstration and Proof-of-Concept.
papers.authors: Ozen AC, Liu S, Ilbey S, Bock M, Emir U, Shih YI.
papers.abstract: Conventional EPI-based fMRI relies on the BOLD contrast to map activity changes, but is limited by high acoustic noise, susceptibility artifacts, and distortion near air-tissue interfaces. Ultra-short and zero-echo-time (ZTE) sequences have gained considerable attention in animal fMRI studies due to their robustness against susceptibility effects, low acoustic noise, and ability to capture signal sources distinct from those of conventional BOLD imaging. In this study, we present a feasibility-level proof-of-concept technical demonstration of ZTE-based fMRI in humans at 3T, while maintaining many of the advantages observed in preclinical studies. Phantom measurements demonstrate that the ZTE protocol is sensitive to oxygenation-related T1 changes at 3T, supporting its feasibility for detecting related functional signals. In five healthy volunteers, task-based visual stimulation and finger tapping experiments elicited activation in primary visual and motor cortices, respectively, using the ZTE sequence, demonstrating proof-of-concept feasibility in this small cohort. Resting-state components with spatial patterns consistent with canonical visual and sensorimotor networks were identified using independent component analysis in the same cohort. Compared to BOLD-EPI, ZTE showed significantly reduced acoustic noise and was largely insensitive to susceptibility-induced signal loss in this feasibility study. While this work represents our initial experience using ZTE for human fMRI at 3T, the presented results will motivate future studies to refine and extend this approach to explore complementary functional contrast mechanisms.

papers.title: Sustained Seizure Freedom After Stereo-Electroencephalography Without Definitive Intervention: Evidence for Network Modulation by Invasive EEG.
papers.authors: Harland TA, Farmer S, Ferrari C, Terry M, Cullen M, Bunch M, Adamo MA.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society
papers.abstract: Summary Stereo-electroencephalography (sEEG) is a diagnostic technique used to localize seizure-onset networks in drug-resistant epilepsy, typically guiding resection, ablation, or neuromodulation. Sustained seizure freedom after diagnostic implantation alone is rarely described. We describe two patients who achieved long-term remission after sEEG monitoring without definitive surgical intervention. A 39-year-old man with posttraumatic right hemispheric epilepsy underwent implantation of 11 depth electrodes, during which no habitual seizures were captured despite medication withdrawal and provocation. After electrode explantation, he discontinued all antiseizure medications and has remained seizure-free for 71 months. A 63-year-old woman with left temporal epilepsy underwent implantation of 12 depth electrodes; monitoring again failed to capture habitual seizures, although abundant mesial temporal interictal discharges were recorded. After explantation, which was complicated by a small tract hemorrhage, she has remained seizure-free for 20 months on stable cenobamate therapy. These cases add to a limited body of evidence suggesting that sEEG implantation may induce microlesional or network-modulatory effects capable of interrupting seizure propagation, analogous to remission reported after intracranial electrode placement in prior series. Recognition of this phenomenon is clinically important. When no habitual seizures are recorded and early postoperative improvement is observed, a period of extended follow-up may be warranted before pursuing resection, ablation, or neuromodulation. Further study is needed to define predictors of remission, clarify underlying mechanisms, and guide patient counseling regarding this uncommon but meaningful effect of invasive EEG.

papers.title: Acute Onset Orolingual Choreoathetosis and Auditory Hallucinations in a Healthy Young Adult Following High Melatonin Dose.
papers.authors: Bain HL, Yanez AM, Bartlett SI.
papers.abstract: Melatonin is considered a safe OTC sleep aid with rarely reported adverse effects despite limited data. We present a case of acute orolingual choreoathetosis and auditory hallucinations following 132 mg ingestion of melatonin in an otherwise healthy, 22-year-old active-duty male in IBOLC training. The patient developed abrupt, predominantly orolingual choreoathetosis and mild auditory hallucinations, 1 hour after waking. Three days earlier, he began taking 24 mg of melatonin nightly for insomnia and ingested 132 mg the night before presentation. He denied alcohol, illicit drug, or other medication use. On ED arrival, he was hemodynamically stable with continuous orolingual choreoathetosis. Initial labs demonstrated mild acute kidney injury and transaminitis. Head CT was unremarkable. MRI head showed a nonspecific left frontal white matter hyperintensity. Lumbar puncture revealed normal protein and WBC, negative culture, and negative oligoclonal bands, though CSF processing difficulties prevented autoimmune panel completion. Neurologic symptoms resolved by the next morning without recurrence, and a subsequent EEG was unremarkable. This case documents a temporal association between high-dose melatonin exposure and acute neurologic symptoms but does not establish melatonin as the cause. The clinical presentation also occurred in the setting of substantial confounders, including sleep deprivation and heat exposure. This observation supports further investigation of uncommon neurologic presentations occurring after high-dose melatonin intake.

papers.title: Predicting IGD treatment outcomes across interventions using a whole-brain functional connectome biomarker.
papers.authors: Wei M, Luo X, Fu J, Li S, Ni H, Liu J, Dong GH.
papers.abstract: Background Although treatment approaches have been explored in internet gaming disorder (IGD), however, little is known about the specific neural activity that is associated with treatment outcomes. This study aims to establish a treatment-sensitive network that reliably predicts treatment outcomes across different interventions for IGD. Methods Resting-state fMRI data were collected from 90 individuals with IGD who received one of three different intervention protocols (mindfulness meditation, approach bias modification, or retrieval-aversive conditioning training). Connectome-based predictive modelling (CPM) was used to build a treatment-sensitive network to predict individual symptom reduction, then validated them on the external dataset. Results The negative (r = 0.401, p <.001) and combined network (r = 0.480, p <.001) can significantly predict a reduction of addiction severity (baseline minus post-test). Specifically, the negative network was primarily centred on the motor, subcortical, and salience networks. The positive network primarily involved cerebellar-related connections. Incorporating these into a combined model significantly improved predictive accuracy, suggesting that cerebellar-related connectivity may contribute to the prediction of intervention-related clinical improvement. Finally, the treatment-sensitive network was validated in a separate data. Conclusions This study established a treatment-sensitive network based on the whole-brain connectome. These findings provide valuable empirical evidence for identifying biomarkers for IGD treatment and advance personalised therapeutic strategies. Clinical trials registration The trial protocol was pre-registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (www.chictr.org.cn; ChiCTR2300077831(MM), ChiCTR2300075869(ApBm), ChiCTR2500095444(R-AC), ChiCTR2400090834(SAE)).

papers.title: Venlafaxine modulates white matter integrity in dorsal and ventral language pathways after subcortical stroke: a longitudinal TBSS study.
papers.authors: Li C, Liu L, Wang L, Zhang W, Liu L, Xie Q, Liu Y.
papers.abstract: Background Subcortical aphasia results from disrupted cortico-subcortical language networks after left-hemispheric infarction. Venlafaxine, an SNRI, may accelerate language recovery, but its effects on white matter plasticity remain unclear. We used diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to assess early venlafaxine effects on dorsal and ventral language pathways in subacute stroke. Methods Thirty-two patients with first-ever left subcortical infarction and mild-to-moderate aphasia were randomized to venlafaxine (n=16; 75 mg/day, day 7-week 4) or control (n=16). DTI was acquired at 30±7 and 90±7 days post-stroke. TBSS compared fractional anisotropy (FA) in language-related tracts using permutation testing with TFCE (corrected p<0.05). . Results At Visit 2, venlafaxine recipients had higher FA in right superior longitudinal fasciculus/arcuate fasciculus (SLF/AF), bilateral inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi (IFOF), and left inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF), but lower FA in left SLF and uncinate fasciculus (UF). At Visit 3, FA increases extended to SLF/AF and UF, yielding bilateral dorsal and ventral enhancement; only right ILF FA decreased. FA changes positively correlated with aphasia quotient, spontaneous language fluency, and picture-naming improvements. . Conclusion Early venlafaxine induces biphasic white matter remodeling: initial contralesional and bilateral ventral enhancement, followed by bilateral integration, suggesting optimized language network reorganization.

papers.title: Striatal network dysfunction underlying speech impairment in early Parkinson's disease.
papers.authors: Rogers CP, Mournet S, Gallea C, Biondetti E, Mangone G, Sambin S, Chougar L, Villain N, Gaurav R, Arnulf I, Habert MO, Petrovska-Delacrétaz D, Corvol JC, Benali H, Vidailhet M, Lehéricy S, Jeancolas L.
papers.abstract: The pathophysiology underlying Parkinson's disease (PD) speech impairments and its potential sex differences remain unclear. We investigated sex-specific alterations in speech and striato-cortical networks in 104 patients with early PD (68M/36F), and 44 healthy controls (23M/21F), using quantitative speech markers and multimodal neuroimaging. Speech features related to prosody, phonation, articulation, fluency, and rhythm, were extracted from voice recordings; striatal dopaminergic loss was quantified using DaT-SPECT, and functional connectivity between striatal and cortical language networks was analyzed with resting-state fMRI. Results showed that PD-related speech impairments were more pronounced in males. Functional connectivity was globally reduced in PD, but female patients exhibited higher caudate-cortical connectivity. In males, speech deficits were associated with both dopaminergic loss and connectivity disruption, whereas in females, only connectivity changes were involved. These findings revealed sex-specific pathophysiological mechanisms in early PD speech disorders, emphasizing the need for sex-stratified approaches in research and clinical practice.

papers.title: Abnormal resting-state EEG microstates correlate with objective sleep parameters in insomnia disorder.
papers.authors: Wu Q, Weng L, Lei X.
papers.abstract: Background Insomnia is a common sleep disorder, and Electroencephalogram (EEG) microstates, which mirror transient cerebral cortical functional activity, are linked to sleep disorder pathophysiology. The microstate characteristics in insomnia patients and correlations with objective sleep parameters remain to be further explored. Method This study enrolled 45 insomnia disorder (ID) patients and 48 healthy controls (HC), collecting awake resting-state EEG for microstate analysis; 27 ID and 13 H C participants additionally completed overnight polysomnography (PSG), and exploratory correlation analyses of microstate and PSG data performed for the ID group. Results Compared with HC, ID patients had markedly shorter duration of microstate A and B, higher occurrence and contribution of microstate C, and reduced duration, occurrence and contribution of microstate D (p < 0.05). ID patients also showed significantly lower transition probabilities of A→D, B→D, D→A and D→B (p < 0.01), and higher probabilities of A→C, B→C, C→A and C→B (p < 0.05). Correlation analyses revealed that in the ID, microstate D occurrence was negatively correlated with rapid eye movement sleep proportion (REM Sleep%, r = -0.427, p = 0.026) and positively correlated with non-rapid eye movement sleep stage 1 proportion (S1%, r = 0.385, p = 0.047). Conclusion ID patients present significant abnormalities in EEG microstates, and the occurrence of microstate D is correlated with objective sleep indicators of PSG. These findings suggest that EEG microstate parameters may reflect abnormalities in the sleep architecture of ID and may provide references for analyzing the cortical hyperarousal mechanism of chronic insomnia, constructing objective assessment schemes, and developing targeted neuroregulation interventions.

papers.title: Temporal interference stimulation for treating Wilson disease: A prospective clinical and functional MRI study.
papers.authors: Cheng N, Wang Y, Du H, Yu G, Han X, Huang Y, Xu C, Qiu B, Dong T.
papers.journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics
papers.abstract: Wilson disease (WD) is an inherited disorder of copper metabolism caused by ATP7B mutations, and persistent neurological deficits, especially dystonia and motor disability, may remain despite standard anti-copper therapy. The putamen is a deep gray-matter nucleus frequently affected by copper deposition in WD and may therefore represent a plausible target for non-invasive neuromodulation. This prospective, single-arm, open-label study evaluated the clinical efficacy and neural mechanisms of right putamen-targeted temporal interference stimulation (TIS) in patients with WD. Twenty-five patients received right putamen-targeted TIS once daily for 10 sessions. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the Unified Wilson's Disease Rating Scale (UWDRS) total score and its neurological, hepatic, and psychiatric subscale scores. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI) was used to evaluate regional homogeneity (ReHo) and seed-based functional connectivity (FC) of the right putamen. Paired tests compared pre- and post-treatment changes, and Spearman correlation analysis examined associations between imaging changes and clinical improvement. After treatment, the UWDRS total score decreased significantly from 59.40 ± 30.54 to 44.12 ± 24.96, with concurrent improvements in neurological, hepatic, and psychiatric subscale scores. The rsfMRI analysis showed increased ReHo in the right putamen and enhanced FC between the right putamen and right Rolandic operculum. After correction for multiple comparisons, greater increases in right putamen ReHo correlated significantly with larger reductions in UWDRS total and neurological scores. In this exploratory study, these preliminary findings suggest that right putamen-targeted TIS may improve clinical symptoms in WD, potentially through enhanced local functional synchronization within the putamen.

papers.title: Attenuated attention engagement and sensorimotor resonance to social events in first-episode adolescent depression: Evidence from EEG oscillations.
papers.authors: Tang E, Zhang S, Qin W, Xu Y, Zheng J, Chen X, Wu R, Zhao H, Fu Y, Zhao C, Song W, Li J, Liu C, Liu Y, Yin J, Huang M, Chen H.
papers.abstract: Background Depressive symptoms may disrupt social brain development during adolescence, resulting in adverse long-term quality of life. Yet, little is known regarding the cognitive and neural changes during the processing of social interactions in adolescents with first-episode depression, particularly from an allocentric perspective. Methods We used electroencephalography (EEG) to assess two neural indicators during the observation of others' interactions, including sensorimotor mu suppression and occipital alpha-band activity, in 22 adolescents with first-episode major depressive disorder (MDD) and 23 healthy counterparts. Participants observed animated motions wherein actions were directed toward animate (human-like) or inanimate (rock) targets, comprising social (giving) and kinematically matched control events (disposing, taking and acquiring). Results Healthy controls (HCs) exhibited stronger central-parietal mu suppression in the lower sub-band during observation of socially interactive giving events than disposing events. In contrast, adolescents with MDD manifested no corresponding difference in mu suppression. Additionally, depressive adolescents demonstrated significantly higher occipital alpha power when viewing social (patient) than non-social (rock) targets, and this alpha power was significantly higher than that observed in HCs. Exploratory correlation analyses revealed that attenuated sensorimotor resonance of social interactions was significantly associated with increased severity of depressive symptoms in the MDD group. Conclusions Adolescents with first-episode depression showed difficulties in efficiently encoding social information and implicitly extracting the social-relational meaning of observed social interactions. These findings critically extend current understanding of neurocognitive mechanisms underlying social cognitive alterations in this population, and provide potential avenues for early screening and targeted interventions of social functioning impairment in adolescence.

papers.title: Therapeutic strategies in vascular cognitive impairment: Insights from the bilateral common carotid artery stenosis mouse model.
papers.authors: Hattori Y, Yamamoto Y, Mun J, Ihara M.
papers.abstract: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) is a major consequence of cerebrovascular disease, but disease-modifying therapies remain limited. Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion is increasingly recognized not simply as reduced cerebral blood flow, but as a sustained disturbance of oxygen delivery, capillary perfusion, neurovascular coupling, blood-brain barrier integrity, glial homeostasis, white matter maintenance, and synaptic network function. The bilateral common carotid artery stenosis (BCAS) mouse model is a central experimental platform for studying hypoperfusion-related VCI, as it exhibits reproducible cerebral blood flow reduction, white matter pathology, gliovascular injury, and cognitive impairment while permitting genetic manipulation, longitudinal imaging, retinal readouts, omics profiling, and therapeutic testing. This review synthesizes therapeutic studies in BCAS model mice across vascular/endothelial and hemodynamic mechanisms, oxidative and ferroptotic stress, ion-water transport, neuronal excitability and synaptic support, remote ischemic conditioning, regenerative and cell-based approaches, and biomarker-driven model refinement. Across these domains, successful interventions frequently converge on interconnected network nodes rather than isolated linear pathways, linking endothelial function, blood-brain barrier stability, redox-lipid balance, astrocytic ion-water regulation, microglial repair states, oligodendrocyte maturation, myelin integrity, and circuit plasticity. However, methodological heterogeneity concerning surgery, animal characteristics, behavioral testing, treatment timing, and outcome selection restricts translation. Future BCAS studies should prespecify treatment windows, particularly delayed-treatment paradigms initiated after objectively documented hypoperfusion, white matter injury, or cognitive impairment. Studies should also incorporate systemic dose-response assessments, biomarker-guided treatment stratification, clinically relevant comorbidities, and rational combination therapies. Such approaches may convert mechanistic insights from chronic hypoperfusion models into clinically credible therapeutic strategies for VCI.

papers.title: Multimodal visual question answering in neuro-oncology and gastroenterology: A domain-specific feasibility study.
papers.authors: Shehzad F, Mennella C, Fujita H, Esposito M, Minutolo A.
papers.abstract: Medical Visual Question Answering (Med-VQA) requires models to combine image content with the clinical intent expressed by a question, yet domain-specific resources and controlled analyses of modality use remain limited. This study introduces two expert-validated Med-VQA datasets for brain tumor MRI and gastrointestinal endoscopy and evaluates a dual-stream architecture that combines BERT question representations and ViT image features through Modular Co-Attention on Attention (MCAoA). The model formulates answer prediction as closed-vocabulary classification and is assessed through overall, question-type, disease-class, baseline, ablation, and usability analyses. The complete fine-tuned model with product fusion achieved accuracies of 80.86% (WUPS 81.32%) on the brain tumor dataset and 75.95% (WUPS 76.77%) on the gastrointestinal dataset. It exceeded the question-only and image-only baselines by 23.86 and 43.16 percentage points, respectively, on brain tumor MRI, and by 18.54 and 35.92 percentage points on gastrointestinal endoscopy. Product fusion provided a small but consistent advantage over concatenation, while end-to-end encoder fine-tuning improved accuracy over frozen encoders on both datasets. A complementary study with clinical experts indicated positive perceived usability in a controlled setting. These findings show that performance cannot be reproduced from either modality alone and support the complementary use of image and question information. However, the ablations establish modality-level dependence rather than spatially correct anatomical grounding, which requires targeted counterfactual and attribution-based evaluation.

papers.title: Reading Intention Where There Is None: Neurobehavioral Correlates of Intention Attribution of Morally Ambiguous Scenarios in Borderline Personality Disorder.
papers.authors: Sen B, Giannini G, Kulakova E, Lipka R, Villringer A, Wingenfeld K.
papers.journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Background Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterized by altered social cognition, including a tendency to bias intention attribution in ambiguous situations. However, the neurobehavioral mechanisms underlying this tendency remain poorly understood. Here, we examined whether intention attribution is disturbed in BPD and reflected in behavioral bias and altered neural processing of morally ambiguous social information. Methods A total of 71 individuals with BPD (55 female, 16 male) and 72 healthy controls (56 female, 16 male) were included. Participants viewed harm-based scenarios depicting intentional and accidental actions while electroencephalography was recorded. Behavioral responses and event-related potentials were analyzed exploratorily to examine group differences in intention attribution and neural differentiation. Results Behaviorally, individuals with BPD were more likely to misinterpret accidental harm as intentional, whereas responses to intentional harms did not differ between groups. Mass-univariate event-related potential analyses revealed group differences in early frontocentral (approximately 200-250 ms) and later centroparietal (734-789 ms) time windows. Healthy controls showed greater accidental-intentional differentiation in the early windows, whereas individuals with BPD exhibited reduced neural differentiation. In contrast, the later effect showed greater differentiation in the BPD group. Conclusions These condition-specific findings indicate a selective intention-attribution bias in BPD alongside altered neural differentiation of ambiguous social information at earlier and later time points. More broadly, social judgment disturbances in BPD may be particularly evident when harmful outcomes conflict with innocent intentions, rather than reflecting generalized response differences.

papers.title: Genomic structural equation modeling of impulsivity and risk-taking traits reveals three latent factors associated with brain structure and development.
papers.authors: Shishikura M, Liu L, Yu E, Zhu R, Vilar-Ribó L, Cupertino RB, Palmer AA, Sanchez-Roige S, Vainik U, Morys F, Gan-Or Z, Misic B, Dagher A.
papers.journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Background Impulsivity is a multifaceted transdiagnostic trait that emerges in childhood. Research has identified genetic loci and brain systems associated with different facets of impulsivity and risk-taking. However, how these genetic underpinnings overlap across different facets, and how they are associated with brain development during childhood remain unknown. Methods Using genomic structural equation modeling on 17 impulsivity and risk-taking traits, we identified latent factors capturing underlying genetic architecture. We then calculated polygenic scores for these factors using Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study data (N = 4,142) and examined their associations with brain structure, development, and behavior in children aged 9-14 years. Finally, we tested whether socioeconomic status modulated the associations between latent polygenic scores and brain structures. Results We identified three distinct genetic latent factors, which we label lack of self-control, reward drive, and sensation seeking. In children, polygenic scores for the three factors showed associations with partly differentiated brain patterns: lack of self-control associated with reduced prefrontal cortical thickness, reward drive with increased subcortical cellular density, and sensation seeking with increased cortical surface area and white matter integrity. Longitudinally, lack of self-control predicted variation in white matter development. We found little evidence that socioeconomic factors modulated associations between polygenic scores and brain structure. Conclusions Using genome-wide association study data of European genetic ancestry samples, we identified three genetically distinct dimensions of impulsivity and risk-taking. These genetic predispositions showed association with brain structure as early as ages 9-10, with limited evidence that these associations varied across socioeconomic context.

papers.title: Excitation-Inhibition Balance and Fronto-Limbic Connectivity Distinguish TMS Treatment Outcomes in Refractory Depression.
papers.authors: Momi D, Wang Z, Oveisi MP, Kadak K, Bastiaens SP, Lissemore JI, Noda Y, Downar J, Rodriguez FV, Strafella R, Daskalakis ZJ, Zrenner C, Zomorrodi R, Rolle CE, Saggar M, Williams N, Keller CJ, Blumberger DM, Voineskos D, Griffiths JD.
papers.abstract: Background Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is effective for treatment-resistant depression, but outcomes remain variable. The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying response remain poorly understood, limiting precision neuromodulation. Methods We combined transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and connectome-based Jansen-Rit neural mass modeling to investigate the mechanistic basis of treatment efficacy in 90 patients with treatment-resistant depression. Individualized whole-brain models were fitted to pre- and post-iTBS TMS-evoked potentials, yielding subject-specific estimates of synaptic connectivity, excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance, and cortical dynamics. Brain states were defined by singular value decomposition of the model's population activity, and partial least squares analysis with nested cross-validation identified the brain-state pattern distinguishing responders from non-responders. Results We identified two neurophysiological signatures associated with treatment response. First, responders showed greater post-treatment reductions in 3-10 Hz oscillatory power, driven by shifts in E/I balance toward greater inhibitory control through reduced excitatory drive and increased inhibitory-to-pyramidal connectivity. Second, a pre-treatment brain state characterized by opposite-polarity dynamics between subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) and left DLPFC distinguished responders from non-responders, consistent with prior fMRI findings on frontolimbic anticorrelation. Neural trajectory analysis further revealed greater dynamical reorganization and increased attractor stability in responders following treatment. Conclusions These findings provide a neurophysiologically-informed framework linking iTBS treatment efficacy to specific changes in cortical E/I balance and frontolimbic circuit dynamics, pointing toward candidate markers that, with subject-specific structural connectivity and independent validation, may inform personalized neuromodulation approaches in treatment-resistant depression.

papers.title: Individual susceptibility to disgust modulates neural and systemic immune responses to virtual infections.
papers.authors: Born M, Akselrod M, Trabanelli S, Girondini M, Papadopoulou G, Vanoni G, Cornu A, Bertoni T, Jandus C, Serino A.
papers.abstract: Disgust is a key psychological mechanism for avoiding pathogen exposure and constitutes a central component of the behavioral immune system. While disgust is thought to reduce infection risk through avoidance, it remains unclear how individual differences in disgust sensitivity shape downstream neuroimmune responses to perceived pathogen threats. Here, we show that lower disgust sensitivity is associated with stronger activation of type 1 innate lymphoid cells during exposure to infectious, compared with neutral, avatars in virtual reality. Disgust sensitivity further correlated with circulating signaling factors involved in immune regulation, including hormones related to the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, and eicosanoids. Linear models incorporating disgust sensitivity and threat exposure predicted these signaling factors, which in turn enabled accurate prediction of type 1 innate lymphoid cells responses using a pretrained neural network. Recreating this putative pathway, we were able to predict immune responses solely by disgust scores. Additionally, resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed that exposure to infectious avatars altered hypothalamic connectivity with brain regions involved in visual processing, peripersonal space representation, and social cognition, and these effects were modulated by individual disgust sensitivity. Together, these findings suggest that disgust sensitivity modulates multiple levels of the neuroimmune response to perceived pathogen threats. Across two complementary experiments, our results are consistent with a model linking sensory threat detection, hypothalamic signaling, and systemic immune activation. Rather than uniformly amplifying immune responses, higher disgust sensitivity appears to bias pathogen defense toward neural processing, whereas lower disgust sensitivity is associated with stronger physiological immune activation.

papers.title: Toddler EEG power reflects behavioral social engagement state during naturalistic parent-child interaction.
papers.authors: Manning BL, Roberts MY, Wakschlag LS, Norton ES.
papers.abstract: Social engagement is a critical process for children's language and social development and is altered in neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism. Although previous EEG studies have investigated correlates of children's social development in closely controlled experimental studies, few studies have examined how the brain reflects meaningful behavioral states, such as social engagement, within naturalistic parent-child interaction. This study collected EEG from typically developing toddlers of varying language ability and their parent (n = 49, 24-44 months) during the Social EEG paradigm; dyads completed contexts of dyadic interaction (book reading and puzzle play) and baseline (movie watching) during EEG recording. Videos of the interaction session were coded for social engagement using moment-by-moment behavioral coding and applied to the EEG data. As predicted, child EEG alpha power decreased (p < .001) and theta power increased (p = .01) during social engagement relative to baseline movie engagement. Further, the same pattern was replicated in an independent sample (n = 24, 25-47 months) including children diagnosed with autism, who showed the same pattern of power. These results demonstrate for the first time that EEG power is associated with naturally occurring moments of parent-child social engagement across a range of social/linguistic abilities and ages. This opens avenues for study of more naturalistic and meaningful developmental constructs.

papers.title: Revisiting cortical language and praxis representations in males and females.
papers.authors: Kanert J, Króliczak G.
papers.abstract: Although the past few decades have seen numerous researchers questioning the nature of sex differences in cognition, the answers remain surprisingly unclear. For example, there is evidence against the long-standing hypothesis that women have more bilateral language representation than men. Indeed, the nature and extent of sex differences in language representation remain largely controversial. So are potential sex differences in praxis representation. In this study, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data obtained from 64 females and 61 males during word generation and tool use pantomime were analyzed. The majority of participants had typically organized functions. Whole-brain activity maps and laterality indices (LIs) from regions of interest (ROIs) were examined, using both voxel count and signal intensity. The fMRI results for the language task indicated significantly different activity only for a small region within the female's left occipital cortex. Additional exploratory statistical analysis revealed some, but weak evidence for significant sex difference in the lateralization of the fusiform gyrus. Meanwhile, the statistical analysis of LIs obtained during the praxis task, as well as the whole-brain activity contrasts suggested no sex differences in praxis representation. Moreover, the results from both tasks did not differ depending on the LI calculation method, despite voxel-count based LIs being consistently larger than those based on signal intensity. In conclusion, this study provides new insights into sex differences in cognitive functions, challenging the long-standing assumptions about their nature and extent.

papers.title: From Contrasts to Representations: Rethinking fMRI Approaches for Cortico-Cerebellar Networks.
papers.authors: Irving CN, King M, LeBel A.
papers.abstract: The relationship between the cerebellum and cerebrum remains poorly understood in the neuroimaging literature, despite decades of functional magnetic resonance (fMRI) research. In this opinion article, we argue that this gap reflects fundamental methodological constraints rather than merely a lack of scientific interest. We first discuss challenges in acquiring fMRI data and analysis, with an emphasis on the cerebellum. We then critically evaluate the most common analysis approaches including functional connectivity, univariate contrasts, multivariate pattern analysis, and encoding models, examining the contributions and limitations of each to identify and quantify cortico-cerebellar networks. Through the lens of language processing, we briefly review how these approaches have been applied to characterize cortico-cerebellar networks underlying cognitive function. We conclude by proposing that encoding model frameworks, combined with ecologically valid naturalistic paradigms, offer advantages that can help resolve longstanding debates about cortico-cerebellar network function and organization.

papers.title: Reduced structural connectivity in age-related hearing loss aligns with the sensory deprivation theory.
papers.authors: Boons JHC, De Luca A, Dingemanse G, Vinke EJ, Kremer B, Vernooij MW, Goedegebure A.
papers.abstract: Age-related hearing loss (ARHL) may contribute to cognitive decline through structural degeneration and brain reorganization, as posited by the sensory deprivation theory. These processes can be characterized by topological changes, such as strengthening and weakening of structural connections between brain regions. Stronger connections are more relevant to reorganization, as reorganization is thought to support speech processing by recruiting additional brain networks as a compensatory mechanism. We investigated connectivity changes associated with ARHL to improve the understanding of the sensory deprivation theory. Similar to the lateralization of speech processing, we hypothesized that structural reorganization associated with ARHL would be most evident in the left hemisphere. We assessed whole-brain structural connectivity using 1.5 Tesla diffusion-weighted MRI and structural T1 images in 2402 participants (median age = 66.1 years, females = 54.7%) from the population-based Rotterdam Study. Pure-tone audiometry was performed, and pure-tone averages (PTAs), for different frequency ranges including PTAlow (250-1000 Hz) and PTAall (250-8000 Hz), were determined for the better-hearing ear to reflect ARHL. ARHL was primarily associated with weaker connections involving frontal and subcortical gray matter regions. Contrary to our hypothesis, no lateralization in the connectivity alterations was observed. PTAlow and PTAall yielded the strongest associations, likely driven by low-frequency hearing thresholds. Adjusting for cardiovascular risk factors attenuated associations, especially for PTAlow . In conclusion, the findings contradict the hypothesized compensatory structural reorganization expected from the neural effects of sensory deprivation. While the observed weaker connectivity aligns with the sensory deprivation theory, the results also suggest cardiovascular health as a common risk factor.

papers.title: Leveraging traditional and advanced machine learning for comprehensive oncology data integration and outcome prediction.
papers.authors: Hey G, Del Sesto M, Still M, Patel G, Crlenjak N, Dagra A, Wu Y, Guo Y, Ghiaseddin AP.
papers.abstract: Background Outcome prediction in neuro-oncology remains challenging due to heterogeneity in tumor biology, imaging characteristics, treatment response, and patient-specific clinical factors. Although molecular databases have advanced understanding of brain tumor biology, many datasets lack broader data necessary for generalizable predictive modeling.
