We hypothesized that greater stenosis or remodeling is associated with impaired hemodynamics, increased WMH burden, and poorer cognition.MethodsCross-sectional study of 452 memory clinic patients (median age 74 [IQR 68-78], 53% female) who underwent 3T MRI with time-of-flight MRA and pseudo-continuous ASL. Automated quantification derived global stenosis and brain arterial remodeling (BAR) scores. CBF and spatial coefficient of variation (sCoV) assessed hemodynamics; WMH volume from FLAIR; cognition from a validated neuropsychological battery. Structural equation modelling (SEM) evaluated associations, adjusting for demographics and cardiovascular risk factors.ResultsHigher sCoV was associated with higher BAR (β = 0.14, 95% CI:0.06-0.23). WMH was associated with stenosis (β = 0.20, CI:0.12-0.28) and BAR (β = 0.07, CI:0.001-0.140). Lower CBF (β = -0.26, CI:-0.36 to -0.15) and higher sCoV (β = 0.27, CI:0.17-0.36) were associated with greater WMH burden. Higher BAR was associated with better global cognition (β = 0.07, CI:0.00-0.14). SEM indicated indirect associations with cognition via WMH and CBF.ConclusionsVascular remodeling and stenosis are associated with cerebral hemodynamics, WMH, and cognition, with CBF and WMH as potential mediators, underscoring the importance of vascular health in Alzheimer's disease. These direct and indirect associations are not mutually exclusive: higher BAR was associated with better cognition directly, while also relating to poorer cognition indirectly through greater WMH burden and perfusion heterogeneity.

papers.title: Neuroanatomical correlates of the CDT-14: A voxel-based morphometry study exploring incremental information beyond conventional clock drawing scores.
papers.authors: Sawada Y, Satoh T, Saba H, Kato Y, Kuwada T, Shima S, Murakami K, Sasaki M, Abe Y, Harano K.
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe Clock Drawing Test (CDT) is widely used for cognitive screening but lacks unified scoring standards and neuroanatomical validation.ObjectiveWe examined the neuroanatomical correlates and incremental validity beyond conventional CDT scoring of CDT-14, a psychometrically refined 14-item system with three subfactors (Circle, Numbering, and Hand), using voxel-based morphometry (VBM).MethodsWe analyzed 985 participants from a heterogeneous memory-clinic cohort. Whole-brain VBM compared CDT-14 total and subfactor scores with three conventional scoring systems. Models adjusted for age, sex, education level, and total intracranial volume. Incremental validity was assessed after controlling for a principal-component-derived conventional composite score, with sensitivity analyses adjusting for white matter lesion volume (WMLV).ResultsCDT-14 was associated with gray matter volume (GMV) in distributed clock-drawing regions, including the right anterior hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, bilateral precuneus, and prefrontal regions. Primary incremental analyses identified additional associations in bilateral ventral temporal, right occipito-temporal, and dorsal anterior cingulate regions after accounting for conventional CDT performance. These associations were attenuated after WMLV adjustment, and no clusters survived FWE correction in the WMLV-adjusted incremental model. Subfactor analyses suggested partially distinct but overlapping patterns involving frontostriatal and cingulate regions for Circle, thalamic and limbic-related regions for Numbering, and hippocampal, parietal, and occipital regions for Hand.ConclusionsCDT-14 showed cross-sectional GMV associations beyond conventional scoring in primary analyses. However, the incremental associations were not robust to WMLV adjustment at the FWE-corrected threshold and should be interpreted cautiously. Longitudinal, biomarker-informed, and externally validated studies are needed to establish predictive validity, disease specificity, and clinical utility.

papers.title: Acculturation is associated with cognitive performance but not changes in cognition among middle-aged and older Hispanic/Latino adults: Findings from the HCHS/SOL and SOL-INCA.
papers.authors: Stickel AM, Tarraf W, Kuwayama S, Xue Y, Breton J, Medina LD, Morlett Paredes A, Gallo LC, Cai J, Lamar M, Pirzada A, Daviglus ML, Isasi CR, Kaplan R, Wassertheil-Smoller S, González HM.
papers.abstract: BackgroundHispanic/Latino adults are not a monolithic group. Individuals vary in a range of factors, including levels of acculturation (adoption of Anglo-American culture).ObjectiveTo investigate the relationships between acculturation with cognition, changes in cognition, and risk for mild cognitive impairment (MCI).MethodsWe included Hispanic/Latino adults (unweighted n = 5976) from the Study of Latinos - Investigation of Neurocognitive Aging (SOL-INCA), a Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos ancillary study. Three acculturation measures were collected at Visit 1 (Short Acculturation Scale for Hispanics (SASH) - Social and Language subscales and the MESA Acculturation score). Participants were grouped into quartiles per measure with higher scores reflecting greater acculturation. Outcomes included cognition and MCI prevalence 7-years after Visit 1 and 7-year change in cognition from Visit 1 to 2. Survey linear regressions were performed to model the associations between acculturation measures and cognitive outcomes, controlling for sociodemographic factors.ResultsThe lowest SASH Social and Language acculturation groups had lower global cognition scores than all other groups (all p -values<0.01). The lowest MESA Acculturation score group had lower global cognition scores relative to those in the highest quartile (b = 0.10; SE = 0.04; p < 0.05). However, there were no acculturation differences in cognitive change or MCI.ConclusionsThough low acculturation was associated with lower cognitive performance, it does not seem to be related to increased risk for cognitive decline or pathological cognitive aging (i.e., prevalent MCI).

papers.title: Melatonin as a potential biomarker for subclinical epileptiform activity in Alzheimer's disease: An exploratory study.
papers.authors: Nous A, Seynaeve L, Feys O, Wens V, De Tiège X, Van Mierlo P, Baroumand AG, Mangelschots S, Michiels V, De Witte S, Wittens MMJ, Bjerke M, Ceyssens S, Gordijn M, De Weerdt S, Van Eekchaut A, Nagels G, Smolders I, Engelborghs S.
papers.abstract: BackgroundMelatonin levels are altered in elderly people and might become even more disrupted in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients. An inverse correlation between cerebrospinal fluid melatonin levels and severity of AD neuropathology has been described. There is an increased prevalence of subclinical epileptiform activity (SEA) in AD. Baseline melatonin levels have been described to be lower in epilepsy patients as compared to controls, suggesting antiepileptic effects.ObjectiveTo compare melatonin levels between AD participants and controls, to evaluate melatonin's potential use as biomarker for disease stage in AD and to evaluate the link between melatonin levels and SEA in AD.MethodsAD subjects (n = 20) and healthy volunteers (n = 8) underwent a 24-h-electro-encephalography (EEG), during which multiple blood and saliva samples were taken. Melatonin levels were analysed using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (plasma) and radioimmunoassay (saliva). A subset of participants underwent 50-min resting magnetoencephalography and/or high-density-EEG to detect SEA.ResultsPlasma melatonin levels were significantly lower in AD as compared to controls at 23:00PM. Melatonin levels were similar between patients with AD dementia, MCI due to AD and preclinical AD subjects. Plasma and saliva melatonin levels at 04:00AM and 01:00AM, respectively, were significantly higher in AD participants with SEA as compared to those without.ConclusionsNight-time melatonin levels might serve as a potential biomarker to identify AD patients at risk for SEA, based on exploratory findings. Whether this increase could be a compensatory feedback mechanism against SEA or whether melatonin rather has pro-epileptic effects, remains to be elucidated by further research.

papers.title: Multimodal MRI insights into glymphatic clearance and blood-brain barrier integrity in healthy aging.
papers.authors: Bhattarai A, Zhu YD, Albuhwailah B, Maillard P, DeCarli C, Fan AP.
papers.abstract: Aging is associated with impaired CSF clearance in preclinical models, but its impact on blood-brain barrier (BBB) health and glymphatic function in humans remains unclear. The BBB and glymphatic functions are complementary and may partially overlap, yet their interaction is yet to be fully elucidated. In this study, we aimed to compare BBB integrity, extracellular free water, and glymphatic function between healthy young and older adults, and to examine mechanistic relationships among these measures using multimodal MRI techniques. 30 healthy participants with no known neurological or psychiatric disorders, including 12 younger (26 ± 3 years) and 18 older individuals (75 ± 7 years), underwent MRI scans on a 3T Siemens Prisma scanner. Multimodal MRI techniques were used, including diffusion-prepared arterial spin labeling to measure the water exchange rate (Kw) across the blood-brain barrier (BBB); free water (FW) imaging to quantify extracellular free water in white matter; and diffusion tensor imaging along perivascular spaces (DTI-ALPS) to assess glymphatic function. These measures were compared between younger and older individuals. Mediation analysis was performed to assess the mechanistic relationship between BBB integrity and glymphatic function and to test whether this relationship was mediated by free water. Older individuals showed reduced whole-brain Kw (p = 0.021), increased white matter FW (p = 0.002), and reduced DTI-ALPS (p < 0.001) compared to younger adults. Kw was positively associated with DTI-ALPS (β = 0.402 × 10-2 , p = 0.022) and negatively associated with FW (β = -0.676 × 10-3 , p = 0.008). DTI-ALPS was negatively associated with FW (β = -3.487, p = 0.001). Significantly reduced Kw was also observed in the cortical grey matter of older adults. Reduced Kw may reflect impaired BBB function, while reduced DTI-ALPS and increased FW indicate impaired glymphatic clearance. FW mediated the relationship between Kw and DTI-ALPS (95% CI [0.00014, 0.00404], p = 0.035), suggesting a potential mechanistic link between BBB function, extracellular water content, and glymphatic clearance efficiency. Overall, this study provides novel multimodal MRI insights into BBB and glymphatic alterations in healthy aging and may inform the development of MRI biomarkers to preserve cognitive health.

papers.title: Refractory Status Epilepticus Following Erroneous Intrathecal Injection of Tranexamic Acid: A Case Report and Long-Term Follow-Up and Narrative Review.
papers.authors: Yousfi H, Nobile L, Gaspard N, Taccone F.
papers.abstract: Introduction Accidental intrathecal injection of tranexamic acid (TXA) is a rare but catastrophic preventable adverse event associated with high mortality and severe neurological consequences. It represents a major neurological emergency that requires immediate specialized management. Case presentation A 32-year-old man erroneously received an intrathecal injection of 300 mg of TXA instead of bupivacaine during a saphenous vein stripping procedure. He rapidly developed refractory myoclonic status epilepticus, sympathetic hyperactivity, and rhabdomyolysis. Management included multiple antiseizure medications, continuous EEG-guided sedation, and targeted use of neuromuscular blockade. The patient recovered without immediate neurological deficit but developed persistent cognitive impairment and posttraumatic stress disorder at follow-up. Conclusions This case highlights the severe neurotoxicity of intrathecal TXA and the importance of early and aggressive intensive care management. It also underscores the need for long-term multidisciplinary follow-up for the assessment of anesthetic procedure-related complications.

papers.title: Topographical Patterns of Slow Wave Activity in Sleep Talking: An Exploratory Polysomnographic Investigation.
papers.authors: Pellegrini E, Camaioni M, Mangiaruga A, Pumo D, Alfonsi V, Annarumma L, Scarpelli S, Sanguineti C, Castelnovo A, De Gennaro L, D'Agostino A, Gorgoni M.
papers.abstract: Sleep talking (ST) is a parasomnia characterized by the utterance of unaware linguistic activations during sleep. Electrophysiological evidence is scarce, and it remains unclear whether local electroencephalographic (EEG) alterations characterize the sleep of STs outside of parasomnia episodes. Findings from NREM parasomnias suggest that local slow-wave activity (SWA) abnormalities may characterize a full night's sleep beyond behavioural manifestations. Accordingly, this study investigates SWA topography and the spatial distribution of the single SWA bins across sleep stages in a group of 12 young STs compared to 10 healthy controls (HCs) matched for sex and age, who underwent overnight laboratory polysomnographic recordings. The relationship between SWA pattern and parasomnia frequency was explored, and the overnight decline in SWA was examined to assess the potential impact of homeostatic processes. Our findings point to a peculiar SWA pattern characterized by a substantially stable central increase across sleep stages and a frontopolar decrease primarily in N2 sleep, suggesting a local and frequency-specific (≥ 1 Hz) SWA regulation in STs that may interact with homeostatic processes. These results provide new insights into the sleep electrophysiology of STs and shed light on trait-like regional alterations in SWA that may facilitate parasomnia events. Our findings align with the concept of local sleep, which posits that distinct cortical regions may simultaneously exhibit diverse functional states. In this view, different parasomnias may be characterized by specific SWA topographical patterns reflecting the peculiar behaviours enacted during sleep.

papers.title: Cross-Subject Localization of Epileptogenic Zone for Drug-Resistant Epilepsy Based on the Causal Brain Network.
papers.authors: Wang Y, Kong W, Liu Y, Shi Z, Li Q, Wang T, Chen W, Hu B.
papers.abstract: Objective While neurosurgical treatment is the primary intervention for Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) patients, its success rate is limited to approximately 60%. Precise localization of epileptogenic zone (EZ) is a critical factor for surgical success. This study aims to achieve cross-subject localization of the EZ in DRE patients using causal brain network features extracted from stereotactic electroencephalography (SEEG). Methods We collected SEEG recordings from 12 DRE patients who achieved complete seizure freedom (Engel Class I). The causal coupling algorithm, full convergent cross mapping (FCCM), was applied to both ictal and interictal states to extract causal brain network features from SEEG recordings. We fed these features into multiple machine learning models to achieve automated identification of EZ within a leave-one-patient-out cross-validation framework. Under a unified evaluation protocol, FCCM was compared with directed information, frequency-domain convergent cross mapping (FD CCM),high-frequencyoscillation-based methods, source-sink con nectivity, and SEEGformer. Results At the individual level, the Mann-Whitney U test demonstrated that the raw FCCM values sig nificantly differentiated the EZ from the non-epileptogenic zones (NEZ) in 83.3% (10/12) of patients during the ictal state and in all patients (12/12) during the interictal state (p < 0.001). Per mutational multivariate analysis of variance on the 8 dimensional statistical features revealed significant global network variations in 83.3% (10/12) of ictal and 91.7% (11/12) of interictal states (p < 0.001). The combined model, which integrated both ictal and interictal features using the logistic regression classifier, achieved the best performance among all evaluated methods This approach achieved the highest accuracy (0.83 ± 0.10), recall (0.87 ± 0.09), and F1-score (0.80 ± 0.12), while the second-best baseline (FD CCM) yielded an accuracy of 0.79 ± 0.15, a recall of 0.81 ± 0.20, and an F1-score of 0.75±0.18. These results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Conclusion Causal brain network features extracted by FCCM are robust biomarkers for localizing the EZ. Significance This study could support the development of more personalized treatment strategies for DRE patients. It is expected to promote the development of precision medicine for DRE.

papers.title: A Structured Framework for Translation of the ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology Into Spanish.
papers.authors: Rubinos C, San-Juan D, Alva-Diaz C, Beato M, Bender Del Busto JE, Balugo Bengoechea P, Bermudez R S, Bogantes S, Calle-Lopez Y, Cibils L, Contreras G, Cordero JC, Fernandez V, Florentín C, Galvez HH, Gaona I, Del Carmen Garcia M, Garofalo Gomez N, Gonzalez R, Gutierrez A, Hernandez L, Legnani M, Lizcano A, Magos D, Malpartida N, Mateos JA, Mendoza L, Milan A, Montenegro Lopez R, Martin Palomeque G, Paredes-Aragon E, Perassolo M, Ramirez E, Ramos A, Rivas V, Sanchez Ortiz N, Servin O, Silva-Soto S, Su H, Thompson A, Thonon V, Ulate-Campos A, Uribe-San-Martin R, Vergara JP, Vides-Rosales M, Viñan Vazquez I, Zavala-Reina ÁA, Daily J, Grant J, Frasso R, Fernandez A, Bruzzone MJ, Consorcio Hispano de Monitoreo Electroencefalográfico.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society
papers.abstract: Purpose The American Clinical Neurophysiology Society (ACNS) Critical Care EEG Terminology provides standardized language for describing electroencephalographic (EEG) patterns in critically ill patients but has not been formally translated into Spanish. We aimed to develop a consensus-based Spanish translation of the ACNS Critical Care EEG Terminology using a multi-phase methodology involving physicians from Spanish-speaking countries. Methods This qualitative study aimed to establish a standardized Spanish ACNS Critical Care EEG terminology through a three-phase process: Phase 1: Initial iterative translation by 14 Spanish-speaking physicians working in subgroups. Discrepancies were documented for further discussion. Phase 2: Focus groups with specialists practicing in Spanish-speaking countries, guided by qualitative research experts. Sessions explored terminology preferences, implementation challenges, and regional variations. Phase 3: Qualitative analysis and final consensus using a modified Delphi methodology. Ranked choice voting analysis to achieve ≥75% consensus was used and when needed, a two-option runoff determined the final selected term. Results Forty-five physicians from all Spanish-speaking countries except Nicaragua participated in 10 focus groups to review 25 terms. Seven terms generated two possible Spanish translations, four generated three, five generated four, and nine generated five. A consensus-based Spanish terminology was established, prioritizing semantic fidelity to the ACNS terminology while also accounting for terms already in wide regional use. Examples of final consensus terms included: Generalized Periodic Discharges → Descargas Periódicas Generalizadas (98%, Round 1); Lateralized Rhythmic Delta Activity → Actividad Delta Rítmica Lateralizada (100%, round 1); and Sharp Wave → Onda Aguda (82%, round 1). The outdated term periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges remained widely used because of familiarity among intensivists. Conclusions This effort provides the first structured Spanish adaptation of the ACNS Critical Care EEG terminology. The resulting lexicon reflects linguistic diversity across regions and supports consistent communication, training, research, and broader adoption of evidence-based continuous EEG practices.

papers.title: Correlation of blood biomarkers with microstructural brain injury in survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
papers.authors: Laaksonen MV, Posti JP, Hollmén CC, Blennow K, Zetterberg H, Rinne JK, Virtanen SM, Saunavaara JP, Parkkola RK, Laitio RM, Arola OJ, Hynninen MS, Ylikoski EK, Martola JA, Tiainen MS, Roine RO, Scheinin H, Maze M, Roine T, Vahlberg T, Laitio TT, Xe-HYPOTHECA Working Group, Xe-HYPOTHECA Working Group .
papers.abstract: In-hospital mortality among resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients remains high. Identifying patients who will benefit from intensive care while avoiding prolonged, potentially unnecessary treatments is essential. Blood-based biomarkers provide a novel method for evaluating brain injury. The ability of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), neuron-specific enolase (NSE) and total-tau (t-tau) to measure white and grey matter injury is unestablished in comatose OHCA survivors treated with targeted temperature management (TTM) or xenon combined with TTM. We examined correlations between the biomarkers and white and grey matter injury assessed with diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). This was a randomized, single-blind, phase 2 clinical drug trial involving two multipurpose intensive care units in Finland. It was conducted between August 2009 and March 2015. One hundred and ten comatose OHCA patients aged 24 to 76 years were randomly assigned to either inhaled xenon treatment combined with 24-h TTM (33°C) (n = 55, xenon group) or TTM alone (n = 55, control group). MRI data were available from 96 patients, with a median imaging time of 53 h (interquartile range, 47-64 h) after OHCA. Biomarker data were obtained from 105 patients. In the control group of 48 patients, after adjusting for age, sex and site, a disruption of white matter microintegrity as measured by decreased fractional anisotropy (FA) of DTI, the primary endpoint of the trial, showed a significant negative correlation with NfL at 24, 48 and 72 h (ρ = -0.28 to -0.37; P < 0.05), NSE at 48 and 72 h (ρ = -0.30 to -0.35; P < 0.05) and t-tau only at 72 h (ρ = -0.30; P < 0.05). In the xenon group (n = 48), these correlations were absent at all timepoints. The NfL-FA partial correlations showed progressive divergence between the xenon and control groups, with a statistically significant between-group difference observed at 72 h (ρ = -0.37 versus ρ = 0.14; P = 0.016). Cortical or basal ganglia grey matter mean diffusivity did not have a consistent correlation with biomarker levels at different time points. No statistically significant differences were found between the xenon and control groups in the adjusted geometric mean levels of GFAP, NfL, NSE or t-tau at various time points following OHCA. In conclusion, NfL correlated with FA in controls but not in the xenon group. This between-group difference reached significance at 72 h, suggesting that xenon may modify the relationship between axonal injury and white matter microstructure after OHCA.

papers.title: Lateral habenula hyperactivity and network dysfunction underpin stress-induced depressive-like behaviors in mice.
papers.authors: Li Y, Ning W.
papers.abstract: Objective The lateral habenula (LHb) is a critical hub for encoding aversive signals and regulating negative motivation in depression, yet the systemic alterations in functional connectivity and topological architecture of LHb-centered whole-brain networks induced by chronic stress remain unclear. Methods This study characterized LHb-associated network changes in chronic social defeat stress (CSDS)-induced depressive-like male mice using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging, including fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF), static/dynamic functional connectivity (sFC/dFC) and graph theory analysis, combined with a battery of behavioral assessments. Results CSDS-susceptible mice exhibited typical depressive phenotypes (social avoidance, anhedonia, behavioral despair), accompanied by elevated spontaneous neuronal activity in the LHb, robust hyperconnectivity between the LHb and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, and significantly reduced dFC variability between the LHb and subcortical regions (hippocampus, hypothalamus, midbrain). Graph theory analysis further revealed a disrupted small-world topology of the LHb-centered network, with decreased global/local efficiency, reduced clustering coefficient and increased characteristic path length. Conclusions Our findings reveal that chronic stress exposure is associated with LHb hyperactivity and widespread fronto-limbic and subcortical network remodeling. The functional and topological LHb signatures identified herein may serve as candidate biomarkers indicating stress susceptibility. This study offers multi-layered interpretative clues for network-level alterations linked to stress-associated depressive manifestations, and identifies the LHb connectome as a promising circuit candidate for follow-up targeted interventional research of mood disorders.

papers.title: Neuropsychological assessment in functional cognitive disorder: a scoping review.
papers.authors: Mammì A, Reuber M, Pascarella A, Abelardo D, Cutellé R, Bulgari A, Ferlazzo E, Gasparini S.
papers.abstract: Background Functional cognitive disorder (FCD) involves potentially reversible cognitive complaints characterized by internal inconsistency, where subjective cognitive difficulties exceed or are incompatible with observed performance and cannot be explained by other neurological or psychiatric disorders. Although some patients perform below expected levels on formal tests, the role of neuropsychological assessment in FCD diagnosis remains unclear. Objectives This review aimed to synthesize evidence on formal neuropsychological assessment in FCD and provide guidance for practitioners involved in its diagnosis. We investigated whether: 1) a typical pattern of cognitive performance can be identified in this condition; and 2) clinically relevant features may emerge during comprehensive neuropsychological evaluation. Methods MEDLINE, Scopus, and PsycINFO were searched for English-language empirical studies on FCD up to January 9th, 2025. Quality appraisal was conducted using JBI tools. A narrative synthesis was performed analysing cognitive outcomes, clinical and behavioural features identified during neuropsychological evaluation. Results Of 226 screened articles, 23 met inclusion criteria; quality was mixed. Cognitive performance in FCD is heterogeneous, and standalone tests have limited diagnostic utility. Key clinical features include mid-life onset, psychiatric comorbidities, and links to stress or adverse life events. Distinctive communicative and behavioural features may support diagnosis, though not diagnostic alone. Conclusion The diagnosis of FCD requires a multidimensional approach integrating cognitive, behavioural, linguistic, and contextual observations. Neuropsychological evaluation can identify positive signs and internal inconsistencies through a combination of standardized cognitive testing, behavioural and linguistic observation, psychodiagnostics measures. Further research is urgently needed to validate potential cognitive markers and refine assessment strategies.

papers.title: Dynamic functional abnormalities of cerebellar networks in adolescents with obsessive-compulsive disorder.
papers.authors: Jia A, Yuan X, Zhang K, Zhang C, Li R, Fu C, Wang B, Li K.
papers.abstract: Background Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) commonly begins during adolescence, yet its neurobiological basis remains unclear. Beyond the classical cortico-striatal framework, the cerebellum has been implicated in cognitive, affective, and motor regulation, relevant to OCD. However, it is unknown whether adolescent OCD involves abnormal dynamic coordination of large-scale cerebellar networks. Methods Thirty-eight adolescents with OCD and 29 matched controls underwent dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) analysis of cerebellar networks using a sliding-window approach and k-means clustering. Connectivity states, temporal properties, and the standard deviation of dFNC across sliding windows were quantified and examined in relation to clinical symptoms through exploratory partial correlation analyses. Results Compared to healthy controls, adolescents with OCD showed fewer state transitions, indicating reduced network flexibility. They also exhibited lower dFNC variability in networks, including dorsal attention network (DAN)-visual network (VN), DAN-salience network, default mode network (DMN)-VN, and DMN-somatomotor dorsal network connections. Exploratory partial correlation analysis revealed that DAN-VN dFNC variability was negatively correlated with OCI-CV neutralizing scores, whereas DMN-VN dFNC variability was positively correlated with CDI negative mood scores, and CDI total scores. Conclusions Adolescent OCD shows reduced intra-cerebellar dynamic connectivity flexibility and variability associated with obsessive-compulsive and depressive symptoms, suggesting impaired cerebellar reconfiguration.

papers.title: Anxiety sensitivity, psychological vulnerability, and brain volumes in borderline personality disorder.
papers.authors: Kılıçaslan AK, Uğur K, Sun T, Taşçı İ, Maçin G, Yıldız S.
papers.abstract: Aim This study compared AS, psychological vulnerability, and brain volumes in BPD and healthy controls and examined clinical-volumetric associations within BPD. Method Twenty-seven patients with BPD and 28 healthy controls completed the Anxiety Sensitivity Index-3 and the Psychological Vulnerability Scale. Three-dimensional T1-weighted images were acquired using a 1.5-Tesla MRI scanner, and regional volumes were calculated. Results In raw analyses, the BPD group had higher psychological vulnerability and total, cognitive, and social AS scores. After covariate adjustment, only social AS remained significant (p = 0.035). Bilateral putamen, anterior insula, caudate, nucleus accumbens, and total gray matter volumes were larger in the BPD group, persisting after adjustment (all p ≤ 0.018). Differences in left amygdala, posterior and total insula, posterior cingulate gyrus, and white matter volumes lost significance after adjustment. In the BPD group, posterior insula volumes were negatively correlated with total and social AS scores, remaining significant after controlling for confounders (r=-0.471 to -0.611; p = 0.004-0.036). Psychological vulnerability and cognitive AS were not associated with regional volumes. Conclusion Social AS may represent a specific dimension of BPD. Group-level differences in anterior insula and striatal volumes, together with dimensional associations between posterior insula volumes and AS, suggest distinct roles for insular subregions in BPD-related clinical and structural processes.

papers.title: Thalamocortical connectivity associated with fatigue after accounting for depressive symptoms in stroke survivors and controls.
papers.authors: Stilling J, Gillies C, Kim JH, Jamison K, Kuceyeski A.
papers.abstract: Background Post-stroke fatigue is common and disabling, yet rarely distinguished from co-occurring depression, limiting understanding of its neural substrates. We examined resting-state fMRI correlates of post-stroke fatigue while accounting for depressive symptoms. Methods We studied 103 stroke patients and 29 age-matched controls from a longitudinal neuroimaging cohort. Fatigue was assessed via the SF-36 Vitality subscale and depression via the Geriatric Depression Scale - Short (GDS-15). Linear mixed-effects models evaluated associations between vitality and resting-state functional connectivity, adjusting for depression and covariates. Residualized vitality models served as sensitivity analyses to isolate fatigue variance independent of depressive symptoms, with FDR correction applied within feature families. Results In depression-adjusted models, higher vitality (lower fatigue) was associated with increased frontoparietal-limbic connectivity (β = 0.0013, FDR q = 0.048), though this did not survive depression residualization. In a residualized sensitivity analysis, higher vitality (lower fatigue) was associated with reduced thalamus-insula and thalamus-ventral attention network connectivity (thalamus-insula: β = -0.0071, FDR q = 0.011; thalamus-VAN: β = -0.0043, FDR q = 0.012); these associations were attenuated and did not survive correction in the primary depression-adjusted model (q ≈ 0.075). Conclusions Fatigue was associated with both frontoparietal-limbic and thalamocortical connectivity, although the thalamic associations were attenuated after adjustment for depressive symptoms in the primary analysis and were most evident in residualized sensitivity analyses. These findings suggest that fatigue and depressive symptoms may involve both shared and potentially distinct neural correlates. Point estimates were smaller in stroke participants than controls, providing no evidence that the observed associations were stroke-specific. Future work should determine whether these relationships are unique to stroke or reflect broader neural correlates of fatigue across clinical populations.

papers.title: TMRKP: Trustworthy MRI-based radiology knowledge-aware prediction framework for stroke-associated pneumonia and hemorrhagic transformation.
papers.authors: Zhao C, Yu Y, Xia T, Yuan M, Yang Y, Hu C.
papers.journal: Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society
papers.abstract: Prediction of stroke-associated pneumonia (SAP) and hemorrhagic transformation (HT) is critical for improving the prognosis of acute ischemic stroke patients. However, current brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based models narrowly focus on generic visual patterns, and frequently overlook the radiology-informed knowledge critical for predicting SAP and HT. To address this limitation, we propose a trustworthy MRI-based radiology knowledge-aware prediction (TMRKP) framework equipped with radiology knowledge-aware masked modeling (RKMM) and evidential multi-sequence fusion (EMF). Specifically, TMRKP first organizes four MRI sequences into a 2 × 2 super-sequence configuration, mimicking the diagnostic perspective of radiologists who simultaneously analyze multiple imaging modalities. Second, to introduce radiology knowledge into representation learning, we focus on white matter hyperintensities (WMH), a well-established biomarker of chronic small-vessel disease and long-term ischemic injury that is clinically relevant to SAP and HT. During pre-training, RKMM segments WMH masks from the MRI sequence to steer the model toward WMH regions, enabling it to learn meaningful representations of these clinically relevant pathological areas. Third, for SAP and HT prediction, EMF models the predictive uncertainty using evidence derived from both the super-sequence and the WMH-aware masked super-sequence, and fuses the resulting multi-sequence evidence based on Dempster-Shafer theory (DST). Extensive experiments on the collected Jiangdu dataset, together with independent external validation on the Zhongda dataset, demonstrate the superiority and generalizability of TMRKP over the state-of-the-art models.

papers.title: White matter hyperintensity burden is associated with neuroaxonal injury in acute ischemic stroke.
papers.authors: Ramis D, Bennouna N, Jové B, Girona A, Cabero-Arnold A, Brengaret O, Rosa-Batlle I, Bartolomé-Arenas I, Doncel-Moriano A, Vargas M, Urra X, Rudilosso S, Chamorro Á.
papers.abstract: Background and purpose White matter hyperintensities (WMH) reflect accumulated microvascular brain injury in small vessel disease, yet their impact on acute-phase circulating biomarker profile after ischemic stroke remains poorly defined. We examined whether WMH burden is associated with greater circulating biomarker levels in acute ischemic stroke, independent of infarct size. Methods We retrospectively analyzed a cohort from a prospective single-center registry of patients with MRI-confirmed ischemic stroke without large-vessel occlusion who were treated with intravenous thrombolysis. WMH and infarct volumes were quantitatively measured on MRI. Circulating neurofilament light chain (NfL) and selected inflammatory and endothelial biomarkers were obtained at the time of thrombolysis. Associations between WMH burden and biomarker levels were assessed using multivariable linear regression. Results Among 168 patients (median age 69 years; 39% women), greater WMH volume was independently associated with higher circulating NfL levels (fold-change 1.25, 95% CI 1.12-1.41; p < 0.001), even after adjustment for infarct volume. The standardized effect of WMH volume on NfL was comparable to that of infarct volume. In contrast, associations between WMH burden and inflammatory or endothelial biomarkers were weak and inconsistent after adjustment. Conclusions WMH burden is independently associated with higher NfL in the acute phase of ischemic stroke. These findings suggest that NfL levels in the hyperacute stroke setting may reflect acute ischemic injury but also pre-existing chronic microvascular brain damage, supporting consideration of WMH burden when interpreting neuroaxonal biomarkers after stroke.

papers.title: Maternal language barriers and preterm infants' general movements: Evidence from a multilingual population.
papers.authors: Huening B, Jaekel N, Dathe AK, Middendorf L, Bialas J, Felderhoff-Mueser U, Jaekel J.
papers.abstract: Aim To assess whether immigrant mothers' language barriers are associated with the motor development of infants born preterm, assessed using the Prechtl General Movement Assessment. The assessment of these spontaneous movements allows the prediction of cerebral palsy and neurodevelopmental delay. Methods The study included 508 infants born at 22-36 weeks gestation. At a corrected age of three to five months, general movements were assessed according to Prechtl, and a subsample of 251 infants also underwent coding with the Motor Optimality Score - Revised. Language barriers were measured using continuous linguistic distance scores between mothers' first languages and German (range 0-102.40). Results Of all mothers, 53.94% had an immigrant background and 45.10% reported a first language other than German. Higher linguistic distance was associated with a lower likelihood of fidgety movements being present (OR = 0.99, p < .05), although this association did not remain significant after adjustment for confounders. In contrast, higher linguistic distance was negatively associated with the Motor Optimality Score - Revised, an association that remained significant after adjustment for confounders, in both the univariate (B = -0.02 [-0.03, -0.01], β = -0.20, p < .001) and fully adjusted model (β = -0.17, p < .01; adjusted for gestational age, infant sex, severe brain lesions and maternal education). Conclusions Language barriers in the form of linguistic distance between mothers' first languages and their host country's majority language are associated with the early motor development of infants born preterm. Future research needs to disentangle how language barriers, intersectional vulnerabilities, and potential assessment biases affect infant development and follow-up services.

papers.title: The brain before the herd: Pre-Decision EEG prediction of herd-consistent investment choices among bilingual investors.
papers.authors: Loang OK, Jiyang H, Azar AS.
papers.abstract: This study examines whether pre-decision electroencephalographic (EEG) activity provides incremental information for explaining and predicting herd-consistent investment choices when social and fundamental signals conflict. A controlled 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 within-participant factorial experiment involving 80 English-Mandarin bilingual Chinese investors who met a predefined English-proficiency threshold equivalent to IELTS 6.5 or TOEFL iBT 80 and had prior experience in U.S. equity markets manipulated language, information format, social-media sentiment, and information consistency. Herd-consistent choice was conservatively defined as alignment with the social signal when it contradicted fundamental information. Behavioural and single-trial EEG responses were analysed using mixed-effects models, while machine-learning models were evaluated through nested participant-disjoint validation. The findings indicate that Mandarin-language presentation and short-form financial information are associated with greater conformity to social signals under informational conflict. Conflict between social and fundamental information also elicits stronger frontal-midline theta activity, consistent with heightened demands on cognitive control and conflict monitoring before choice. Pre-decision P300 and theta provide distinct predictive information beyond contextual and participant characteristics, indicating that attentional updating and conflict processing contribute differently to subsequent herd-consistent decisions. These findings support a process-based account of investment conformity in which information architecture, social influence, and pre-decision neurocognitive processing jointly shape herd-consistent choices.

papers.title: Corrigendum to "When Chinese verb transitivity meets wrong syntactic category" [Brain Lang. 281 (2026) 105820].
papers.authors: Zhang Y, Piao Q, Yang Y, Boland JE, Du Y, Wang Y, Han M.

papers.title: Delirium after Aortic Arch Surgery with Hypothermic Circulatory Arrest: Clinical and Neuroimaging Insights from the GOT ICE Randomized Trial.
papers.authors: Hughes GC, Browndyke JN, Chen EP, Szeto WY, DiMaio JM, Brinkman WT, Markovic J, Gaca JG, Blumenthal JA, Karhausen JA, James ML, Yanez D, Li YJ, Mathew JP.
papers.abstract: Background Postoperative delirium (POD) is a complication of arch surgery with hypothermic circulatory arrest (HCA) and may contribute to long-term cognitive decline, but prospective data are limited. We examined its incidence, predictors, and neurocognitive and neuroimaging correlates. Methods The Cognitive Effects of Body Temperature During Hypothermic Circulatory Arrest trial compared deep versus moderate hypothermia during elective arch repair. Delirium was assessed preoperatively and on postoperative days 1-3 using the Confusion Assessment Method. Thirty-day outcomes, cognition, quality of life, and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging at 4 weeks and 1 year were compared by POD status. Results Of 269 patients with complete assessments, POD occurred in 34.6% and did not differ significantly between hypothermia groups (p=0.45). Patients with POD had higher stroke rates (9.7% vs 0.6%; p<0.001), prolonged ventilation (3.2% vs. 0%; p=0.017), and longer hospitalization (8.5 vs. 5.9 days; p<0.001). Affected patients had worse cognition and quality of life (p<0.001) at 30 days, with partial recovery at 1 year. Baseline imaging demonstrated reduced thalamo-cerebellar connectivity in patients who developed POD (p<0.01, p-FWE<0.05), with persistent abnormalities at 1-year. Higher baseline cognition and ejection fraction were protective against POD (OR<1), whereas longer antegrade cerebral perfusion time increased risk (OR 1.03; 95% CI, 1.005-1.05; p=0.019). Conclusions POD affects >one-third of patients after arch surgery with HCA and is associated with worse 30-day and 1-year cognitive outcomes with enduring imaging abnormalities. Reduced preoperative thalamo-cerebellar connectivity suggests a preexisting neural vulnerability, indicating that delirium may unmask rather than cause long-term cognitive decline.

papers.title: Multimodal MRI markers of white matter hyperintensities and their impact on cognition in cerebral small vessel disease: a systematic review.
papers.authors: Aryal B, Pendem S, P S P, Kadavigere R, Priyanka, Ranjan R.
papers.abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) is a leading cause of stroke, dementia, and age-related cognitive decline, with white matter hyperintensities (WMH) being a key imaging feature in MRI. This review aims to evaluate the association between multimodal magnetic resonance imaging markers of white matter hyperintensities and cognition in cerebral small vessel disease. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science (2016-2026) was done. Studies involving adults with MRI visible CSVD markers who underwent MRI standardized cognitive assessment were eligible. Fifteen studies were included with a total of 5752 participants. Included studies used conventional and advanced MRI techniques to evaluate the association of WMH with cognitive function. The findings were synthesized narratively according to MRI techniques. Conventional MRI studies showed that greater WMH burden and CSVD severity were associated with poorer cognition, particularly processing speed and global cognition, with individual studies reporting β values of - 0.371 (p < 0.001) and - 0.363 (p < 0.001), with good predictive accuracy reported in one study (AUC = 0.800, 95% CI: 0.710-0.891). While Advanced MRI also showed associations with microstructural and microvascular damage in white matter and with reduced blood flow was associated with poorer cognitive performance, individual studies reported β values of 0.268-0.273, moderate-to-strong associations (r = 0.310-0.441), good diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.86-0.89), and significantly lower scores on cognitive assessments (Mini-Mental State Examination: p < 0.001; Montreal Cognitive Assessment: p < 0.05). These findings suggest that WMH burden and disrupted white matter microstructure are associated with cognitive impairment. Larger, standardized studies are needed to determine the clinical value of MRI markers as reliable biomarkers for early detection and monitoring of cognitive impairment in CSVD.

papers.title: Local repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) induces whole-brain functional dynamic remodeling.
papers.authors: Fan L, Li Y, Duan SQ, An S, Wu Y, Yao N, Zhu Q, Zhang M, Huang ZG, Zhang SP.
papers.abstract: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a proven tool to modulate brain functional dynamics and treat neurological and psychiatric diseases. However, it remains unclear how local rTMS affects whole-brain functional dynamics. Here, we investigated the stimulation effects of rTMS using two data-driven approaches. By constructing multi-layer networks from resting-state fMRI data acquired before and after 1 Hz stimulation over the left frontal (FRO-TMS) and occipital cortex (OCC-TMS), we found significantly decreased dynamic interaction after FRO-TMS. We further characterized whole-brain functional hierarchy by computing nonreversibility and observed a significantly flattened hierarchy after FRO-TMS, whereas OCC-TMS did not induce significant changes. We then systematically investigated the association between these distinct modulatory patterns and structural network organization by fitting a large-scale brain computational model. Using noise- and synchronization-based perturbation protocols, we found that the simulated perturbation distance correlated significantly with the local dominance and controllability of the stimulated node in the structural network, providing a potential mechanistic account for the empirical observations. Specifically, driving hub nodes induced relatively small perturbation distances, whereas driving weakly connected regions yielded larger distances. This study provides a heuristic strategy for modeling and optimizing stimulation protocols in noninvasive brain stimulation. Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10568-3.

papers.title: A geometric rs-fMRI connectome descriptor reveals individual stability without robust autism group differences.
papers.authors: M S SP, A ST.
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has resisted reproducible case-control characterization in resting-state functional connectivity, leaving open whether reported group differences reflect genuine biology or methodological variability. We introduce a geometric framework that represents functional connectomes on the symmetric positive-definite Riemannian manifold and quantifies individual deviation as tangent-space dispersion, complemented by normative modeling of graph topology. Using the multi-site Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE I) cohort (N=1035 subjects), we evaluate this descriptor under stringent robustness conditions and report three findings. First, individual connectome geometry is a stable, individually unique descriptor. The magnitude of a subject's deviation is highly reliable across split halves (intraclass correlation ICC[Formula: see text]) but is dominated by an acquisition-site scale, whereas its high-dimensional shape identifies subjects within-session with 98.9% accuracy once that scale is removed. Second, the case-control difference in dispersion is null and, by two one-sided equivalence tests against Cohen's d = 0.2 , statistically equivalent to zero in all ABIDE I analysis cohorts (full cohort d = -0.007 , N = 1035 ; strict cohort d = +0.038 , N = 635 ); a nominal single-atlas effect (dispersion ratio 1.05, p = 0.046 ) does not survive multi-atlas reanalysis. Third, acquisition site explains 69% of dispersion variance while diagnosis explains 0.0001% ; deviations form no discrete subtypes and do not predict symptom severity (minimum p=0.15 across tested graph-deviation predictors). Geometric dispersion is therefore a reproducible, individually unique connectome descriptor but not a case-control biomarker of ASD, which helps to explain the inconsistency of connectomic findings in autism.

papers.title: Cerebellar Crus I and Crus II Structure and Excitation/Inhibition Balance in Autism Spectrum Disorder.
papers.authors: Hegarty JP, Komaki H, Gu M, Young K, Ogbonnaya N, Spielman DM, Hardan AY.
papers.journal: Journal of autism and developmental disorders
papers.abstract: Purpose Cerebro-cerebellar network dynamics are highly implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), particularly the posterolateral cerebellar hemispheres. Cellular alterations in the cerebellum are also consistently reported in post-mortem research, suggesting potential impacts on the balance between excitatory glutamatergic (Glu) and inhibitory GABAergic signaling (E/I). Emerging evidence further indicates that the cerebellum supports multiple cognitive and behavioral domains associated with the diagnostic criteria for ASD. Methods The current study collected structural T1-weighted MRI and novel 1 H MR spectroscopy data (MEGA-SPECIAL) to examine neurometabolites of Glu and GABA from the cerebellar hemispheres of autistic (n=13) and neurotypical children (n =16). We also explored preliminary comparisons with autistic adolescents (n=7) and assessed relationships for social communication, restricted and repetitive behaviors, and sensory processing differences. Results Crus I and II were significantly thinner in autistic children compared to neurotypical children. While there were no significant group differences in the subset of participants with quality neurometabolite measurements, p > 0.05, there were salient relationships between E/I, cerebellar structure, and core ASD domains. Thinner Crus I grey matter and smaller Crus II volume were correlated with higher E/I, especially for Glu in left Crus I and right Crus II. Morphometric properties and E/I were also associated with self-injurious and other restricted and repetitive behaviors. Conclusion Our preliminary findings are limited by the small sample size but suggest a potential relationship between cerebellar structure, the balance of excitation-inhibition in cerebro-cerebellar networks, and the core domains of autism spectrum disorder.

papers.title: Resting-state BOLD fMRI-derived cerebrovascular reactivity for detecting crossed cerebellar diaschisis.
papers.authors: Xu J, Shan Y, Cui B, Yin Y, Li J, Liu J, Ma Y, Lu J.
papers.abstract: Purpose To study cerebellar cerebrovascular reactivity (CVR) derived from resting-state (RS) blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) as a potential imaging biomarker for crossed cerebellar diaschisis (CCD). Methods Thirty-nine patients with symptomatic unilateral cerebrovascular occlusion and eighteen age-matched healthy subjects underwent a simultaneous PET/MR scan. CCD was diagnosed as a contralateral cerebellar metabolic reduction present on 18 F-FDG PET semi-quantitatively. RS BOLD-CVR maps were derived by extracting signals within specific frequency bands of RS BOLD. The cerebellar asymmetry index (CAI) calculated from RS BOLD-CVR and 18 F-FDG PET data were compared using receiver operating characteristic and Bland-Altman analysis. Neurological function was determined with NIHSS and mRS. Results In our cohort, CCD was diagnosed in 21 of 39 (53.8%) patients on 18 F-FDG PET. CCD+ patients exhibited larger infarct volume, more severe supratentorial CVR impairment, and worse functional status than CCD- patients at admission and 3.5 years follow-up. The area under the curve for RS BOLD-CVR CAI was 0.862 (95% confidence interval: 0.747-0.978) with a cutoff value of 8.2%, achieving a sensitivity of 81.0% and a specificity of 83.3% to detect CCD. The Bland-Altman analysis showed no significant proportional bias between PET CAI and CVR CAI (P = 0.848). CVR CAI was correlated with NIHSS (ρ = 0.352, p = 0.033) and mRS (ρ = 0.360, p = 0.029) at admission after adjusted for age and infarct volume. Conclusion RS BOLD-CVR demonstrates good sensitivity and specificity to detect diaschisis-related cerebellar cerebrovascular reactivity in patients with symptomatic unilateral cerebrovascular occlusion. Furthermore, participants with cerebellar CVR impairment and metabolic reduction tended to have poorer neurological function.

papers.title: Differences in Intracranial Artery and Brain Impairment Between Pediatric and Adult Moyamoya Disease: A Comparative MRI Study.
papers.authors: Du X, Zhang H, Li B, Liu Y, Liu S, Han C, Sheng F, Duan G, Zhao X, Lu M, Cai J.
papers.journal: Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
papers.abstract: Background Moyamoya disease (MMD) exhibits incidence peaks in children and adults, but the age-related differences in MR imaging features remain unclear. Purpose To determine the differences in intracranial artery and brain impairment between pediatric and adult patients with MMD using MR imaging. Study type Retrospective. Population Four hundred and three patients (median age, 42 years [IQR, 29-51 years]; 268 adults) diagnosed with MMD by digital subtraction angiography (DSA), with routine clinical brain MRI and high-resolution intracranial vessel wall imaging within 1 week of DSA. Field strength/sequence Pre- and post-contrast 3D T1 SPACE and routine brain MRI sequences including T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, diffusion weighted imaging, and 3D time-of-flight at 3.0 T. Assessment Three neuroradiologists (10, 6, and 11 years of neurovascular imaging experience) assessed vessel wall enhancement grades and patterns, basal ganglia and centrum semiovale perivascular spaces, white matter hyperintensities, lacunes, infarction, hemorrhage, and intracranial arterial luminal stenosis. Statistical tests Student's t-test, Mann-Whitney U test, Chi-square test, or Fisher's exact test, and logistic regression analysis. A two-sided p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Adult patients were significantly more likely to have bilateral intracranial internal carotid artery stenosis (90.7% vs. 81.5%), Grade 2 enhancement in the posterior cerebral artery (9.0% vs. 2.2%), and significantly higher risk of intracranial hemorrhage (odds ratio (OR) = 5.216, 95% confidence interval (CI): 2.312-11.767), periventricular WMHs (OR = 2.634, 95% CI: 1.263-5.494), and lacunes (OR = 2.012, 95% CI: 1.179-3.432) compared to pediatric patients. In contrast, pediatric patients were significantly more prone to bilateral anterior cerebral artery (ACA) stenosis and vessel wall enhancement, and had significantly higher prevalence of Grade 1 enhancement at the origins of the middle cerebral artery and ACA, as well as significantly higher odds of PVSs in the centrum semiovale (OR for adults = 0.447, 95% CI: 0.210-0.949) compared to adult patients. Data conclusion The intracranial arterial and brain impairments assessed by MR imaging significantly differed between adult and pediatric patients with MMD. Evidence level 3. Technical efficacy Stage 5.

papers.title: Pragmatic screening for autoimmune-associated epilepsy in drug-resistant epilepsy of unknown etiology in resource-limited settings: A hypothesis-generating study.
papers.authors: Frezatti TOHM, Saute RL, Júnior VA, Nakano FN, Dalio MTRP, Velasco TR, Leite JP, Dos Santos AC, Marques VD, Sakamoto AC.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
papers.abstract: Objective To evaluate the feasibility of investigating autoimmune etiology in adults with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) of unknown origin in resource-limited settings and to develop a pragmatic, hypothesis-generating screening approach to guide autoantibody testing. Methods A prospective observational study including adults with DRE of unknown etiology was conducted at a tertiary epilepsy center in Brazil. All patients underwent standardized assessment including inflammatory and autoimmunity markers, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), electroencephalography (EEG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and application of the APE2 and ACES scores. Clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings were analyzed in the context of published autoimmune-associated epilepsy (AAE) profiles to inform a pragmatic screening strategy. Results Twenty-six patients (46.2% female; median epilepsy duration: 18.5 years) were included. EEG findings were nonspecific. Six patients developed mesial temporal abnormalities on follow-up MRI. CSF protein elevation was observed in 37.5%, oligoclonal bands in 13.6%, and elevated IgG index in 18.2%. Antinuclear antibodies were detected in 26.9%. APE2 score ≥ 4 was present in 57.7%, while ACES score ≥ 2 occurred in 11.5%. Due to limited access to antibody testing, only one patient underwent CSF autoantibody analysis, confirming high-titer anti-GAD65. Based on integrated clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings, a pragmatic screening algorithm was proposed to prioritize candidates for autoantibody testing. Significance In resource-limited settings, systematic use of accessible clinical and laboratory markers may help identify patients with higher pre-test probability of AAE. A pragmatic screening approach may improve diagnostic efficiency and support individualized decision-making when comprehensive antibody testing is not readily available.

papers.title: Ceramide Transporter Syndrome
papers.authors: Regan-Fendt K, Gehin C, Knerr I, D'Angelo G, Gennarino VA.
papers.abstract: Clinical characteristics Ceramide transporter (CerTra) syndrome is characterized by a spectrum of developmental delay, intellectual disability, neurobehavioral abnormalities (autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, self-injurious behavior), hypotonia, infant feeding difficulties, seizures, and brain abnormalities (most commonly involving white matter). Some individuals have poor weight gain, microcephaly, and developmental regression (predominantly affecting speech). Affected individuals reported to date range in age from infancy to a few individuals age 40 years or older. Diagnosis/testing The diagnosis of CerTra syndrome is established in a proband with suggestive findings and a heterozygous pathogenic variant in CERT1 identified by molecular genetic testing. Management Treatment of manifestations: Multidisciplinary care is recommended by specialists in developmental delay, intellectual disability, neurobehavioral/psychiatric manifestations, feeding/gastrointestinal issues, and epilepsy; as needed, care by specialists for individuals with cerebral visual impairment and other vision issues, musculoskeletal manifestations, sleep dysregulation, hearing loss, transition to adult care, and family support. Surveillance: At each visit, assess developmental progress, educational needs, neurobehavioral manifestations, measurement of growth parameters, nutritional status, safety of oral intake, and gastrointestinal manifestations; neurologic evaluation in those with seizures and assessment for new manifestations such as changes in tone and ataxia at each visit; ophthalmology evaluation with frequency per treating ophthalmologist; physical medicine and occupational and physical therapy assessment of mobility, self-help skills, presence or progression of scoliosis, pes planus, and other foot abnormalities at each visit; annual assessment of sleep issues; hearing evaluation per treating clinician; assessment of family needs for social services support at each visit. Genetic counseling CerTra syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder typically caused by a de novo pathogenic variant. Rarely, individuals diagnosed with CerTra syndrome have the disorder as the result of a CERT1 pathogenic variant inherited from a parent. If the CERT1 pathogenic variant found in the proband cannot be detected in the leukocyte DNA of either parent, the recurrence risk to sibs is estimated to be 1% because of the possibility of parental gonadal mosaicism. Once the CERT1 pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.

papers.title: Shifts in neural representations, not gaze, track how people reinterpret ambiguous social scenes
papers.authors: Sava-Segal CA, Benson TG, Finn ES.
papers.abstract: How do we come to “see” the same thing differently after hearing someone else’s perspective? Revising an interpretation could reflect changes in how the brain represents the meaning of what we see, changes in how we visually sample the input, or both. To disentangle these mechanisms, we developed MindLibs, an adaptive fMRI and eye-tracking paradigm in which participants generate interpretations of ambiguous photographs and then view alternative interpretations chosen in real time to vary in semantic content from their own. Exposure to semantically distant alternatives revealed a strong link between reinterpretation as reported behaviorally and representational shifts in association cortex, but no systematic relationship between reinterpretation and changes in gaze. In particular, representational shifts in lateral default-mode network regions (DMN-B) predicted reinterpretation independently of shifts in frontoparietal, attention, and visual networks, and independently of whether gaze changed. In contrast, shifts in visual cortex tracked reinterpretation only when gaze also shifted, and contributed no unique variance beyond DMN-B. These findings identify higher-order conceptual reconfiguration, rather than perceptual resampling, as the primary account of how people revise the meaning of an ambiguous scene.

papers.title: Feature-Engineering Strategies for EEG-Based ADHD Classification in Children: A Controlled Benchmark of Expert, LLM-Guided and Full-Space Comparators
papers.authors: Rohani F, Alhatab H, Jarrud M, Salous N, Kasimoğlu S, Mueller A.
papers.abstract: EEG-based machine-learning studies of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are vulnerable to optimistic performance estimates when feature selection or model choice is informed by data outside the training fold. We compared expert-reconstructed, large language model (LLM)-guided and full-space feature strategies under leakage-controlled subject-level validation in a frozen cohort of 77 children (45 ADHD, 32 controls) represented by 1,185 gamma-free EEG features. Four classifiers (SVM, GMM, random forest [RF] and XGBoost) were evaluated with nested leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOOCV), with all data-dependent operations restricted to outer-training subjects. Across 100 repetitions of stratified 10-fold cross-validation, RF/expert achieved mean accuracy 62.8% (SD 3.5%; empirical 95% interval 55.8%–69.5%), mean balanced accuracy 62.3% and mean AUC-ROC 0.618. The corresponding LOOCV point estimate was 71.4% accuracy and 71.0% balanced accuracy (AUC-ROC 0.673). GMM/expert achieved the highest AUC-ROC (0.699), indicating metric-dependent model ranking. The expert-reconstructed strategy achieved the highest accuracy and balanced accuracy for every classifier, whereas the LLM-guided strategy showed no consistent advantage over the full feature space. Pairwise classifier differences were not significant after Holm correction. A pre-specified 200 µV artifact gate reduced RF/expert accuracy to approximately 55.8%, below the 58.4% no-information rate; this drop may reflect removal of artifact-related signal and/or reduced epoch counts leading to noisier feature estimates. These findings support cautious benchmarking and external validation rather than claims of algorithmic or LLM superiority.

papers.title: MRI improves global outcome prediction after moderate or severe traumatic brain injury
papers.authors: Shi H, Curley WH, Gjyzari M, Nanda A, Bodien YG, Sun X, Stubbs JL, Amorim E, Temkin NR, Mukherjee P, Zimmerman KA, Bertolini G, Magnoni S, Dunet V, Oddo M, Moro F, Mallas E, Graham NSN, Sharp DJ, Manley GT, Jain S, Fox MD, Edlow BL, Snider SB, the TRACK-TBI Investigators.
papers.abstract: Importance Brain MRIs are routinely acquired following moderate or severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) because of their high sensitivity for detecting traumatic brain lesions. However, there is no standard framework for their interpretation, and their clinical utility is unproven. Objective Here, we test whether MRI-based quantification of traumatic brain lesions improves outcome prediction relative to the best tools currently available to clinicians. Design, Setting and Participants We analyzed hemorrhagic contusions and axonal injury in four prospective studies of moderate or severe TBI: BIOmarkers of AXonal injury after traumatic brain injury (BIOAX) 2017-2021; Resting and Stimulus-based Paradigms to detect Organized NetworkS and predict Emergence of consciousness (RESPONSE Pilot and RESPONSE 2) 2012-2022; Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury (TRACK-TBI) 2014-2020. External validation in a fifth, prospective single-center study (Brigham and Women’s Hospital) 2024-2026. Exposure Contusion volume was measured via manual segmentation. Axonal injury volume was quantified with diffusion tensor imaging, by measuring the volume of skeletonized fractional anisotropy significantly lower than that of healthy controls. Main Outcomes and Measures Functional outcomes were assessed at 6 months with the Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended; values 4 were considered unfavorable. Results Among 201 patients with MRI (mean age: 41, median Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS] score on admission: 7, MRI obtained median 14 days post-injury), MRI-measured contusion volume discriminated outcomes better than CT Marshall score (AUC 0.81 vs 0.64; p=0.001), and remained associated with unfavorable outcomes controlling for multiple commonly-measured clinical variables. Quantitative axonal injury volume discriminated outcomes better than manual MRI grading (AUC 0.82 vs 0.62; p<0.001) and remained associated with unfavorable outcomes independent of other clinical predictors. The prognostic discrimination of traumatic lesion volumes was not improved by accounting for the location or normative connectivity of either lesion type. In a multivariate model, contusion and axonal injury volumes were independently predictive, with age-dependent volume thresholds for 90% probability of unfavorable outcome, and strong discrimination in an external cohort (N=27; AUC 0.83, p<0.001). Replacing all CT-based measures with MRI lesion volumes in the IMPACT model significantly improved out-of-sample prognostic performance (AUC 0.85 vs 0.64; p<0.05). Conclusions and Relevance MRI-based lesion quantification improves prognostic discrimination relative to measures currently available to clinicians treating patients with TBI. Global functioning at 6 months is driven more by the volume than the location or connectivity of traumatic lesions. These findings support integrating MRI-based lesion quantification into clinical workflows and updated TBI classification frameworks.

papers.title: Multiscale structural MRI differences among collegiate American football players, cross-country runners, and non-athletes
papers.authors: Guchait A, Chen C, Muggleton NG.
papers.abstract: Structural differences observed in collision-sport athletes may reflect repetitive head-impact exposure, broader effects of athletic training, or pre-existing individual variation, making inclusion of a non-collision athlete group important for interpretation of any differences seen. Here, structural T1-weighted MRI data from 17 collegiate American football players, 16 cross-country runners, and 9 non-athletes were analyzed using FSL voxel-based morphometry (VBM), FIRST subcortical volumetry and vertex-wise shape analysis, and FAST whole-brain tissue segmentation. Spatial inference used permutation testing with threshold-free cluster enhancement and family-wise error correction, while scalar analyses used multiplicity-corrected procedures. FAST-derived absolute tissue volumes were also examined in a sensitivity analysis adjusting for FreeSurfer estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV). VBM showed recurrent brainstem-centered differences, with non-athletes showing greater local gray matter measures than both athlete groups, whereas football players showed greater brainstem measures than runners. FIRST vertex-wise analysis identified corrected differences involving the brainstem and selected subcortical structures, while no total FIRST structure volume survived false discovery rate correction. Unadjusted FAST analysis identified a CSF group effect, F (2, 24.38) = 11.46, p < .001, q = .001. After eTIV adjustment, the CSF group effect remained, F (2, 38) = 14.30, q < .001, and a white matter group effect was also identified, F (2, 38) = 9.59, q < .001; gray matter and total segmented tissue did not show corrected adjusted effects. These findings indicate that structural variation depends on anatomical scale, comparison group, and head-size adjustment and cannot be attributed uniquely to collision-sport exposure.

papers.title: Multimodal Glymphatic Imaging in Multiple Sclerosis: Associations with Sleep and Disability
papers.authors: Sharifpour R, Elands S, Hrabovecky J, Rovai A, Borrelli S, de Bourgoing G, Perrotta G, De Tiège X, Strauss M.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system is the waste clearance pathway in the central nervous system. Although its dysfunction has been associated with several neurological disorders, its role in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains poorly understood. This system is thought to be particularly active during sleep, yet the relationship between sleep metrics and MRI-derived markers of glymphatic activity has been scarcely explored. In this study, we aimed to perform a multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment of glymphatic function in MS and investigate its association with sleep parameters, clinical disability, disease duration and MRI-derived structural markers. The study included 22 patients (34.3±10.1 years; 16 female) with relapsing-remitting MS and 26 healthy controls (32.2±5.7 years; 18 female), all of whom underwent 3.0 Tesla MRI. Glymphatic function was assessed using diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and global blood-oxygen-level–dependent (BOLD) signal–cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coupling. In addition, sleep micro- and macrostructural features, clinical disability, disease duration, along with mean diffusivity (MD), lateral ventricular, choroid plexus volumes and lesion load were evaluated. Patients showed reduced DTI-ALPS index, though this difference became only a trend after controlling for MD. No significant group differences were observed in global BOLD signal-CSF coupling. However, in patients, the weaker coupling was associated with longer total sleep time, lower arousal index, greater disability and lateral ventricle enlargement, whereas the DTI-ALPS index showed no significant correlations with any of the measures. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that DTI-ALPS can serve as a reliable marker of glymphatic function in demyelinating diseases such as MS, where disease-related alterations in white matter microstructure can confound diffusion-based measures. In contrast, gBOLD–CSF coupling showed associations with sleep, clinical disability and structural changes in patients, despite the absence of a significant group-level difference. This finding suggests that gBOLD–CSF coupling may capture individual variability in glymphatic-related dynamics relevant to sleep and the clinical expression of MS.

papers.title: The Semantic Shift in Autobiographical Memory and Aging: Do Retrieval Goals Contribute to Age-Related Memory Differences?
papers.authors: Cohen DE, Puig Rivera VA, Andrews-Hanna JR, Grilli MD.
papers.abstract: Relative to young adults, cognitively healthy older adults typically include more semantic details when narrating remembered, personal events. This age difference in autobiographical memory is mostly interpreted in the literature as a sign of cognitive and brain decline, and the consequences are largely assumed to be negative. Complementing decline-based accounts, the current perspective builds on a recent proposal that developmental changes in memory-guiding motives may help shape how and why older adults reflect on their personal past (Grilli & Sheldon, 2022). We identify theoretical support and accumulating empirical evidence suggesting that young and older adults may pursue distinct goals when retrieving autobiographical memories. A closer examination of these goals raises the possibility that young adults’ goals may be especially well served by episodically specific memories, whereas older adults’ goals may be better aligned with semantic autobiographical knowledge. Although experimentally causal evidence remains limited and an important direction for future research, the reviewed literature identifies age-related changes in retrieval goals as a plausible contributor to the semantic shift and yields testable predictions for distinguishing this account from decline-based explanations.

papers.title: Large Language Model-Based Identification of Subjective Cognitive Decline in Electronic Health Records Among Older Adults With Normal Cognitive Testing: Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.authors: Wang L, Amariglio RE, Varghese S, Tian J, Seger D, Zhou L, Marshall GA.
papers.abstract: Background Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) typically refers to self- or informant-reported decline in cognition despite the absence of objective impairment on standardized testing. Older adults with documented normal cognitive test performance provide a pragmatic anchor cohort for electronic health record (EHR)-based SCD phenotyping. However, cognitive concerns are primarily recorded in unstructured notes and are inconsistently documented, making it unclear how often and in whom concerns are captured in routine care. Objective This study aims to operationalize EHR-based SCD phenotyping in an objectively normal-testing cohort using a large language model (LLM)-based natural language processing approach and to examine the frequency and clinical and sociodemographic correlates of cognitive concern documentation. Methods We conducted an EHR-based observational study of patients aged 65 years or older with a first normal cognitive test recorded in EHR flowsheets between January 2019 and April 2024 in a large health care system. We developed and iteratively refined a 2-stage LLM-based natural language processing pipeline to identify documented cognitive concerns in unstructured notes during the 12 months prior to the index date, and evaluated performance against manual review. We quantified the frequency of documented concerns within this normal-testing cohort and used multivariable logistic regression to assess associations with sociodemographic factors (age, marital status, insurance, and neighborhood Area Deprivation Index), sequentially adjusting for clinical comorbidities and relevant medications. Results Among 15,750 older adults with normal cognitive test scores, 13.8% (n=2175) had at least 1 documented cognitive concern in the prior year, captured in 1.2% (7394/605,177) of notes. On manual validation, the 2-stage pipeline (Med42-v2-8B screening followed by GPT-4o confirmation) achieved a sensitivity of 0.957, positive predictive value of 0.935, specificity of 0.985, and F 1 -score of 0.945 for cognitive concern identification. Documentation was more likely in older individuals, those with commercial (vs Medicare) insurance, and those with neurological and psychiatric conditions. In fully adjusted models, Parkinson disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.29, 95% CI 3.60-7.77), traumatic brain injury (aOR 4.63, 95% CI 3.15-6.81), stroke or transient ischemic attack (aOR 3.46, 95% CI 3.15-4.18), epilepsy (aOR 2.52, 95% CI 1.83-3.49), depression (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.36-1.75), and excessive alcohol use (aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.06-2.06) were among the strongest correlates of cognitive concern documentation. In contrast, obesity (aOR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65-0.82), hyperlipidemia (aOR 0.59, 95% CI 0.51-0.67), and residence in more deprived neighborhoods (higher Area Deprivation Index) were associated with lower odds of documented cognitive concerns. Conclusions A 2-stage LLM pipeline enabled accurate identification of documented cognitive concerns consistent with SCD among older adults with normal cognitive testing. Documentation was uncommon and selectively captured by clinical and sociodemographic factors, with implications for equity and the validity of EHR-based phenotypes.

papers.title: Feasibility and Safety of Transcranial Focused Ultrasound on Language Impairment in a Patient with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Case Report.
papers.authors: Yan C, Zhu G, Liang S, Zhao Y, Chen W, Xia Q, Jian J, Wang Z, Zhang B, Ao L.
papers.abstract: Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is defined by persistent difficulties with social communication and language, and a subset of children stay minimally verbal despite intensive interventions. The left amygdala and ventral-anterior superior temporal sulcus (STSva) form a key circuit for social-language integration, but how transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) might modulate in minimally verbal ASD has not been explored. Case presentation An 11-year-old minimally verbal ASD boy received 4 weeks of sequential tFUS stimulation (0.5 MHz). The treatment targeted the left amygdala and STSva, five times per week. Outcome assessments included the Mandarin Clinical Evaluation of Language for Preschoolers' Core Scale (MCELP-CS), Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC), and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) at pre-tFUS, post-tFUS, and a 4-week follow-up. The boy tolerated the intervention well, with no adverse events. Significant improvements in key language skills (vocabulary naming +10%, sentence structure imitation +22%) and reduced ASD symptoms (ABC language -40%, social interaction -26%) were observed post-tFUS and sustained at follow-up. fNIRS confirmed altered cortical activation and reorganized functional connectivity in language-related brain regions.
