Results Seventeen neuroimaging reports arose from nine independent cohorts (321 enrolled patients with MDD, 293 in imaging analyses, 144 healthy controls). The most reproducible finding was bidirectional normalization in striatal-cortical reward-circuit regions across four cohorts, qualified by null nucleus accumbens and putamen seed findings in one cohort. Default-mode-network regions were implicated in seven of nine cohorts, with heterogeneous directions. The only anterior insula effect surviving between-group correction was confined to an acute stimulation-state paradigm, and stimulation-state connectivity changes were frequency-band-specific. Twenty-seven of the coded effects were explicitly null. The sole machine-learning model (AUC = 0.856) was evaluated only by internal cross-validation. Quality appraisal rated two reports high, fourteen moderate, and one low. Conclusion The evidence remains strictly hypothesis-generating: auricular vagus neuromodulation is accompanied by distributed treatment-associated brain changes, but establishes neither causal pathways nor clinically actionable imaging markers. Confirmatory multi-center, sham-controlled trials with preregistered imaging endpoints, harmonized stimulation parameters, explicit null-result reporting, and independent external validation are needed. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261421762, identifier CRD420261421762.

papers.title: Resting-state functional connectivity of hippocampal subregions in predicting escitalopram treatment outcome in major depressive disorder.
papers.authors: Zhang F, Li X, Zhang L, Zhou Y, Zhou J, Feng Y, Wang G, Yu A, Wang Y.
papers.abstract: Objective To examine whether pretreatment resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) of hippocampal subregions is associated with 12-week escitalopram treatment outcomes in major depressive disorder (MDD). Methods A total of 87 patients with MDD received 12 weeks of escitalopram monotherapy and underwent resting-state functional MRI before treatment. Based on the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-17) score at week 12, patients were classified into the remission depression group (RD, n = 42) or the nonremission depression group (NRD, n = 45). Seed-based whole-brain rsFC analyses were performed using eight bilateral hippocampal subregions as seeds. Group differences in rsFC were examined, and exploratory logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analyses were conducted to assess the discrimination of remission. Partial correlations between differential rsFC and the HAMD-17 reduction rate were calculated controlling for age, sex, and education level. Results Compared with NRD, RD showed higher pretreatment rsFC between the left hippocampal tail and the right inferior parietal lobule and lower rsFC between the right hippocampal body and the left middle occipital gyrus and between the right hippocampal tail and the right cuneus. An exploratory combined model integrating the three differential rsFC measures showed discrimination between the RD and NRD groups, with an area under the curve of 0.841 (95% confidence interval: 0.755-0.915). The HAMD-17 reduction rate was negatively associated with right hippocampal body-left middle occipital gyrus rsFC and right hippocampal tail-right cuneus rsFC, but positively associated with left hippocampal tail-right inferior parietal lobule rsFC. Conclusion Patterns of pretreatment rsFC involving the hippocampal body and tail and parietal and visual cortical regions were associated with 12-week escitalopram treatment outcomes in MDD. These connectivity measures may represent candidate imaging features for further investigation, although validation in larger independent samples is required.

papers.title: Stroboscopic light stimulation as a controllable probe of the psilocybin state: a mechanistic framework and a falsifiable prediction.
papers.authors: Żełabowski K, Wieczorek T, Hamed A.
papers.abstract: Stroboscopic light stimulation (SLS) and psilocybin each induce altered states whose phenomenology and neurophysiology partly overlap, including posterior alpha-band changes and visual imagery. The two states engage the alpha band through different operations - pharmacological suppression under psilocybin and frequency-selective visual drive under SLS. We formalize their possible interaction for prediction and falsification. The framework proposes that, by relaxing the precision weighting of high-level cortical priors and, through 5-HT2A activation, suppressing posterior alpha-band power, psilocybin creates a state in which an exogenous, frequency-controlled visual rhythm can modulate the perceiver's experience. The thesis concerns precision rather than response amplitude. Because existing neuroimaging comes mostly from eyes-closed rest, where directional evidence is contested, the falsification does not depend on which sensory-inclusive model, Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS) or cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical (CSTC), is correct. The framework predicts that, within a prespecified near-peak psilocin window, rhythmic SLS raises the Visionary Restructuralization dimension of the five-dimensional Altered States of Consciousness questionnaire (5D-ASC) relative to a luminance- and rate-matched arrhythmic control - an increase a precision framework predicts even if evoked amplitude does not rise. A complementary, report-independent endpoint, the intermodulation response to two-frequency stimulation, is proposed. State-dependence is tested as the drug-by-rhythmicity interaction in a 2 × 3 factorial design (placebo or psilocybin × rhythmic SLS, arrhythmic control, or no stimulation), with the sign of any interaction evaluated on a pre-declared scale. An adequately precise negative interaction would count against the central state-dependence prediction for the tested conditions. The framework organizes five axes around this prediction: titration of experiential intensity at fixed dose, content shaping through frequency specificity, modulation of difficult-experience phenomenology, testing whether resting-state signatures depend on sensory context, and individual-difference profiling of SLS responsiveness. The framework makes no claim of therapeutic enhancement. Its aim is mechanistic and methodological.

papers.title: Temporal association between adjunctive repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and seizure reduction in a pediatric patient with DNM1L-associated EMPF1: a case report.
papers.authors: Chen X, Sun P, Ren X, Liu G, Bai X, Guo F, Guo R, Wu S, Wang H.
papers.abstract: Background Encephalopathy, lethal, due to defective mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission 1 (EMPF1) is a rare, severe mitochondrial disorder characterized by acute-onset refractory seizures that rapidly progress to status epilepticus and are associated with a poor prognosis. Conventional therapies, including antiepileptic drugs and the ketogenic diet, exhibit limited efficacy. Although repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has shown promise in other forms of drug-resistant epilepsy, its potential role in managing EMPF1 remains unexplored. Case presentation A 7-year-old boy, previously healthy with normal development, presented with right-hand clonic movements and impaired consciousness, which progressed to status epilepticus. Brain MRI revealed diffuse cytotoxic edema involving the bilateral frontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, basal ganglia, and thalami. EEG recording showed generalized periodic spike-wave discharges with background slowing. Genetic testing identified a novel de novo DNM1L mutation (c.1949T > C, p.Leu650Pro), which was classified as likely pathogenic according to ACMG/AMP guidelines and provided strong support for the diagnosis of EMPF1. In addition to a regimen of antiepileptic drugs and a metabolic "cocktail," 1-Hz rTMS (90% of the resting motor threshold, 40 trains daily) was applied over the left primary motor cortex on Day 16. Following initiation of this combined therapy, seizure frequency was temporally associated with a marked reduction, decreasing from ∼20 to 5-6 episodes/day after one day, 2-3 by Day 27 (12 days after rTMS initiation), and 0-1 by Day 36 (21 days after rTMS initiation). Despite this reduction in clinical seizure burden, the patient developed progressive pneumonia leading to sepsis and acute heart failure, and died on Day 65 (hospital day 65). Conclusions In this case, adjunctive rTMS applied alongside standard antiepileptic and metabolic "cocktail" therapy was temporally associated with a pronounced reduction in seizure frequency in a patient with DNM1L-associated EMPF1. This temporal association is hypothesis-generating and does not permit attribution of the observed seizure reduction to rTMS; further investigation in larger cohorts is warranted.

papers.title: Case Report: Right frontal periventricular heterotopia underlying secondary network epilepsy with a Lennox-Gastaut phenotype: multimodal SEEG, CCEP, and rs-fMRI evidence.
papers.authors: Wang C, Hong J, Ji J, Zhang C, Chen W, Xu J.
papers.abstract: Objective Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) is generally regarded as a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy involving distributed brain networks, although a focal structural abnormality may occasionally recruit bilateral cortical and thalamic circuits and produce an LGS phenotype. We characterized the spatiotemporal organization of such a network and its changes after focal SEEG-guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RF-TC). Methods A 50-year-old woman with drug-resistant epilepsy, multiple seizure types, diffuse slow spike-and-wave discharges, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, intellectual impairment, and right frontal periventricular heterotopia (PVH) underwent stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG). Cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) were acquired before and after SEEG-guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RF-TC). Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI), obtained before and 3 months after RF-TC, was analyzed using three seeds: the entire right frontal PVH and the right and left centromedian thalamic nuclei (CM). Results SEEG identified the earliest sustained ictal activity within the sampled right frontal PVH-related medial contacts, accompanied by high-frequency activity. This was followed by ipsilateral lateral frontal recruitment, contralateral frontal synchronization, and subsequent bilateral CM involvement. Two-stage RF-TC of the onset and early-recruited networks was followed by seizure freedom through 9 months. After RF-TC, right-sided stimulation produced markedly attenuated lesion-related CCEP responses, whereas left-sided responses and responses between thalamic contacts showed little appreciable change. Descriptive rs-fMRI difference maps demonstrated decreased local frontal connectivity around the treated territory and increased long-range connectivity for the PVH seed; both CM seeds showed predominantly increased connectivity with distributed cortical and cerebellar regions. Conclusion In this patient, a focal PVH-related epileptogenic network was associated with secondary bilateral cortical and thalamic recruitment underlying an LGS phenotype. CCEP and rs-fMRI captured complementary aspects of postoperative network change: attenuation of stimulation-evoked propagation and postoperative changes in intrinsic functional connectivity, respectively.

papers.title: Decoding user satisfaction during reading of pre-defined question-answer pairs: BCI approach using delta and gamma EEG.
papers.authors: Park W, Mansour S, Kim L, Eid M.
papers.abstract: Introduction The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has intensified the need for robust evaluation frameworks to align artificial intelligence (AI) behavior with human expectations. While current reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) strategies heavily rely on explicit, post-hoc self-reports, these metrics are fundamentally limited by subjective biases and user non-compliance. Methods To address this, the current study presents a novel brain-computer interface (BCI) framework that systematically characterizes the continuous, implicit neural correlates of user satisfaction and dissatisfaction during a reading-based evaluative task involving pre-validated LLM-generated question-answer pairs. Sixty-four-channel electroencephalography (EEG) data were recorded from 30 participants while they read and evaluated various LLM-generated responses. To capture genuine subjective experiences, individual trials were relabeled based on post-trial 5-point Likert scale ratings into five distinct evaluative states, and spatiotemporal spectral analyses were performed. A ShallowFBCSPNet architecture was further used to evaluate single-trial classification between the very satisfied and very dissatisfied conditions under a subject-mixed cross-validation scheme. Results Spatiotemporal spectral analyses revealed distinct neural oscillatory dynamics that temporally dissociate satisfaction and dissatisfaction. When reading highly satisfactory responses, a pronounced, sustained enhancement of low-frequency delta power was observed within the bilateral frontotemporal areas during the middle (4-8 s) and late (8-12 s) reading intervals, indexing high-order cognitive consolidation and reward processing. Conversely, processing highly dissatisfactory responses led to a localized suppression of high-frequency gamma power in the right frontotemporal region during the early interval (0-4 s), reflecting an immediate affective appraisal and expectation violation. Utilizing the ShallowFBCSPNet architecture, the system successfully discriminated between the "very satisfied" and "very dissatisfied" states, achieving an average accuracy of 81% under a subject-mixed cross-validation scheme. Discussion These findings demonstrate that user evaluative states are encoded via distinct frequency-specific cortical networks over differing temporal windows. By bridging cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence, this study establishes the conceptual and empirical foundation for passive BCI-driven implicit feedback channels, laying groundwork toward future real-time paradigms for next-generation LLM alignment; the classification result should be interpreted as a feasibility demonstration rather than an estimate of real-world decoding accuracy.

papers.title: Complementary white matter networks support flexible concept learning.
papers.authors: Gumus M, Alizadeh Saghati N, Mack ML.
papers.abstract: Introduction Concept learning is not an isolated act of cognition; it recruits a host of core mechanisms, including working memory, decision making, and attention. A wide range of brain networks spanning cortical and subcortical areas support these operations, which have been identified via activation patterns related to concept learning. A critical open question, however, is whether the white matter architecture connecting these regions serves as the structural scaffold that makes such flexible learning possible. Methods We employed a rule-plus-exception learning paradigm wherein participants categorized visually complex stimuli. While some items closely followed the rules, exceptions violated them, acting as a behavioural index of flexible learning. We quantified the integrity of white matter tracts across the whole human brain using diffusion-weighted imaging and leveraged correlational tractography to uncover their behavioural relevance. Results Correlational tractography revealed two distinct white matter networks associated with individual variability in either rule or exception learning. The network supporting exception learning was predominantly subcortical-limbic, comprising the fornix, thalamic radiations, and forceps minor alongside the left frontal-parietal cingulum, a pattern consistent with hippocampal-prefrontal communication and cognitive control over atypical exemplars. Conversely, the network for rule-based items was distinguished by long-range cortico-cortical and cortico-cerebellar pathways, including the right frontal-parietal cingulum, the middle longitudinal fasciculus, and the middle cerebellar peduncle, reflecting the integration of visual features with abstract rule representations and their gradual automatization. Discussion These findings provide novel evidence that complementary white matter networks support flexible concept formation and offer a neuroanatomical basis for characterizing individual differences in flexible concept learning.

papers.title: CLSP-REQA: a real-time quality-aware closed-loop seizure prediction framework with Mamba-BiLSTM and confidence-gated intervention.
papers.authors: Chen M, Wu Q, Huang B, Lai X, Chen Z, Ouyang X, Ren Q.
papers.abstract: Introduction Reliable seizure prediction is a prerequisite for closed-loop neurostimulation therapy, yet existing methods rarely account for the variability in EEG signal quality encountered in real-world deployment, and the overwhelming majority adopt non-strict evaluation protocols that overestimate generalization performance. Methods We propose CLSP-REQA (Closed-Loop Seizure Prediction with Real-time EEG Quality Assessment), a unified framework that embeds a lightweight signal quality estimator directly within the prediction pipeline. A Real-time EEG Quality Assessment (REQA) module runs in parallel with a Mamba-BiLSTM backbone, producing a scalar quality score q ∈ [0, 1] that modulates output confidence through a tiered non-linear fusion function (ECLO). We conducted dedicated experiments testing whether this learned score reflects genuine signal quality rather than a redundant proxy for the prediction task, and a sensitivity analysis of the fusion thresholds against standard calibration baselines. The framework was evaluated under strict cross-patient evaluation on the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG Database (n = 23 subjects, 198 seizures) and the SIENA Scalp EEG Database (n = 14 subjects, 47 seizures). Results On CHB-MIT, CLSP-REQA achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.7426 ± 0.0199, exceeding the unadapted cross-patient baseline of 0.69 reported by Jemal et al., using only 16 EEG channels compared to 23 in prior work, and without requiring any target-patient data or domain adaptation. On SIENA, CLSP-REQA achieved an AUC of 0.7012 ± 0.0249, exceeding the best domain-adapted cross-patient result of 0.61 on the same dataset under a strictly harder information constraint, since domain adaptation methods are given access to unlabelled target-patient data that CLSP-REQA does not use. Discussion The framework outputs a structured four-tuple 〈p, q, c , ΦSHAP 〉 designed for compatibility with closed-loop neurostimulator interfaces. As both evaluation datasets are retrospective recordings from controlled hospital settings, we report this study as a feasibility demonstration rather than evidence of prospective, real-world clinical readiness, and the comparison with domain adaptation should not be read as unconditional superiority.

papers.title: A consistent vigor network in Parkinson's disease: a potential target for brain stimulation effects.
papers.authors: Kavian Z, Hajipour Sardouie S, Arasteh E, Mirian MS, Sreenivasan V, Yazdani M, McKeown MJ.
papers.abstract: Introduction In motor tasks with repetitive trials, motor vigor varies substantially from trial to trial in people with Parkinson's disease (PD). A key question is whether neural variability reflects behavioral variability or whether additional variability emerges as the neural signal is translated into movement. We aimed to identify a vigor-related neural network that could provide a candidate target for brain stimulation. Methods We analyzed individual-trial fMRI data from 18 participants with PD who performed an overlearned ballistic hand-squeeze task in OFF- and ON-medication sessions while receiving subthreshold galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS) with different stimulus waveforms. Single-trial fMRI responses were estimated using GLMsingle and entered into a constrained optimisation framework designed to identify a network that was task-active, encoded behavior, showed low trial-to-trial variability, and was spatially coherent. Results The analysis identified a distributed vigor network whose activity remained related to behavioral vigor while showing lower variability than behavior itself. The network included motor, striatal, cerebellar, thalamic, parietal, temporal-limbic, and orbitofrontal regions and showed limited overlap with the standard task-activation map. GVS waveforms associated with faster responses were accompanied by corresponding changes in vigor-network activity, but not in the broader task-activation network. Dopaminergic medication was also associated with stronger local functional connectivity within the vigor network. Discussion These findings suggest that movement variability in PD may arise partly when a relatively stable central vigor-related command is translated downstream into movement. The identified network may therefore provide a potential target for neuromodulation approaches aimed at increasing motor vigor in people with PD. Independent validation and future causal testing are needed.

papers.title: Exploring partially shared valuation-related neural responses between abstract desirability and food incentive evaluation.
papers.authors: Chen R, Wang F.
papers.abstract: Motivational evaluation can generalize across diverse goals, while the incentive value of biologically relevant stimuli such as food is dynamically modulated by physiological need. The present study examined whether cross-category desirability evaluation under a non-deprived baseline condition and food incentive evaluation under experimentally manipulated Hunger and Satiety states show partially similar valuation-related neural responses within the same individuals. Participants underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) while completing two complementary experiments: an abstract desirability judgment task involving objects, events, and persons, and a food evaluation task conducted under Hunger and Satiety states. In the DESIRE experiment, neural responses associated with desirable versus undesirable judgments were examined across three semantic categories to identify candidate neural patterns related to abstract desirability evaluation. In the HUNGER experiment, analyses examined both baseline food incentive value and hunger-related increases in food desirability. Exploratory whole-brain analyses identified activation patterns involving medial frontal and cingulate valuation-related regions, including the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC), during abstract desirability evaluation. Exploratory maps in baseline food incentive-value evaluation analysis also implicated medial frontal and cingulate valuation-related regions. In addition, food items whose desirability increased under hunger showed greater activation than rating-stable food items in the left inferior orbitofrontal cortex, together with visual, cerebellar, and sensorimotor regions. However, formal conjunction-null analyses, ROI-based convergence analyses, whole-brain overlap analyses, and permutation-based tests did not provide evidence for a statistically robust shared neural representation across abstract desirability and food valuation. These findings suggest that cross-category desirability evaluation and homeostatically modulated food incentive evaluation may involve partially overlapping valuation-related processes while remaining sensitive to semantic context and physiological state. The results provide preliminary support for the possibility that abstract motivational cognition may partially engage valuation-related processes that are also involved in physiological incentive evaluation.

papers.title: Differential mechanisms of continuous theta burst stimulation and low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for chronic tinnitus: preliminary efficacy dissociation by local focalization vs. network dispersion.
papers.authors: Zhang M, Qin L, Jin E, Shi C, Ni J, Wang J, Gao S, Ma Y, Li X, Li Y.
papers.abstract: Objective This study aimed to preliminarily compare clinical efficacy and neural mechanisms of continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) and low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) targeting the auditory cortex in chronic subjective tinnitus. Differential effects on tinnitus loudness and distress, as well as the moderating role of disease duration, were explored. Methods Twenty-nine patients were randomly assigned to cTBS (n = 16) or rTMS (n = 13) groups. Neuronavigation-guided stimulation was applied to the individualized auditory cortex peak activation site. Outcome measures included the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at baseline, post-treatment, 1-month, and 3-month follow-ups. Resting-state fMRI was used to analyze amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF) and regional homogeneity (ReHo). Functional connectivity (FC) analysis was performed to explore the network-level changes. Results Clinically, cTBS was associated with a rapid reduction in VAS-rated tinnitus loudness (p = 0.004), while low-frequency rTMS demonstrated sustained improvements in THI scores up to the 3-month follow-up (p = 0.007). Mixed-model ANCOVA yielded significant time-by-group interactions for THI and VAS, verifying different therapeutic profiles between cTBS and rTMS. Resting-state fMRI uncovered separable brain plasticity: cTBS induced focal changes in left auditory cortex, whereas rTMS remodeled extensive limbic-cognitive networks. Two-way ANCOVA confirmed shared left prefrontal interaction signals, supporting stronger prefrontal suppression by cTBS. Baseline tinnitus duration was negatively correlated with 3-month THI improvement rates. Collectively, clinical and dual resting-state imaging results identified separable therapeutic and neuromodulatory signatures of cTBS and low-frequency rTMS. Conclusion Our exploratory results suggest that cTBS may facilitate a rapid reduction in tinnitus loudness possibly through focal auditory modulation, while low-frequency rTMS eases persistent tinnitus distress through large-scale network remodeling. Our findings provide preliminary evidence for the divergent prefrontal inhibitory profiles of the two inhibitory protocols. Shorter tinnitus duration predicts better therapeutic outcomes, highlighting the value of early intervention. These exploratory results provide evidence for personalized TMS-based neuromodulation in chronic tinnitus.

papers.title: Increased visual reliance for postural control in multiple sclerosis: preliminary evidence from task-related cortical desynchronization.
papers.authors: Braunsmann L, Stolz I, Rosiny F, Pöhlau D, Abeln V, Schneider S, Abel T, Knaepen K.
papers.abstract: Background Balance impairment is one of the most disabling symptoms in multiple sclerosis (MS), yet the underlying cortical mechanisms remain poorly understood. This exploratory study investigated how postural demands modulate brain activity in MS. Methods Seven individuals with MS (mean age: 51.1 ± 9.7 years; 5 women; median Expanded Disability Status Scale: 5.5, IQR: 4.5-6.0) and seven age- and sex-matched healthy controls (mean age: 51.0 ± 9.6 years) performed three static balance tasks on a force plate: quiet stance with eyes open, quiet stance with eyes closed, and narrow stance with eyes open. Electroencephalography (EEG) and center of pressure (COP) were simultaneously recorded. Group differences were assessed using Linear Mixed Models. Significant effects are reported with false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected q -values, and otherwise with uncorrected p -values. Results MS patients demonstrated greater postural sway than healthy controls, with FDR-corrected group × condition interactions across COP parameters (semi-partial R 2 = 0.225-0.441; all q < 0.05), most pronounced during eyes closed (semi-partial R 2 = 0.124-0.282; all p < 0.05). Resting-state EEG revealed no consistent group differences except for an uncorrected elevation of occipital theta power in MS patients (p = 0.017; r = -0.76). During stance, uncorrected group × condition interactions indicated that MS patients exhibited a greater task-induced decrease of theta, alpha, and beta power relative to their matched resting baseline compared to healthy controls (semi-partial R 2 = 0.193-0.318; all p < 0.05). These effects were specific to the eyes-closed condition. Conclusion These preliminary findings are consistent with an increased reliance on visual information for postural control in MS, accompanied by a task-related cortical desynchronization specifically upon visual deprivation. The observed effect sizes, while likely subject to inflation given the small sample size, suggest that oscillatory EEG parameters warrant investigation in larger confirmatory studies.

papers.title: Comparative evaluation of diffusion models for detecting gray matter microstructural alterations in post-stroke depression patients.
papers.authors: Zhang F, Zhang J, Zhang L, Jin H, Li D, Zhao W.
papers.abstract: Background Post-stroke depression (PSD) is often underdiagnosed because its gray matter microstructural abnormalities can be subtle. This study compared four diffusion models (DTI, DKI, MAP, and NODDI) to identify objective imaging biomarkers for the early detection of PSD. Methods Sixty-four participants were enrolled, including 23 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC), 26 patients with acute cerebral infarction without PSD (non-PSD; HAMD-21 < 7), and 15 patients with PSD (HAMD-21 ≥ 7). Clinical assessments (HAMD-21, ADL, MoCA, and MMSE) and diffusion spectrum imaging were performed. Intergroup differences in gray matter microstructure, diagnostic performance based on the area under the curve (AUC), and partial correlations adjusted for age, sex, and years of education were analyzed. Infarct location was not included as a covariate. Results Significant differences among the three groups were observed in age, years of education, and all clinical scale scores (p < 0.05). Altered gray matter microstructure was primarily identified in the middle frontal gyrus, posterior cingulate gyrus, paracingulate gyrus and amygdala. For group discrimination, the left anterior cingulate DKI MD_p10 demonstrated the best performance for distinguishing HC from non-PSD (AUC = 0.916). The left putamen NODDI ODI_p10 showed the highest AUC (0.916) for distinguishing HC from PSD, whereas the left putamen NODDI ODI_p50 yielded the highest AUC (0.856) for distinguishing non-PSD from PSD. After FDR correction, multiple diffusion metrics were significantly correlated with MMSE and MoCA scores, whereas no imaging parameter showed a significant correlation with HAMD-21. Conclusion Multimodal diffusion MRI detects microstructural abnormalities within emotion- and cognition-related circuits, particularly the amygdala and cingulate cortex, across the three groups. Temporolimbic NODDI parameters showed relatively higher AUC values in distinguishing PSD from HC, whereas anterior cingulate DKI metrics showed relatively higher AUC values in differentiating non-PSD stroke patients from HC. Combining multiple diffusion models may aid in the identification of PSD; however, these findings require further validation because infarct location was not adjusted for in the analyses.
keywords: Neurite Orientation Dispersion And Density Imaging

papers.title: An innovative framework based on GMV-ALFF multi-modal MRI and Gaussian data augmentation for psychiatric disorder classification.
papers.authors: Zhu W, Jiang X.
papers.abstract: Objective Schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) exhibit significant overlap in clinical symptoms, posing substantial challenges to accurate diagnosis. This study proposes an innovative multi-modal fusion framework based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), integrating structural and functional MRI biomarkers-gray matter volume (GMV) and amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF). Methods Total 31 patients with schizophrenia, 48 patients with bipolar disorder, and 38 healthy controls (HC) were enrolled and underwent resting-state fMRI scans. The framework comprises three core components: Gaussian data augmentation to mitigate the limitation of small sample sizes; a dedicated CNN architecture for processing GMV and ALFF features to generate class probability outputs for SZ, BD, and HC; and DempsterShafer (D-S) evidence theory for robust multi-modal decision fusion. Results Extensive 5-fold cross-validation confirms the framework's efficacy: it achieves superior performance metrics (Accuracy: 0.9656 ± 0.0324, Precision: 0.9698 ± 0.0319, Recall: 0.9656 ± 0.0324, F1-Score: 0.9661 ± 0.0324) and outperforms traditional machine learning methods (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, KNN). Conclusion The findings demonstrate that the proposed multi-modal fusion approach enhances the ability to differentiate among SZ, BD, and HC compared to unimodal classification methods, providing a reliable technical support for the auxiliary diagnosis of psychiatric disorders.

papers.title: Resting-state cortical alpha frequency in Parkinson's disease and multiple system atrophy: associations with diagnosis, age, and symptom burden.
papers.authors: Chen D, Tang H, Pan Y, Sang H, Gu S, Wang X, Li K, Li F, Sun Y, Chen J, Sun W, Zhang J, Wang Z, Wei L.
papers.abstract: Background Parkinson's disease (PD) and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are clinically overlapping neurodegenerative disorders that present with a complex, heterogeneous burden of motor and non-motor symptoms. Resting-state EEG reveals that cortical alpha slowing is a hallmark of pathological aging, yet its specific presence and clinical significance in these distinct synucleinopathies remain incompletely understood. Therefore, precisely quantifying the individual alpha frequency serves as a critical, non-invasive approach to characterize cortical network dysfunction across synucleinopathies and evaluate how aging moderates its association with clinical symptom burden. Methods We analyzed source-reconstructed resting-state EEG data from 104 participants, comprising patients with PD, patients with the parkinsonian (MSA-P) and cerebellar subtypes (MSA-C) of MSA, and healthy controls. To accurately capture oscillatory dynamics, a data-driven masking empirical mode decomposition approach was applied to extract the individual alpha frequency across canonical cortical networks. General linear models tested diagnostic group differences, age-related effects, and age-dependent associations between individual alpha frequency and clinical symptom scores. Results Relative to healthy controls, both PD and MSA-C exhibited significant lower cortical IAF, whereas MSA-P showed no significant global IAF difference. At the network level, significant reduction of IAF was detected in the visual and dorsal attention networks in both PD and MSA-C. Advancing age independently contributed to alpha slowing across all participants without accelerating the disease-related trajectories. Notably, chronological age significantly moderated the relationship between alpha slowing and non-motor symptoms. In older patients, reduced individual alpha frequency was strongly associated with a higher burden of overall non-motor, autonomic, and psychiatric/cognitive symptoms, a relationship not observed in younger patients or with motor symptom severity. Conclusion Cortical alpha slowing was detected in PD and MSA-C, but not in MSA-P. Age independently contributes to alpha slowing and strengthens its association with non-motor symptom burden, supporting age-aware interpretation of resting-state electroencephalography biomarkers in synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Delusion-related aberrant prediction errors are bottom-up
papers.authors: Fan S, Castiello S, Meyer M, Suthaharan P, Kenney J, Hauke DJ, Adams R, Bansal S, Waltz J, Erickson MA, Gold J, Corlett PR.
papers.abstract: Background: Delusions are the fixed false beliefs that characterize serious mental illnesses like schizophrenia. Prediction errors are surprise signals that guide learning. They have been observed during causal learning in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC). They are registered inappropriately in people with delusions, driving learning towards irrelevant events. This learning correlates with delusion severity. We do not know, however, whether the rDLPFC is receiving the error signal, bottom-up, from other nodes, or, alternatively, whether rDLPFC prediction errors are communicated top-down from rDLPFC. It is also possible that the direction of processing differs between patients with delusions compared with otherwise healthy individuals who espouse delusion-like beliefs but are not delusional per se. Methods: Here, we attempt to distinguish these possibilities using cognitive computational neuroimaging, functional, and effective connectivity analyses of task-based fMRI data in people with schizophrenia (SZ, n=29), people with extreme esoteric beliefs (EEB, n=25), and controls with neither (CTR, n=24), focusing on prediction error processing. Results: During Kamin Blocking of causal learning people who endorse delusions evince aberrant prediction error signals in right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and anterior insula which correlate with delusion severity. Psychophysiological interaction analysis reveals errant coupling between these regions in people with delusions. Effective connectivity analysis locates the dysfunction in schizophrenia to bottom-up prediction error drive from insula to DLPFC. Conclusion: These data provide quantitative computational metrics for distinguishing delusions from other less problematic beliefs and establish that, in schizophrenia, aberrant prediction errors during causal learning arise from errant bottom-up drive from the insula to the rDLPFC. This may then serve as a marker for clinically relevant odd belief and a target for treatment.

papers.title: Human similarity judgments reveal fine-grained representations of relationships and actions in dynamic social scenes
papers.authors: Garcia K, Isik L.
papers.abstract: How does the human mind organize dynamic social scenes? Existing accounts typically rely on pre-defined social-affective or action-based taxonomies, yet whether humans use these dimensions to structure their representations remains largely unknown. We collected 53,223 odd-one-out triplet similarity judgments from 232 participants on 250 naturalistic dyadic-interaction videos and trained a sparse-positive embedding model to recover the underlying latent dimensions. We show the learned dimensions explain twice as much variance in similarity judgments as pre-labeled annotations, capture interpretable fine-grained social-event structure (combining information about social relationships with actions), and fractionate broad semantic content (e.g., parent-child interactions separate into caregiving versus affectionate play). The same dimensions predict fMRI responses in the visual cortex, including lateral visual pathway and superior temporal sulcus, better than pre-labeled annotations. Together, these results suggest that human representations of social scenes combine social relationships and actions in ways that pre-defined taxonomies miss, offering a behaviorally grounded target for future studies of social vision.

papers.title: Beyond Fuel: Metabolic Intermediates as Signaling Molecules in Neuroinflammation and Neurodegeneration.
papers.authors: Wang S, Wang S, Sun Y, Zhang S, Wu J, Xie D.
papers.abstract: Historically, research has viewed substantial brain metabolic activity through the lens of energy production, primarily treating metabolites as substrates and products in bioenergetic pathways. However, this paradigm is now evolving. Key metabolic intermediates are recognized not only as components of Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) synthesis, but also as potent signaling molecules that establish intricate communication networks. This "metabolic signaling language" profoundly influences inflammation, epigenetics, and cell fate by translating cellular metabolic conditions into certain functional outcomes. In this review, three prototypical metabolites, namely succinate, itaconate, and α-Ketoglutarate (α-KG), were discussed. We investigated succinate accumulation during ischemia and mitochondrial stress, which serves as an early alarm that drives inflammation through both intracellular and extracellular receptor-mediated mechanisms. Conversely, itaconate, an inducible metabolite produced by myeloid cells, exerts inhibitory effects and actively alleviates inflammation by covalently modifying proteins. Finally, we highlighted α-KG, a central metabolic hub that links metabolic status to cellular identity and aging by epigenetically regulating DNA and histone demethylase activity. By summarizing the functions of these metabolites across neurological disorders, including ischemic stroke, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis, we delineate a fundamental layer of biological regulation. Deciphering and therapeutic modulation of this metabolic language represent a frontier in neuroscience, offering novel targets for intractable neurological diseases.

papers.title: The ballon model revisited
papers.authors: Gore J, Lee T, Jiaao Y, Knutsson AL, boschen w, Li M, Schilling KG, Anderson AW, Ding Z, Gao Y.
papers.abstract: Abstract Functional MRI based on the blood oxygenation level–dependent (BOLD) effect infers neural activity from hemodynamic changes through a hemodynamic response function (HRF). We revisit the balloon model of the BOLD effect and show that Grubb’s empirical flow–volume power law can be used to determine how vascular transit time varies with flow and is governed by a single index of venous distensibility. Linearizing the resulting equations yields an explicit closed-form HRF, expressed in physiologically recognizable parameters, that reproduces the canonical response. The initial dip, time to peak and poststimulus undershoot are each traced to identifiable terms, and the relations assumed in calibrated BOLD signals emerge as outputs. When oxygen consumption is specified independently of flow, as in earlier generalizations, the analytic solution quantifies the specific relationships between the latency and depth of an initial dip and a neurovascular delay. The new model will prove useful for explaining variations in HRF in white matter, across the brain, and between different populations.

papers.title: Language of Hope in Conversations between Pediatric Oncologists, Children with Advanced Cancer, and their Families
papers.authors: Mali NV, Humphrey C, Porter A, Kaye EC, Superdock AK.
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose : Hope is a key driver of coping and decision-making for children with cancer and their families. Prior studies have shown that hope is bolstered, not fractured, by high-quality prognostic communication. However, clinicians describe a tension between conveying hope and honestly discussing poor prognosis. This prospective longitudinal observational study aimed to identify and characterize communication approaches used by oncologists and parents to navigate hope in the context of poor prognosis. Methods : Serial conversations between pediatric patients with poor-prognosis brain tumors, their families, and their medical teams were audio-recorded at disease reevaluation timepoints for up to 24 months or until death. Rapid qualitative analysis was used to characterize the frequency and content of hope-related dialogue. Results : 132 conversations were recorded for 30 brain tumor patient-parent-oncologist triads. Hope-related dialogue was identified in 73 (55%) of encounters. Oncologists introduced hope language in about two-thirds of these conversations. Hope dialogue could be described along two dimensions: temporal orientation and desired outcomes. Temporally, hope appeared in conversations as prospective, retrospective, or negated. Desired outcomes included hope for cure, hope for remission, hope for life prolongation and meaningful experiences, and hope for symptom management and comfort at the end of life. Conclusion : Hope dialogue may be an entry point for aligning with families, exploring prognostic understanding, and opening the door to deeper conversations about reframing hopes and goals of care. Future work should explore development of strategies to elicit and respond to patient and family hopes across the cancer trajectory.

papers.title: The Half of Everything: Glucose Imbalance Hazards and Brain Vulnerability at the Extremes of Life
papers.authors: Canepa M, Panfoli I, Mangini S, Calandrino A, Vinci F, Malova M, Striano P, Gagliardi L, Ramenghi L.
papers.abstract: Glucose is more than an energetic substrate: its homeostasis emerges from continuous interactions between peripheral glucose-regulatory organs and the brain, where glucose availability, sensing, and utilization must be dynamically matched to metabolic demands. This narrative review examines how disruption of this balance may intersect with oxidative stress, inflammation, and brain vulnerability at the extremes of life. In preterm neonates, the definition of pathological glycaemic states remains heterogeneous, while hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia, and particularly glycaemic variability may represent different manifestations of dysglycaemia within an immature homeostatic system. Experimental and clinical evidence links these disturbances, with different degrees of certainty, to oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, adverse neurological outcomes, and white matter vulnerability. The developing brain is particularly susceptible to redox imbalance because of maturation-dependent antioxidant defenses and the vulnerability of developing white matter. At the opposite extreme of life, aging is accompanied by alterations in cerebral glucose and energy metabolism, while neurodegenerative disorders show disturbances in glucose transport and utilization together with mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammation, and neuronal and white matter abnormalities. We propose the Biochemical and Physiological Mirror as a conceptual interpretation of these apparently distant conditions: developmental immaturity and age-related decline represent distinct biological trajectories that may converge on partially shared glucose–redox–inflammatory intersections. Within the Crossword Effect, glucose therefore acquires biological meaning not as an isolated concentration but through its context-dependent relationships with metabolic, redox, inflammatory, cellular, and developmental information. Viewing dysglycaemia as a systems-level disturbance rather than solely as deviation from a numerical threshold may provide a more integrated framework for understanding brain vulnerability across the lifespan.

papers.title: Activity and Functional Connectivity of Lumbar Spinal Interneurons at Rest: Irregular, Sparse yet Structured.
papers.authors: Mousa MH, Zaback M, Lemay MA, Thompson CK.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: Spinal interneurons are central to sensorimotor integration. Even in the absence of overt sensory inputs or motor output, spinal interneurons remain active, yet their functional organization across spatial and temporal scales remains poorly understood. We characterized the discharge properties and functional connectivity of 2,847 lumbar spinal interneurons recorded in vivo from quiescent decerebrate cats (three males, five females) using microelectrode arrays inserted into rostral (L3-L4) and caudal (L5-L7) spinal segments at superficial (0-1,500 µm) and deep (1,500-3,000 µm) depths. Superficial neurons generally discharged at higher and less variable rates than deeper neurons, forming a consistent depth-dependent gradient at both segments. Functional connectivity was sparse yet structured, with distinct depth profiles across timescales. Short-timescale correlations (±10 ms) occurred in ∼2% of neuron pairs, which were predominantly excitatory and prominent caudally at ∼1,500 µm depth. Longer-timescale correlations (∼400 ms) were similarly rare but showed equal proportions of excitation and inhibitory and were more pronounced at deeper depths. Graph-theoretic network analysis showed that timescale-specific correlations are architecturally distinct and nonrandomly organized. Short-timescale networks exhibited depth-specific hubs near 1,500 µm and lower clustering, whereas longer-timescale networks showed more clustering. At the ensemble level, neurons shared low-frequency oscillatory drive, particularly in rostral recordings. Separately, a subset of ensembles with dense short-timescale connectivity were consistently observed near 1,500 µm in the caudal array, linking slow and fast interactions. Together, these findings show that spinal interneuron circuitry exhibits spatially and temporally structured organization even at rest, establishing a critical baseline for studies of spinal injury and disease.

papers.title: Right Brain: Language Without Speech.
papers.authors: Sai Shreya V, Harshil Sai V.
papers.abstract: During a neurology rotation as a second-year internal medicine resident, I encountered a preschool-aged child whose absence of spontaneous speech initially framed my clinical thinking. Although she did not answer direct questions, she demonstrated an unexpected facility with written language, reading words from books with ease and engaging with the world through visual and textual cues. Over subsequent encounters, I witnessed the gradual evolution of her communication and the adjustments made by her mother, whose daily life had become shaped by therapies, routines, and the uncertainties surrounding developmental differences. As diagnostic labels accumulated and interventions unfolded, I found myself relying on familiar developmental frameworks and searching for deficits that would explain what I observed. Yet the child's strengths, her self-taught reading, sustained engagement with books, and emerging use of words and phrases challenged those expectations. Progress appeared not through dramatic milestones but through small changes that accumulated over time. The experience reshaped my understanding of communication and clinical observation. Rather than viewing silence solely as absence, I learned to recognize forms of language that existed outside the pathways I had been trained to expect. The encounter also revealed how much of medical training is oriented toward identifying what is missing and how easily strengths can be overlooked when they do not fit conventional frameworks. This reflection explores the distinction between speech and language and the importance of remaining attentive to the many ways meaning can be expressed.

papers.title: EXPRESS: BOLD Contrast in Cerebral Diffuse Glioma Imaging: Biological Foundations and Clinical Applications - A Review of the Literature.
papers.authors: Strangis F, Schmidlechner T, Jehli E, Bellomo J, Gönel M, Zerweck L, Sebök M, van Niftrik CHB, Ricciardi L, Romano A, Bozzao A, Serra C, Razansky D, Weller M, Kulcsar Z, Bink A, Regli L, Stumpo V, Fierstra J.
papers.journal: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism
papers.abstract: Diffuse cerebral gliomas are the most common malignant brain tumors in adults. In the present work we conducted a narrative review on the role of blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD)-MRI in diffuse glioma imaging, from historical and clinical applications to recent translational studies including approaches to detect vascular and metabolic alterations as well as its expanding potential to enhance tumor infiltration assessment and treatment surveillance. Task-based and resting-state BOLD-MRI enable localization of eloquent cortical areas and assessment of functional reorganization, though their accuracy is challenged by neurovascular uncoupling and patient-related variability. Combination with vasoactive stimuli allows cerebrovascular reactivity mapping to uncover vascular dysfunction propagating beyond visible tumor margins, correlating with tumor grade and hemodynamic impairment. Quantitative and calibrated BOLD approaches as well as oxygen modulation during BOLD sequence acquisition provide noninvasive biomarkers of tissue hypoxia, oxygen metabolism, and tumor aggressiveness. Despite extensive research, BOLD contrast holds unexploited potential for enhancing glioma diagnosis and management by capturing critical vascular and metabolic alterations. Although challenges remain pertaining to accuracy and standardization, emerging techniques offer substantial potential for the assessment of tumor infiltration extent and therapy surveillance. Advancing clinical integration will require robust standardization, large-scale validation, and correlation with clinical, molecular, and histopathological data.

papers.title: Mind the brain age: How segmentation and template selection reshape structural connectomes.
papers.authors: Ferritto C, Lioi G, Jonin PY, Coloigner J.
papers.abstract: Diffusion-weighted MRI samples the directional diffusion of water in vivo, and tractography uses this information to reconstruct brain fiber pathways. Mapping streamlines to an anatomical parcellation yields structural connectomes. However, in older adults, where white matter alterations and atrophy are common, the choice of reference template and tissue segmentation could be particularly consequential for obtaining accurate, interpretable structural connectomes. Using a conventional pipeline, we evaluated how these two factors, the normalization template and the segmentation used to constrain anatomically guided tractography, affect connectome estimates in cognitively healthy elderly participants. These methodological choices produced systematic and significant differences in network topology and their relationships with clinically relevant variables across standard connectome measures, particularly in patients with white matter hyperintensities. Age-appropriate normalization and lesion-aware anatomically constrained tractography yielded networks with more plausible anatomy and more consistent relationships with cognition and imaging measures, whereas unconstrained tracking inflated density without improving interpretability. These findings demonstrate that structural connectome outcomes are contingent upon template and segmentation selection. We, therefore, advocate for explicit reporting of these methodological parameters and recommend the use of age-appropriate templates combined with white matter lesion-aware segmentation incorporating anatomically informed constraints.

papers.title: Brain network differences in second language learning depend on individual competencies.
papers.authors: Skieresz NH, Marca SC, Murray MM, Reber TP, Rothen N.
papers.abstract: Integrating new words into an existing semantic network is a core challenge of second language (L2) acquisition. We investigated how evidence-based learning strategies and individual performance relate to the neurocognitive dynamics of vocabulary learning. Eighty-three adults proficient in German or French learned 48 Finnish (L2) nouns over 14 days using a mobile app that systematically varied retrieval practice, corrective feedback, multisensory learning, and distributed learning. Before and after training, EEG was recorded during a translation recognition task designed to elicit the N400, an index of semantic integration. Vocabulary accuracy increased from 0.41% pre-learning to 75.5% post-learning (dz = 3.96), and the N400 incongruity effect increased significantly, F (1, 75) = 99.52, p < .001, η²g = .32, reflecting successful integration of new L2 words into the mental lexicon. High performers showed larger N400 responses, consistent with more differentiated semantic processing. In addition, performance group differences emerged in event-related potential (ERP) template-map preponderance (i.e., the proportion of epoch time points assigned to a given template map), indicating differences in processing dynamics and network configurations. Despite systematic manipulation of learning strategies, no single approach yielded consistent behavioral or neural advantages, suggesting that overall exposure and cumulative practice, rather than any specific strategy, may have been primary contributors to the observed learning gains. ERP template-map analyses further revealed that learning not only increased neural responses but also shifted map preponderance within the N400 window as a function of Session and Congruency, indicating a qualitative reorganization of semantic processing. These findings suggest that vocabulary learning success is more closely related to the degree of semantic integration than to any single instructional strategy.

papers.title: Authentic participatory research with older adults for cognitive health (APROACH) in rural Botswana and urban Montreal: protocol for a pilot randomised controlled trial.
papers.authors: Andersson N, Cockcroft A, Wilchesky M, Sarmiento I, Batisi O, Chakravarty M, Geddes M, Grimard F, Hachinski V, Mitchell C, Pichora-Fuller K, Abbasgholizadeh Rahimi S, Sawchuk K, Wittich W, Thabane L.
papers.abstract: Introduction Increasing numbers of older adults live with dementia especially in low- and middle-income countries. Most prevention relies on controlling conditions that increase the risk of dementia, such as hypertension, diabetes and sight and hearing loss. Recent pharmacological treatments have limited efficacy and are prohibitively expensive. Social isolation increases the risk of dementia and evidence suggests interventions to increase social engagement can reduce the risk possibly by supporting executive function. Three key features of authentic participatory research - shared governance, use of evidence and innovation - align with elements of executive function. Our pilot tests the feasibility and acceptability of participatory dementia prevention in Montreal, Canada and rural Botswana. Methods and analysis This pilot randomised controlled trial will recruit women and men aged 65 years and older who are socially isolated (not in paid or voluntary employment, not married) in urban Montreal and two rural communities in Botswana. In Botswana, we will randomly allocate participants in one community to receive the intervention immediately while the control community will receive the intervention after 18 months. In Montreal, individual participants will be randomly allocated to immediate or delayed intervention groups before or after their grouping by shared concern. We aim to recruit at least 100 participants in Botswana and 100 in Montreal. The intervention has six steps: individuals identify priority concerns; participants join groups with shared concerns; groups discuss the concern and potential solutions; groups share the concern and possible solutions with other stakeholders; implementation of solutions; and self-evaluation of the process. We will measure executive function using the Frontal Assessment Battery, and apply a questionnaire to measure integral brain health, physical health and social isolation at baseline, at 18 months and at 33 months. We will analyse narratives of change at the end of the intervention periods to understand participants' experience of the intervention. Ethics and dissemination The McGill University Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences Institutional Review Board approved the entire project on 18 September 2024, Study number: A06-M27-24A. The Psychosocial Research Committee (REC) of CIUSSS West-Central Montreal Research Ethics Board (REB) approved recruitment of clinic-related participants in Montreal on 3 March 2025, Project 2025-4112. The Health Research and Development Division of the Ministry of Health, Botswana, approved the study in Botswana on 24 June 2024, Reference number: HPRD 6/14/1.In Botswana, we will disseminate the findings in community meetings in the two pilot communities and with government and non-government stakeholders convened by the Ministry of Health and the Social Development Department of the Ministry of Local Government and Traditional Affairs. In Montreal, we will disseminate the findings in research meetings and in other relevant fora. We will give oral and poster presentations about the study in relevant local, national and international academic conferences and meetings and publish papers about the findings in peer-reviewed, indexed academic journals. Trial registration number ISRCTN14273485.

papers.title: Speech clocks decode dementia phenotypes, social exposome, and biological aging.
papers.authors: Hernandez H, Pedraza LK, Santamaria-Garcia H, Moguilner S, Legaz A, Prado P, Cuadros J, Amoruso L, Gonzalez L, Dellavale D, Espinoza-Puelles JP, Espinosa JP, Jarne C, Mattiussi F, Caccia M, Welford AS, Pelella N, Inchauspe J, Ferrante FJ, Pérez G, Maito MA, Rocatti G, Godoy ME, Migeot J, Orellana P, Caviedes A, Bruno M, Takada L, Slachevsky A, Behrens MI, Bruna B, Aguillon D, Zapata L, Avila-Funes JA, Custodio N, Miller B, Gorno-Tempini ML, Escudero SP, Reyes P, Hu K, de Oliveira MO, Coronel-Oliveros C, Cruzat J, Cardona JF, Corley M, Meier IB, Narayan VA, Tagliazucchi E, Baez S, Duran-Aniotz C, García AM, Ibanez A.
papers.abstract: Biological aging clocks offer estimations of aging and dementia, yet scalability is limited. We introduce a large-scale, cross-national speech clock derived from 2928 individuals across five Latin American countries, spanning healthy controls (HCs), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), Alzheimer's disease (AD), and non-language/language-dominant frontotemporal dementia (nldFTD/ldFTD). Multimodal acoustic and linguistic features were trained with supervised models to estimate chronological age, generating speech age gaps (SAGs) as cross-sectional markers of deviations from chronological age, with positive values interpreted as relatively older-appearing speech profiles. SAGs differentiated diagnostic groups (HCs < patient groups, with AD < nldFTD < ldFTD). This pattern was associated with clinical/cognitive domains. SAGs correlated with phosphorylated tau (p-Tau217) in AD and social exposome in HCs and AD. Brain clocks (structural/functional/combined) were associated with SAG in AD, nldFTD, and ldFTD. Epigenetic age correlated with SAGs in HCs and AD across Hannum, Retroclock, and OMICmAge, whereas ldFTD associations were limited to Retroclock and OMICmAge. These results indicate that SAGs capture cross-sectional multilevel aging-related variation and may offer a scalable, culturally adaptable, low-cost biomarker candidate for research in underrepresented global settings.

papers.title: Population connective field modeling reveals proto-retinotopic visual cortex organization in the prenatal human brain.
papers.authors: Yoo SH, Kieslinger AS, Skeide MA.
papers.abstract: The visual space is sampled by cortical field maps in which nearby neuronal populations encode nearby locations of images received from the retina. Whether retinotopic cortical organization already emerges in the neonatal or even prenatal human brain is currently unknown. To answer this question in vivo, we applied population connective field modeling to 871 resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging datasets ranging from prenatal to young adult age. We found topographically organized eccentricity and polar angle connectivity maps in V2 and V3 of the visual cortex as early as the 21st week of gestation. These results highlight that human proto-retinotopic cortical maps develop in the second trimester of pregnancy, predating visual experience.

papers.title: Effects of visual stimulation on local field potentials in the midbrain medial longitudinal fasciculus nucleus of Cyprinus carpio.
papers.authors: Zhao Y, Zhu M, Zhang Y, Zhang W, Gao P, Peng Y, Rong X, Tian L, Zhang Y.
papers.abstract: A bio-robot is a hybrid system wherein human-implemented intervention signals delivered through dedicated control techniques modulate the behaviour of a host living organism. Delivering targeted stimulation to specific brain regions of an organism can induce virtual sensory perceptions analogous to those evoked by natural stimuli, thereby eliciting targeted motor behaviours. This strategy constitutes a pivotal control mechanism for bio-robots. Observations of locomotor behaviour in fish following local brain ablation revealed that neurons in the Nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (Nflm) project to the optic tectum and coordinate visually evoked locomotion. This study aimed to advance understanding of the neural rhythm encoding mechanism underlying vision-related local field potentials (LFPs) in common carp (Cyprinus carpio). Light stimulation was applied to the visual organs of carp to elicit tail movements, while LFPs in the bilateral midbrain Nflm regions were recorded simultaneously. Continuous wavelet transform (CWT) was applied for time-frequency analysis of the LFPs, with relative power and Sample Entropy (SampEn) subsequently quantified. The results showed that unilateral visual stimulation of the carp induced elevated relative power of theta, alpha, beta, gamma and high-gamma bands in the LFPs of the contralateral Nflm, and the SampEn of such LFPs was reduced (all adjusted p < 0.05). From an electrophysiological perspective, this study demonstrated that the Nflm is associated with visual signal processing in fish and that the contralateral Nflm regions exhibit a robust response to unilateral visual stimulation. This study provides theoretical support for the regulation of carp robots via Nflm electrical stimulation.

papers.title: Mapping human brain networks using resting-state metabolic connectivity: concepts, methods, and foundational results.
papers.authors: Jamadar S.
papers.abstract: The human brain is a complex network, whose functional properties are constrained by its anatomy and energetic constraints. Metabolic connectivity refers to coherent metabolic interactions between spatially distinct regions, and is most commonly measured using [18F]-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET). While metabolic connectivity as a field predates fMRI-derived functional connectivity measures, it was not until recently that it was possible to estimate a metabolic network at the individual person level. Here, we review the theoretical and historical contexts of metabolic connectivity, its physiological bases, major methodological approaches, and key findings in health and disease. The review highlights that metabolic connectivity yields unique insight into the functional interactions of the brain relative to fMRI, is predictive of cognition and individual phenotype, and displays unique patterns of time-variant state switching and gradient architecture. We conclude the review with a forward-looking perspective of the future of metabolic connectivity, and recommendations for extending the conceptual framework of the measure.

papers.title: COMISA as an Independent Correlate of White Matter Hyperintensities in OSA Patients: A Cross-Sectional Study and Nomogram Construction.
papers.authors: Zhao M, Lu Y, Huang H, Zhong Q, Wei W, Tang B, Chen W, Xie X.
papers.abstract: Background Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a recognized risk factor for white matter hyperintensities (WMH) in cerebral small vessel disease. Identifying risk factors for WMH in OSA patients is important for disease management. Methods This cross-sectional study (2021-2023) enrolled OSA patients and collected PSG, MMSE, and brain MRI data. WMH was diagnosed using STRIVE‑2 criteria. Patients were divided into WMH and non‑WMH groups. Risk factors were identified by between‑group comparisons and multivariate logistic regression; a nomogram was constructed and evaluated by ROC and calibration curves. Results Our findings suggest that COMISA may be the strongest independent correlate of WMH among the factors examined. Higher BMI and increased REM apnea‑hypopnea index were independently associated with higher WMH odds, whereas higher total protein and MMSE scores were associated with lower odds. The nomogram showed potential utility for early screening, though external validation is needed. Conclusion In this study, we identified COMISA as an independent risk factor for WMH in patients with OSA. To our knowledge, this is among the first studies to highlight COMISA as a potentially valuable predictor in this context. These findings may offer a basis for further mechanistic investigations and for identifying individuals at higher risk of WMH, potentially informing early intervention strategies.

papers.title: Psychological and neuropsychological effects of adolescent cannabis use: a structured narrative review.
papers.authors: Miazzi R, Cestonaro C, Terranova C.
papers.abstract: Background Adolescence represents a vulnerable developmental period during which cannabis exposure may be associated with psychological, neuropsychological, and neurobiological alterations. Objective This structured review examines the psychological and neuropsychological effects associated with cannabis use during adolescence, focusing exclusively on human studies. Methods A structured narrative review was conducted using MEDLINE/PubMed. Fifty-five studies meeting the eligibility criteria were included. Results Adolescent cannabis use was frequently associated with increased depressive and anxiety symptoms, psychosis-spectrum experiences, and impairments in memory, attention, inhibitory control, and executive functioning. Neurobiological findings further indicate alterations in cortical maturation, reward-control connectivity, white matter integrity, and neurochemical markers in brain regions involved in cognition and emotion regulation. Although several longitudinal and neuroimaging studies support a possible contributing role of cannabis exposure, causal interpretation remains limited by confounding factors, polysubstance use, heterogeneous exposure measures, and differences in study design. Conclusions These findings highlight adolescence as a vulnerable developmental period and underscore the need for prevention strategies and further longitudinal research.

papers.title: Long-term clinical and biomarker observations following rituximab exposure in two siblings with CSF1R-related leukoencephalopathy: a preliminary familial case series.
papers.authors: Balevicius R, Smertinaite LM, Kourie M, Wszolek Z, Mickeviciute GC, Harris R, Granberg T, Zhuravleva N, Han J, Karrenbauer VD.
papers.abstract: Background Colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R)-related leukoencephalopathy (CRL) is a rare microgliopathy, characterized by progressive neurodegeneration. Impaired STAT3 signaling reduces microglial numbers and limits their ability to clear cellular debris, leading to persistent inflammation and brain tissue damage that activates peripheral CD20⁺ B cells. These cells migrate into the CNS and secrete interleukin-6 (IL-6), amplifying inflammation and further disrupting STAT3 signaling in a self-reinforcing cycle that drives white-matter injury. Methods We describe two siblings from a single family, both carrying the same heterozygous CSF1R variant (c.2562 T > A, p.Asn854Lys), who received four infusions of rituximab (RTX;500 mg) on a compassionate, off-label basis between 2014-2017. The long-term disease trajectory was evaluated using standardized clinical rating scales and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). As a secondary biomarker outcome, serum and CSF neurofilament light chain (NfL) concentrations were assessed. Results In both siblings, RTX exposure was followed by EDSS stability at 6.5 and 7.0, respectively, over 5 years, with mixed trajectories in other functional and cognitive domains. Over the 23-year MRI follow-up period, patients developed cerebral atrophy. During the post-treatment period, no new focal lesions were observed on brain MRI, and levels of CSF-NfL and CSF-CXCL13 were normalized. Conclusions In this preliminary familial case series of two siblings carrying the same CSF1R variant, RTX exposure was followed by long-term clinical stability and favorable biomarker trajectories. Patient 1 had a pre-treatment disease course of approximately 13 years, indicating an inherently slow disease progression that cannot be entirely separated from the treatment effect in an uncontrolled observation.

papers.title: A population code for semantics in human hippocampus.
papers.authors: Franch M, Mickiewicz EA, Belanger JL, Joiner B, Katlowitz KA, Zhu H, Chavez AG, Chericoni A, Goldman AM, Krishnan V, Maheshwari A, Paulo DL, Bartoli E, Kemmer S, Piantadosi ST, Provenza NR, Hennig JA, Sheth SA, Hayden BY.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the successes of large language models (LLMs), we hypothesized that semantic information in the brain may be expressed in distributed patterns of neural activity. We recorded responses of hippocampal neurons while individuals listened to narrative speech. Here, using an encoding model approach, we find robust encoding of semantics, even after controlling for phonemics and grammar. Individual words had complex selectivities that included multiple words in multiple semantic categories. Similar to embedding vectors in LLMs, distance between neural population responses correlated with semantic distance. For semantically similar words, even contextual embedders showed an inverse correlation between semantic and neural distances; we attribute this pattern to the noise-mitigating benefits of contrastive coding. Finally, neural population activity aligned most closely with GPT-2 embeddings, and variation in response patterns correlated with LLM-derived polysemy measures, indicating that semantic encoding is largely contextualized. Ultimately, these results provide a neurocomputational account for understanding how hippocampal neurons encode word meaning during language listening.

papers.title: Altered semantic prediction error processing with increasing schizotypal and autistic traits.
papers.authors: Sterner EF, Demler VF, Lenz R, MacGregor LJ, Mathys C, Knolle F.
papers.abstract: Predictive processing has been proposed as a framework for symptom development in autism (ASD) and schizophrenia (SSD) spectrum disorders, with ASD being associated with an overweighting of (low-level) sensory evidence whereas SSD is characterized by an overweighting of (high-level) prior beliefs, both resulting in altered prediction error processing. This study investigated these hypotheses and their electrophysiological correlates in subclinical expressions of ASD and SSD during language processing. Participants completed an auditory comprehension task that manipulated the precision of high-level semantic prior beliefs and low-level sensory evidence. Hierarchical Bayesian belief-updating modeling and electroencephalography were used to examine whether imbalances in the weighting of prior beliefs and sensory evidence were reflected in altered processing of semantic prediction errors, characterized by mean N400 amplitudes. Computational modeling revealed that increasing schizotypal traits were associated with significant overweighting of prior beliefs, while autistic traits did not show a significant shift. Linear mixed-effect models of mean N400 amplitudes indicated that schizotypy-related overweighting of semantic prior beliefs was reflected in a reduced semantic prediction error signal, indexed by smaller N400 differences between high predictability sentences and both low predictability and high predictability mismatch sentences. A similar but weaker and less distinct pattern emerged for increasing autistic traits. These findings provide converging computational and electrophysiological support for overweighting of semantic prior beliefs with increasing subclinical schizotypy. In contrast, increasing autistic traits were not associated with overweighting of sensory evidence, with electrophysiological results instead suggesting subtle alterations in the weighting of semantic prior beliefs.

papers.title: Functional connectivity recovers canine-human network homology along the evolutionary cortical hierarchy.
papers.authors: Warioba CS, Carroll TJ, Christoforidis GA.
papers.abstract: Mapping functional brain organization between species is a prerequisite for translating connectivity biomarkers from animal models to patients, but connectivity-based correspondence has been demonstrated almost exclusively in primates. We tested whether canine-human network homology can be recovered from functional connectivity alone, using only five network-level anatomical priors, and benchmarked a spectral manifold alignment framework (Laplacian-eigenmap embedding with Procrustes alignment on network centroids) against a simple connectivity-signature matching baseline. Data comprised resting-state fMRI from 15 canines with endovascular permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (pre-occlusion baseline and hyperacute post-occlusion sessions) and two public OpenNeuro datasets: 29 chronic-phase post-stroke aphasia patients scanned before and after rehabilitation (ds003999) and 10 healthy controls (ds000224). Held-out canine-human network homologies were recovered well above chance (top-5 network correspondence up to 54.5% vs. permutation null ≈ 18%, p=0.002 ), and correspondence followed the evolutionary cortical hierarchy: visual and somatomotor homologies were recovered several-fold above chance, default-mode only weakly-extending a gradient previously described in primates to a carnivore. Notably, simple signature matching (54.5%) outperformed manifold alignment (35.5%), indicating that the homology signal is strong enough to be captured without embedding machinery at translational cohort sizes. Within species, canine network metrics showed no treatment-arm differences (all p>0.3 ), and chronic-phase patients did not differ from controls in modularity ( p=0.93 ); a sensitivity analysis bounds these nulls. All results are fully reproducible from shared code and public data.

papers.title: DeID-Aligner: fine-grained brain-vision semantic alignment for cross-subject visual decoding from limited fMRI data.
papers.authors: Yin X, Gan JQ, Yang M, Wang H, Wang Z.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in fMRI-based semantic decoding and visual reconstruction have achieved remarkable progress. However, severe inter-subject variability and the scarcity of paired fMRI-image data remain major obstacles to cross-subject generalization. To overcome these challenges, we propose DeID-Aligner, a brain functional alignment framework that enables multi-task visual decoding across subjects under limited fMRI data. The method first constructs a region-of-interest (ROI)-wise fMRI encoder that captures regional functional representations. A dynamic Patch-to-ROI fusion mechanism with Progressive Modal Attention Transition (PMAT) explicitly associates image patches with cortical regions, enabling fine-grained cross-modal semantic alignment while gradually shifting from cross-modal to fMRI-only for robust inference. To remove subject-specific information, we introduce a de-identification task implemented with a graph attention network (DIT-GAT), which models inter-ROI interaction patterns to reduce subject-specific information and suppress identity cues.
